output.text_response:
## Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

---

### ⚠️ Correction of the Delegation's Premise

The guide cannot be limited to church registers and cemetery inscriptions, because **town-level civil vital recording in Massachusetts predates the statewide act of 1841 by two centuries**. The 1841 act created a *statewide reporting* system — it did not create civil registration from nothing. Town clerks throughout Berkshire County had been recording births, marriages, and deaths since the colonial period (ordering from 1639 per the FamilySearch Wiki on Massachusetts Vital Records). A digitized FamilySearch volume of Town Clerk Vital and Town Records for Berkshire County, 1761–1850 (DGS 004500891, 512 images), exists and covers the entire target period. Church registers and cemetery inscriptions are important supplements — but they do not replace the town-clerk series.

---

### Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761 from Hampshire County (pre-1761 records are under Hampshire County)
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **State:** Massachusetts
- **Border counties (confirmed):**
  - **Bennington County, Vermont** (to the north; formed 1779)
  - **Rensselaer County, New York** (to the west/northwest; formed 1791)
- Families near either border routinely generated records on **both sides of the state line**

---

### Record Types by Category

---

#### 1. Vital Records (Civil — Town Level)

**Start date:** 1639 (colonial-era ordering); statewide system added 1841. Town-level records cover the **entire** 1820–1850 window.

**What to search first:**
- **Published compilations:** "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series exists for more than 200 Massachusetts towns; many Berkshire County towns have a volume. These printed transcripts combine town clerk entries *and* local church registers — the fastest single survey of surviving records for a given town. Held at NEHGS, research libraries, and often on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **FamilySearch collection** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (id: 2061550, ~1.7 million images): [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — indexed + images
- **Browse-only volume** DGS 004500891 — Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, Berkshire County, 1761–1850 (512 images, 0% indexed, no full-text): must be paged through image by image
- **Originals** remain with the clerk of each individual Berkshire County town

**Marriage intentions:** Recorded in the bride's home town AND often in the groom's. If spouses came from different towns — or from across a state line — search *both* town's intention records.

**Pre-1841 vs. post-1841:** After 1841 a second (state-level) series begins alongside the town clerk series. Both may record the same event. Search both.

---

#### 2. Church Records

**Confirmed digitized volume:**
- DGS 004500892 — Church Records (Congregational), Pittsfield, 1791–1850 (274 images, 0% indexed, browse-only)

**Broader collection:**
- FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (id: 1921657, ~494,000 images): [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — indexed + images; may include other Berkshire County towns and denominations

**Gap:** Only Pittsfield's Congregational records are confirmed as a digitized browse volume. Records for other towns and other denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker, etc.) are **not confirmed as digitized** in this survey — they likely exist on earlier FamilySearch microfilm and at NEHGS or denominational archives. Verify via the FamilySearch Catalog directly.

**Important note:** Church registers record **baptisms** (often weeks or months after birth), not births. The date in a church register is the baptism date unless the register explicitly records the birth date separately.

---

#### 3. Cemetery Records

- **FindAGrave** ([https://www.findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) is the primary online index; coverage is volunteer-contributed and varies by cemetery
- Physical sexton records and burial registers are held at individual cemeteries, town offices, or local historical societies — not confirmed as digitized in this survey
- **Headstones are often the only dated death record** for years when neither the town clerk nor the church recorded an event — search for every individual in the target window

---

#### 4. Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1820, 1830, 1840 | Names head of household only; others tallied by age/sex | Cannot identify individual children by name |
| 1850 | Names every person, with age, birthplace, occupation | First fully nominative federal census — highest priority |

- **1850 Mortality Schedule:** Lists deaths in June 1849–June 1850 with name, age, sex, cause — functions as a de facto death register for that year
- Access: FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription)

---

#### 5. Probate Records

- Berkshire County Probate Court records begin with the county's 1761 formation
- **FamilySearch collection** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (id: 1678901, ~284,000 images): [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — indexed + images
- A father's probate file naming all children, or a deed from a child who received land from a parent, can supply relationship evidence when vital records are incomplete
- Originals: Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield

---

#### 6. Land Records

- Massachusetts is a **state-land state** (metes and bounds; BLM GLO does not apply)
- County deeds recorded at the Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield, from 1761
- Land records survive in "remarkably complete runs" (Massachusetts Genealogy wiki)
- Deeds frequently name family members and can establish relationships

---

#### 7. Military Records

- **War of 1812** (1812–1815): Pension and bounty-land warrant files extend well into the 1820–1850 window
- **Mexican-American War** (1846–1848): Service records and pensions
- NARA: [https://www.archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)
- **Fold3** (subscription, digitized NARA records including pension files): [https://www.fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)
- Massachusetts state militia records: Massachusetts Archives, Boston

---

#### 8. Passenger Lists & Naturalization

- **FamilySearch** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (id: 1784312, ~617,000 images): [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) — indexed + images
- **FamilySearch** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (id: 1459213, ~173,000 images): [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) — indexed + images
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including Berkshire County courts

---

#### 9. Newspaper Records

- **Newspapers.com** (subscription): [https://www.newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) — obituaries, marriage notices, legal estate notices
- The *Pittsfield Sun* was published from the early 19th century; specific title coverage on Newspapers.com was not confirmed in this survey

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Individual town clerks** (each Berkshire Co. town) | Original town vital records from colonial era | In person or mail to the specific town |
| **Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield** | Probate records from 1761 | In person or mail |
| **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield** | Deeds from 1761 | In person; some online |
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | Colony/state records from 1620s; state vital records from 1841 | In person; online finding aids |
| **NEHGS, Boston** | Published vital-records compilations, microfilmed church registers, local histories, manuscripts | In person; americanancestors.org (subscription) |
| **FamilySearch** | Multiple indexed collections + two browse-only volumes (see above) | Free — familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry** | Federal census, mortality schedules | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| **Fold3** | Military/pension records | Subscription |

---

### Records NOT Online (or Unconfirmed)

- Church registers for towns other than Pittsfield (Congregational) — likely on earlier FamilySearch microfilm; verify via FamilySearch Catalog
- Cemetery sexton and burial registers — physical only
- Town-level tax assessment lists — held at individual town offices
- Local and county histories — NEHGS and research libraries
- Original town vital records — physical at each town clerk's office (a digitized but unindexed copy is on FamilySearch as DGS 004500891)

---

### Research Tips

1. **Start with the "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" published compilation** — if your town has a volume, it is a printed transcript of both town clerk records and local church registers and is the fastest single survey available.

2. **Identify the specific town first.** The digitized Berkshire County volume (DGS 004500891) is entirely unindexed and must be browsed image by image; the FamilySearch indexed collection (id: 2061550) and the published compilations are far more efficient once the town is known.

3. **Search across both state lines.** Records may exist in Bennington County, Vermont and/or Rensselaer County, New York. Each of those counties needs its own separate locality survey before their vital-record coverage can be assessed — do not assume they match the Massachusetts town-level standard.

4. **Check marriage intentions in both towns** — bride's and groom's home towns, which may be in different counties or states.

5. **The 1850 Mortality Schedule is a de facto death register** for June 1849–June 1850 and is often the only named death record for those months.

6. **Do not treat 1820–1841 as a "pre-registration" void.** Town-level recording predates the statewide system by 200 years. Civil records exist; compliance and survival simply vary by town.

7. **Land and probate records establish family relationships** when vital records are missing — search them for every generation.

8. **NEHGS is the regional specialist.** For Berkshire County records not yet digitized online, the NEHGS library in Boston is the best single point of contact.

---

*Known gaps in this survey:* The FamilySearch Catalog (microfilm, books, manuscripts, finding aids) could not be queried with available tools. A direct search of the FamilySearch Catalog at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) for "Berkshire County" is strongly recommended, particularly for microfilmed church registers from individual towns not yet in a digitized collection.

Many Berkshire County towns have a published volume in this series. These are held by the New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) and many research libraries, and are often available on microfilm through FamilySearch.

**Where original records are held:** The originals remain with the clerk of each individual Berkshire County town, per the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page.

**Post-1841 state records:** For 1841–1850, events were also to be reported to the state; the statewide record is a second series alongside, not a replacement for, the town clerk record.

**Gaps:** Compliance before 1841 was uneven. Some towns' records for specific years are incomplete or missing. Where town records are absent, church registers and cemetery inscriptions are the substitutes.

**Records confirmed by tools:** FamilySearch digitized volume DGS 004500892: Church Records (Congregational), Pittsfield, Berkshire County, 1791–1850, 274 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — **browse-only images**. This collection may include records from additional Berkshire County towns and denominations not represented in the single browse-only volume above.

**Coverage gap:** Only Congregational records for Pittsfield are confirmed in the digitized volume returned by `volume_search`. Church records for other Berkshire County towns, and for other denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, and others that likely served the county), are not confirmed as digitized in any tool result in this survey. They may exist on earlier microfilm held by NEHGS or the Massachusetts Archives but were not returned by the tools.

**Baptisms vs. births:** Church registers record baptisms (often weeks or months after birth), not births. The date in a church register is the baptism date unless the register explicitly records the birth date as a separate field.

---

### Census records

**Federal census:** The target period falls within the 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 federal censuses, all of which covered Berkshire County. The 1820, 1830, and 1840 censuses name only the head of household and tally other members by age and sex categories. The 1850 census is the first to name every household member individually with age, sex, birthplace, and occupation. For a family seeking birth, marriage, and death evidence, the 1850 census is therefore the most directly useful.

**Mortality schedules:** Begin with the 1850 census. The 1850 mortality schedule records deaths in the twelve months preceding the census date (June 1849–June 1850) and names the individual, age, sex, and cause of death. This is a de facto death record for that year and can substitute for missing vital records.

**Access:** Federal census images and name indexes are available through FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records

**Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, dower releases, estate distributions.

**Date range:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (Massachusetts Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial): "Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts." Berkshire County Probate Court records therefore cover the full 1820–1850 window.

**FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (id: 1678901, 283,945 images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 — indexed + images.

**Testate vs. intestate:** A person who left a will (testate) will have a will on file; search the will books. A person who died without a will (intestate) will have an administration record — letters of administration, an inventory, and a distribution. Both series name family members and can establish relationships not in vital records.

**Where held:** Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield.

---

### Land records

**Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is a state-land state, not a federal-land state; the BLM GLO website does not apply here).

**Types:** Deeds, mortgages, releases, and related instruments.

**Date range:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (Massachusetts Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial): land records "were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs." Berkshire County's series begins from its 1761 formation.

**Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Massachusetts is a state-land state; land grants originate with the Commonwealth, not the federal government. For the 1820–1850 period, most land in Berkshire County was already in private hands and transactions are deed-to-deed transfers recorded at the Berkshire County Registry of Deeds.

**Where held:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield. No dedicated land-records wiki page was returned (the URL for Massachusetts_Land_and_Property returned only a generic page in this survey).

---

### Military records

**Relevant conflicts:** The War of 1812 (1812–1815) falls immediately before the target period; pension and bounty-land warrant applications often post-date the war by decades and will appear in 1820–1850 records. The Mexican-American War (1846–1848) falls within the target period.

**Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty-land warrants — held at the National Archives (NARA), https://www.archives.gov/ (returned by external_links_search). Massachusetts state militia records may be at the Massachusetts Archives, Boston.

**Online access:** Fold3 (subscription), https://www.fold3.com/ (returned by external_links_search), holds digitized NARA military records including pension files.

---

### Cemetery records

**Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/, returned by external_links_search) is the primary online index for Berkshire County cemetery inscriptions. Coverage is volunteer-contributed and varies by cemetery. No `volume_search` volume was returned for cemetery records specifically.

**Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers for individual cemeteries may be held by the town clerk, historical societies, or the cemetery itself. No tool result named specific Berkshire County cemeteries or their holdings.

**Context note:** The delegation identified cemetery inscriptions as a primary source for 1820–1850, and for deaths in particular they are often more complete than any other source — a headstone may be the only dated death record for a person in a year when neither the town clerk nor the church recorded the event. They should be searched for every individual in the target window.

---

### Newspaper records

**Online coverage:** Newspapers.com (subscription), https://www.newspapers.com/ (returned by external_links_search). Historical Berkshire County newspapers included the *Pittsfield Sun* (published from the early 19th century), but specific title coverage on Newspapers.com was not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.

**Content value for vital events:** Obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices (estate administration notices, land sale announcements) can supply or confirm dates not in other records.

---

### Immigration and emigration records

**Relevant ports:** Boston is the nearest major port of entry.

**FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (id: 1784312, 617,283 images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312 — indexed + images. The date range exactly matches the target period.

**Naturalization records:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (id: 1459213, 172,839 images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213 — indexed + images. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including the Berkshire County courts.

**Content note:** Passenger lists record every person on board including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

---

### Tax records

**Types:** Massachusetts property and poll tax records were assessed at the town level. They can place an individual in a specific town in a specific year and can substitute for missing census years.

**Where held:** Town-level records are held at individual town offices. No dedicated Massachusetts tax-records wiki page was returned in this survey (the URL returned only a generic page).

### Other record types

**NEHGS library:** The FamilySearch Wiki (Massachusetts Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial) identifies the New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) as "the largest genealogical library in the region." It holds published vital-records compilations, microfilmed church registers, and local histories for Berkshire County towns. Their catalog is at https://www.americanancestors.org/ (not returned by external_links_search, cited here because the NEHGS name itself came from a tool result).

**Massachusetts Archives:** Holds original colony records from the 1620s onward (per the same wiki source). For Berkshire County in 1820–1850, relevant holdings include legislative petitions, state census materials (if any), and state-level vital records after 1841.

**Local and county histories:** Published local histories (19th and early 20th century) for Berkshire County towns often reprint early vital records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. These may be the only surviving transcription of records since lost. No specific titles were returned by any tool in this survey.

## Research tips

- **The town clerk is the first stop, not the last.** Per the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records), original records remain with the clerk of each town. The FamilySearch browse-only volume (DGS 004500891) covers Berkshire County as a whole but is unindexed; searching the original town clerk's records may be more efficient once the family's town is confirmed.

- **Look for the "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" published compilation first.** Per the Massachusetts Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial), these published volumes exist for more than 200 Massachusetts towns. If your Berkshire County town has a volume in this series, it is a printed transcript of both town clerk records and local church registers, and is the fastest way to survey the full surviving record for a town.

- **Check marriage intentions in both towns.** The Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) specifies that marriage intentions were recorded in the bride's home town and may also appear in the groom's home town. If spouses came from different towns, search the intention records of both towns — one of which may be across the county line or even across the state line.

- **Search across both state lines.** This family's town is near both the New York and Vermont borders. Confirmed neighboring jurisdictions from this survey are Bennington County, Vermont (formed 1779; standardPlace: "Bennington, Vermont, United States") and Rensselaer County, New York (formed 1791; standardPlace: "Rensselaer, New York, United States"). Family members may have been baptized, married, or buried in a border town on either side. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York and Vermont vital records returned only generic content in this survey, so specific vital registration start dates for those states cannot be cited from these tools — a separate locality survey for the specific border counties is recommended before assuming that record coverage on either side equals the Massachusetts town-level standard.

- **The 1850 census Mortality Schedule is a de facto death register.** For deaths occurring between June 1849 and June 1850, the mortality schedule names the individual and gives age, sex, and cause of death. It is often the only named death record for the period before state-level registration was consistently enforced.

- **Pre-1841 statewide-series gap does not mean no records.** Town-level recording predates the statewide system by two centuries. Do not dismiss 1820–1841 records as "pre-registration" — the period has civil records, they are simply town-level rather than state-level.

- **Land and probate records establish relationships.** Per the Massachusetts Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial), land records at the county level "survive in remarkably complete runs" and probate records begin in the 1630s. For a family where vital records are incomplete, a father's probate file naming all children, or a deed from a child who received land from a parent, can supply the relationship evidence that no vital record provides.

- **NEHGS is the regional specialist.** The Massachusetts Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial) identifies NEHGS as "the largest genealogical library in the region." For Berkshire County specifically, their collections of microfilmed church registers and published town histories are the best single point of contact for records not yet digitized online.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, Barony of Cary, County Antrim, Province of Ulster
- **Administrative center:** Bushmills
- **Church of Ireland diocese:** Connor (Province of Armagh)
- **Poor Law Unions (from 1838):** Ballymoney and/or Coleraine — confirm by townland
- **Political context:** Kingdom of Ireland until 1801; thereafter United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland until 1922

### Economy & Community
A rural, mixed agricultural and coastal-fishing area with a strong domestic linen industry (declining from the 1820s–1840s) and the Bushmills distillery. The population was predominantly **Ulster-Scots Presbyterian**, alongside a Church of Ireland community, a smaller Roman Catholic population, and scattered Methodists. This is the heartland of the **Route Presbytery**, one of the oldest Presbyterian presbyteries in Ireland.

### Key Events
1798 United Irish Rebellion (Antrim was a major site); Act of Union 1800; linen decline 1820s–1840s; Famine emigration 1845–1852.

---

## Boundary Changes

Billy civil parish boundaries were stable in this period. The important change is the **1858 Probate Act**, which moved probate jurisdiction from the Consistorial Court of Connor (for County Antrim) to a civil District Probate Registry in Belfast. Pre-1858 wills and administrations are largely lost in the 1922 Four Courts fire (see Record Losses below).

---

## Record Types Available

### Civil Registration (Vital Records)
| Event | Start Date | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Non-Catholic (Presbyterian) marriages | 1 April 1845 | First civil records for this family |
| All births, marriages, deaths | 1 January 1864 | Full civil registration |

**Everything 1780–1844 is church records only.** Registration districts: confirm whether Billy parish falls under Coleraine or Ballycastle district.

**Where held:** General Register Office of Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast. Freely searchable at **IrishGenealogy.ie**; also on Ancestry.com and Findmypast.

### Church Records

**This is the primary source category for 1780–1864.**

#### Presbyterian *(priority for this family)*

The principal congregation is **Bushmills (Route) Presbyterian Church** — one of the historic congregations of the Route Presbytery. Its baptism, marriage, and session registers are the single most important source for the family.

Other overlapping congregations to check:
- **Dervock Presbyterian Church** (south, Ballybogey area)
- **Armoy Presbyterian Church** (east, toward Ballycastle)
- **Ballywillan Presbyterian Church** (west, toward Portrush)

Presbyterian registers record *baptisms* (not births — note the parents' names and often the townland), and marriages (names of both parties and fathers). **Kirk session minutes** can document individuals through disciplinary cases, poor relief, and transfer certificates.

**Held at:** PRONI (Belfast); Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland (PHSI, Belfast); microfilm at FamilySearch; some uploads to IrishGenealogy.ie.

#### Church of Ireland
The parish of Billy is an important parallel source even for Presbyterian families (especially pre-1845 marriages). Held at PRONI; some images on IrishGenealogy.ie and FamilySearch.

Diocese of Down and Connor; registers typically begin 1820s–1840s. Held at PRONI.

| 1841, 1851 | Largely destroyed in 1922 Four Courts fire; fragments survive at NAI |

For the 1780–1870 period there is no surviving full census. Census substitutes are essential.

### Census Substitutes *(critical sources)*

- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists heads of household with tithable land by townland. Fully indexed at NAI (titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie), Ancestry, and FamilySearch. **Use as your early 19th-century anchor.**
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (c.1859–1862 for County Antrim):** Names every occupier of land or buildings, with townland, valuation, and landlord. Freely available at **AskAboutIreland.ie**; also on Ancestry. **Use as your mid-century anchor.**
- **Poor Rate records (post-1838):** Rate books at PRONI; function as annual tax lists between the Tithe Books and Griffith's.
- **Flax Growers' List (1796):** Lists County Antrim householders who received spinning wheels under a government premium scheme.
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** Detailed manuscript descriptions of each parish — population statistics, occupations, sometimes family names. County Antrim memoirs are exceptionally complete. Published by the Institute of Irish Studies, QUB.

### Probate Records

- **Pre-1858:** Consistorial Court of Connor (small estates) / Prerogative Court of Armagh (larger). **Originals largely destroyed in 1922.** A name index survives at NAI; some abstracts and registered copies survive at PRONI and Registry of Deeds.
- **Post-1858:** Civil District Probate Registry, Belfast. Annual calendars survive at PRONI and indexed on Ancestry.

### Land Records

- **Registry of Deeds** (from 1708): Voluntary registration; weighted toward middling and larger landholders. At King's Inns, Dublin; indexes on Ancestry.

- **Landed Estates Court records (post-1848):** Detailed rental schedules at NAI.

### Military Records

- British Army service records (WO 97) and pension records (WO 22, 116, 120) at **The National Archives, Kew** (TNA) — digitised on Findmypast and Ancestry.
- Antrim Militia records at PRONI.
- **1798 Rebellion records:** Yeomanry muster rolls, rebel lists, compensation claims at PRONI, NAI, and TNA.

### Newspapers

- **Coleraine Chronicle** (from 1844): Closest paper with strong north Antrim coverage. Digitised on British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk / Findmypast).
- **Belfast Newsletter** (from 1737 — one of the world's oldest continuously published newspapers): Major Ulster-wide source. Marriage and death notices indexed by the Ulster Historical Foundation. Freely available via the BNA and QUB Digital Library.
- **Northern Whig** (from 1824): Also held at Linen Hall Library, Belfast.

### Immigration / Emigration Records

North Antrim had **very high emigration rates** to North America throughout the 18th–19th centuries. Records on both sides of the Atlantic may survive:

- US passenger lists from 1820 at NARA and on Ancestry/FamilySearch

- Ulster Historical Foundation (ancestryireland.com) has compiled Ulster emigrant databases
- Ordnance Survey Memoirs sometimes note emigrant destinations for specific parishes

### Other Records

- **National School roll books (from 1831):** Children's names, parents, enrolment dates. At PRONI.
- **Church session minutes:** Presbyterian disciplinary cases, poor relief, transfer certificates — name individuals missing from baptism/marriage registers.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

**Tool-coverage note:** Every FamilySearch Wiki tool — `wiki_read`, `wiki_place_page`, `wiki_search`, and `place_search` — returned a generic placeholder for all Ireland and County Antrim queries in this session. `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `external_links_search` resolved the place to an empty string and returned 0 Ireland-specific results. No collection IDs, volume numbers, record counts, or repository details came from the tools. The sections below are therefore grounded in general knowledge of Irish archival practice; repository names, registration dates, and record survival notes come from that body of knowledge, not from verified tool output. The researcher should confirm current holdings and access directly with PRONI, IrishGenealogy.ie, and the FamilySearch Wiki pages listed under Repository Guide.

---

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, Barony of Cary, County Antrim, Province of Ulster
- **Administrative center:** Bushmills (the principal town of the parish)
- **Church of Ireland diocese:** Connor (in the ecclesiastical province of Armagh)
- **Parent civil jurisdiction:** County Antrim; under the Poor Law structure (from 1838) partly within the Ballymoney Poor Law Union and partly within the Coleraine Poor Law Union
- **Political context:** Kingdom of Ireland until 1 January 1801; thereafter part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland until 1922
- **Population during period:** North Antrim was a rural, mixed agricultural-and-fishing area. The linen domestic industry was active through the late 18th and early 19th centuries. The area was less catastrophically affected by the Great Famine than the south and west but still saw significant emigration in the 1840s–1860s, mainly to North America.
- **Economy:** Agriculture (oats, potatoes, flax), coastal fishing, linen weaving, and distilling (the Bushmills whiskey distillery has operated continuously since at least the 18th century)
- **Ethnic and religious composition:** Predominantly Ulster-Scots Presbyterian settlers and their descendants (concentrated in the town and farming townlands), with a Church of Ireland (Anglican) community, a smaller Roman Catholic population, and scattered Methodists. The Route Presbytery, one of the oldest Presbyterian presbyteries in Ireland, covers this area.
- **Key historical events:** 1798 United Irish rebellion (Antrim was a significant site); Act of Union 1800; linen industry decline with mechanisation from 1820s–1840s; famine emigration 1845–1852; railway expansion reached north Antrim by the 1870s

## Boundary changes

Billy civil parish boundaries were stable across this period. For probate purposes, the relevant boundary change is the 1858 Probate Act, which transferred probate jurisdiction from the ecclesiastical diocesan courts (Consistorial Court of Connor for County Antrim) to the new civil District Probate Registry in Belfast. Pre-1858 wills and administrations for people of substantial means were proved in the Prerogative Court of Armagh; all others in the Consistorial Court of Connor. Both sets were concentrated in Dublin and were largely destroyed in the Four Courts fire of June 1922 (see Known Record Losses below).

The Poor Law Union boundaries drawn in 1838 affect the survival of some administrative records: check both the Ballymoney and Coleraine unions depending on which townland within Billy parish is relevant.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start dates:**
  - Non-Catholic (including Presbyterian) marriages: civil registration began at the county registrar level on 1 April 1845. These are the earliest civil records for a Presbyterian family.
  - All births, marriages, and deaths (all denominations): civil registration began at the county registrar level on 1 January 1864.
  - The registration district covering Billy parish and Bushmills was Coleraine (for the western part) or Ballycastle (for the eastern part) — confirm which district covers the relevant townland via PRONI or the General Register Office.
- **What exists for 1780–1870:** Civil records exist only from 1845 (Presbyterian marriages) or 1864 (all events). The entire period 1780–1844 for a Presbyterian family is covered by church registers only, not civil records.
- **Where held:** Original civil registers from 1864 are held by the General Register Office of Northern Ireland (GRONI), Neville House, Chichester Street, Belfast. Indexes and many images are freely searchable online at IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie). Ancestry.com and Findmypast.com also carry Ireland civil registration indexes.
- **Gaps:** Civil registration for births was under-recorded in rural Ulster in the years immediately after 1864; some births appear in church registers but not in civil records for this early period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Presbyterian kirk session registers and congregational registers; Church of Ireland registers for Billy parish; Quaker registers if applicable.

### Church records

This is the primary source category for 1780–1864 and remains important as a parallel source after 1864.

**Presbyterian (the priority denomination for this family):**

The principal Presbyterian congregation serving Bushmills and Billy civil parish is Bushmills (Route) Presbyterian Church, formally known as the Route congregation, in the Route Presbytery. This is one of the historic congregations of Ulster Presbyterianism. Its registers recording baptisms (not births — Presbyterian ministers recorded the baptism event), marriages, and sometimes burials are the most important single source for this family.

Additional congregations whose catchment areas overlap with Billy parish or whose members could include families from the Bushmills area include:

- Dervock Presbyterian Church (a few miles to the south, in the Ballybogey/Dervock area)
- Armoy Presbyterian Church (east, toward Ballycastle)
- Ballywillan Presbyterian Church (west, toward Portrush)
- Portrush Presbyterian Church (further west)

Presbyterian registers for County Antrim congregations are primarily held at the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), Belfast. Microfilm copies of many registers are held at the FamilySearch Library and may be browsable via FamilySearch.org. The Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland (PHSI), located in Belfast, also holds a collection of registers and minute books. Some registers have been transcribed or indexed and are searchable at IrishGenealogy.ie and on Ancestry.com.

Presbyterian registers record baptisms (typically giving the child's name, parents' full names, and sometimes the townland). They do not record births. Marriage registers record the names of both parties and their fathers. Kirk session minutes sometimes record disciplinary cases and can name individuals not otherwise in the register series.

The starting dates of surviving Presbyterian registers vary by congregation; some begin in the early 1800s, some in the mid-18th century, and a few are incomplete or lost. Confirm the Bushmills (Route) congregation's register start date directly with PRONI or the PHSI.

**Church of Ireland:**

The Church of Ireland parish of Billy covers the same civil parish. Its registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are an important source even for Presbyterian families who occasionally used the established church (for example, before a local Presbyterian meeting was formed, or for legal marriages before 1845 under the Marriage Acts). Church of Ireland registers for Billy are held at PRONI. Many Church of Ireland registers for County Antrim have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. Some are indexed on IrishGenealogy.ie.

**Roman Catholic:**

The Catholic parish serving the Bushmills area was part of the Diocese of Down and Connor. Catholic registers for north Antrim typically begin later than Church of Ireland registers (often 1820s–1840s for baptisms). Held at PRONI and at the relevant diocesan offices.

**Methodist:**

Methodist circuits operated in north Antrim; registers are held at PRONI and at the Methodist Church in Ireland archives in Dublin.

- **Language:** All church registers for this area are in English.

### Census records

The Irish census situation is severely affected by deliberate and accidental destruction:

- **1901 and 1911 censuses:** Survive fully. Fully indexed and freely available online at the National Archives of Ireland website (census.nationalarchives.ie) and at FamilySearch and Ancestry. These post-date the target period but are important for identifying the older generation of the family still living.
- **1891 census:** Deliberately destroyed by the government shortly after collection — does not exist.
- **1881 census:** Deliberately destroyed — does not exist.
- **1871 census:** Deliberately destroyed — does not exist.
- **1861 census:** Deliberately destroyed — does not exist.
- **1851 census:** Survived largely intact until the 1922 Four Courts fire; partially destroyed. Fragments survive (including some County Antrim material). The surviving fragments are held at the National Archives of Ireland, Dublin.
- **1841 census:** Largely destroyed in 1922; fragments survive.
- **1831 census:** Largely destroyed; County Londonderry (adjacent to Antrim) has significant surviving material, which may include families with Antrim connections.
- **1821 census:** Largely destroyed.

For the target period 1780–1870, there is no surviving full census for Billy parish. The researcher must rely on census substitutes (see below and Tax Records section).

### Census substitutes

These are the primary population sources for 1780–1870:

- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists heads of household who occupied tithable land in each townland, with acreage and valuation. Coverage is at the townland level within each civil parish. Billy parish's Tithe Books are held at the National Archives of Ireland and are fully indexed online at the NAI website (titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie) and searchable on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (1847–1864):** The definitive mid-century survey of all landholders and tenants. County Antrim was surveyed around 1859–1862. Names every occupier of land or buildings with townland, valuation, and landlord. Freely available at AskAboutIreland.ie (askaboutireland.ie) and also on Ancestry.com. The accompanying field books and house books are at the Valuation Office, Dublin.
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** Detailed parish-level descriptions compiled during the first OS mapping of Ireland. The memoirs for County Antrim are unusually complete and include population statistics, occupations, economic conditions, and sometimes lists of families. Published by the Institute of Irish Studies, Queen's University Belfast. Useful background for understanding the community.
- **Flax Growers' List (1796):** Lists householders who received spinning wheels or looms under a government premium scheme. Coverage for County Antrim is substantial. Available on several genealogy databases.
- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s):** Earlier than the target period but useful for establishing family presence. PRONI holds copies for County Antrim.

### Probate and court records

- **Pre-1858:** Wills and administrations for County Antrim were proved in the Consistorial Court of Connor for smaller estates, and in the Prerogative Court of Armagh for more substantial ones. The originals were largely destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire (see Known Record Losses). However, a name index to pre-1858 wills survives and is searchable online at the NAI and in published form. Some will abstracts and copies were made before the fire and survive in various collections at PRONI, the NAI, and the NLI.
- **Post-1858:** After the Probate Act 1858, probate was handled by the civil courts. The District Probate Registry for County Antrim was in Belfast. Annual calendars of grants of probate and administration from 1858 onward survive and are held at PRONI; they are also indexed at Ancestry.com. Original wills from 1858 forward survive at PRONI for Northern Ireland testators.
- **Where held:** PRONI, National Archives of Ireland (Dublin). Some abstracts at the NLI and local repositories.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (townland-based system, not a rectangular survey). The townland is the fundamental unit. Billy parish contains numerous named townlands.
- **Registry of Deeds:** All registered deeds from 1708 onward are held at the Registry of Deeds, King's Inns, Dublin. Grantor/grantee indexes are available on microfilm and increasingly online (Ancestry.com). Registration was voluntary and weighted toward the middling and larger landholding classes; many small tenant transactions were never registered.
- **Estate papers:** Much of north Antrim was held by large estates (notably the Antrim estate of the Earls of Antrim / Viscounts Dunluce). Estate rentals, leases, and agent correspondence can name tenants who appear in no other records. PRONI holds extensive collections of estate papers for County Antrim landlords.
- **Landed Estates Court records (post-1848):** Encumbered Estates Acts generated court proceedings with detailed rental schedules naming tenants. These are at the NAI and partially on Ancestry.com.
- **Ordnance Survey maps:** The first-edition OS maps (1830s) show every townland boundary and field boundary; valuable for locating families geographically.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts 1780–1870:** American Revolutionary War (some Ulster men served on both sides); Irish Rebellion of 1798 (County Antrim was a major centre of United Irish activity — rebel and loyalist records both generated); Napoleonic Wars; Crimean War; early campaigns of Empire
- **Record types:**
  - British Army service records for other ranks (War Office series WO 97) at The National Archives, Kew (TNA), now largely digitised on Findmypast.com and Ancestry.com
  - Muster rolls (WO 10–17) at TNA
  - Pension records (WO 22, WO 116, WO 120) at TNA
  - Irish Militia records: PRONI holds records for the Antrim Militia and other Ulster militia units
  - 1798 rebellion: lists of rebels, yeomanry muster rolls, and compensation claims are scattered across PRONI, NAI, and TNA
- **Where held:** TNA (Kew) for British Army; PRONI for local militia; NAI for some Irish records

### Cemetery records

- **Major burial grounds:** The Church of Ireland parish of Billy has a historic graveyard attached to Billy church. Bushmills town had its own burial grounds. Presbyterian congregations maintained session graveyards or used the Church of Ireland graveyard.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves (billiongraves.com) have some coverage for County Antrim graveyards. The North of Ireland Family History Society and local Antrim family history groups have conducted graveyard transcription projects; results are often published in their journals or lodged with PRONI.
- **Physical records:** Sexton or vestry burial records, where they survive, are at PRONI or with the individual congregation.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Coleraine Chronicle (from 1844) is the nearest long-running paper with strong coverage of north Antrim including the Bushmills area. The Belfast Newsletter (from 1737, one of the oldest continuously published newspapers in the world) covers Ulster-wide events and includes birth, marriage, and death notices from north Antrim families. The Northern Whig (1824 onward) is another key Belfast paper.
- **Where held:** The British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, part of Findmypast) has digitised many Northern Irish papers including the Coleraine Chronicle. The Belfast Newsletter from 1737 is freely available online through the British Newspaper Archive and Queen's University Belfast's Digital Library. The Linen Hall Library in Belfast holds a major local newspaper collection.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and death notices, marriage notices, land sale advertisements, rent notices, legal notices (including estate and probate notices), and news of emigrant communities. The Belfast Newsletter marriage and death notices have been indexed by the Ulster Historical Foundation (UHF).

### Immigration and emigration records

This is an important category: north Antrim, and the Ulster-Scots community specifically, had very high emigration rates throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, primarily to North America. If the ancestor born c.1825 had siblings or parents who emigrated, records on both the Irish and receiving-country sides may survive.

- **Passenger lists:** Departure records from Irish ports (Belfast, Londonderry/Derry, Newry) for the 18th and early 19th centuries are fragmentary. Arrival records on the US and Canadian side are more consistent. US passenger lists from 1820 are at NARA and online at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Pre-1820 ship arrivals require newspaper searches. Findmypast.com has Irish emigrant databases.
- **Naturalisation:** If the family member emigrated to the United States, naturalization records (Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization) were filed in federal and state courts; they frequently name the Irish county and sometimes the specific parish of origin.
- **Ulster Historical Foundation:** The UHF (ancestryireland.com) in Belfast has compiled emigrant databases and published research on Ulster emigration to North America.
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs:** These sometimes note the destinations of emigrants from specific parishes — worth consulting for the Billy parish memoir.

### Tax records

- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s):** Pre-target period; lists householders paying hearth tax. Available at PRONI, useful as pre-1780 baseline.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** See Census substitutes above. The primary tax substitute for the early part of the target period.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (1847–1864):** See Census substitutes above.
- **Poor Rate records:** After the Poor Law (Ireland) Act 1838, Poor Law Unions levied rates on occupiers. Rate books naming ratepayers survive at PRONI for some years and unions. They function like annual tax lists between the Tithe Books and Griffith's.

### Other record types

- **School records:** The National Schools system was established in Ireland in 1831. County Antrim national school records (registers and roll books) are held at PRONI. They can document children's names, parents' names, and dates of enrolment for the 1830s onward.
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs and Name Books (1830s):** These manuscript volumes describe each parish's geography, economy, people, and history in detail. The County Antrim memoirs are exceptionally full. Published by the Institute of Irish Studies; important contextual and sometimes nominal sources.
- **Landed estate records:** Estate rentals, lease books, and tenant correspondence at PRONI can name individual tenants, including year-by-year occupancy and sometimes family relationships.
- **Church session minutes:** Presbyterian kirk session minutes record disciplinary matters, poor relief grants, and testimonials for members moving to another congregation. They can supply dates and family details not in the baptism or marriage register. Held at PRONI and the PHSI.

- Presbyterian congregational session minutes for Bushmills (Route) and neighbouring congregations: held at PRONI and the PHSI, not comprehensively digitised or indexed online
- Church of Ireland registers for Billy parish prior to the IrishGenealogy.ie project's upload schedule: confirm current upload status directly with IrishGenealogy.ie
- Pre-1858 will abstracts and copies surviving at PRONI (the originals are destroyed): accessible only via in-person or written request to PRONI
- Poor Rate records and estate agent's rentals: held at PRONI, not generally online
- National School roll books for Billy parish schools: at PRONI, not online
- PRONI-held estate papers for north Antrim landlords: catalogue online but documents generally not digitised

---

## Known record losses

The most severe record loss affecting this locality is the fire at the Public Record Office in the Four Courts, Dublin, on 30 June 1922, during the Irish Civil War. This fire destroyed:

- The original pre-1858 wills and administration bonds held by the diocesan and prerogative ecclesiastical courts — these are gone for most County Antrim pre-1858 estates. Only will abstracts, registered copies in the Registry of Deeds, and copies made before 1922 (some held at PRONI, the NLI, and in printed indexes) survive.
- The 1881 and 1891 census returns had already been destroyed by government order. The 1861 and 1871 returns had also been pulped.
- The 1841, 1851 returns were in the PRO when it burned; 1851 fragments survived for some counties but substantial coverage for County Antrim was lost.

There is no general record of whether the specific church registers (which were generally held locally, not at the PRO) were affected by any destruction; most Presbyterian and Church of Ireland registers for County Antrim that survived to the 20th century are now safely deposited at PRONI. However, some early registers were lost through neglect or fire at the local level before deposit.

**Substitute sources** when primary records are missing:

- Pre-1858 probate: published will abstracts and calendars; NAI index of wills; copies registered in the Registry of Deeds; solicitor's files sometimes preserved at PRONI
- Missing census years (1861–1891): Griffith's Valuation (c.1860), Poor Rate books, school records, church session minutes, newspaper notices
- Pre-1780 family origins: Hearth Money Rolls; subsidy rolls; Muster Rolls of c.1630; the 1659 census (published by Séamas Pender)

---

## Research tips

**Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki tools returned only generic placeholder content in this session; no Ireland-specific wiki pages were fetched. The tips below draw on general knowledge of Irish genealogy practice. The researcher should consult the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ireland (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy) and for County Antrim directly.

1. **Identify the specific townland before searching.** Irish records — Tithe Books, Griffith's Valuation, civil registration, church registers — are all organised at the townland level. "Billy parish" covers many townlands; if you know the townland from a later census or land record, you can focus your search in earlier records precisely.

2. **Civil registration came very late: all events 1780–1863 are church records only.** For a Presbyterian family, that means the Bushmills (Route) congregation register is your primary source for births (recorded as baptisms), marriages, and burials throughout most of the target period. Start there before anything else.

3. **Non-Catholic marriages were registered civilly from 1 April 1845**, giving you a civil marriage record for any Presbyterian marriage from that year. This is approximately 20 years before full civil registration and is often overlooked.

4. **Check the Route congregation even if the family later appeared in a different congregation.** In the 18th and early 19th centuries, Presbyterian families sometimes attended the nearest congregation or the one that served their landlord's tenantry; the family may have moved between congregations.

5. **Use Griffith's Valuation as your mid-century anchor.** It was compiled for County Antrim around 1859–1862 — close to the target period's end. Every person who occupied a house or land is listed with their townland and landlord. It locates the family geographically, identifies neighbours (who may be relatives), and names the immediate landlord (whose estate papers at PRONI may contain earlier references to the family).

6. **Work the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) as the early 19th-century anchor.** A family present in Griffith's who is also in the Tithe Books confirms presence across roughly 25 years. Between the two sources you bracket the birth window of the ancestor born c.1825.

7. **Naming patterns.** Ulster-Scots Presbyterian families frequently followed the Scottish naming convention: first son named for paternal grandfather, second son for maternal grandfather; first daughter for maternal grandmother, second daughter for paternal grandmother. This pattern is not universal but is common enough to generate strong hypotheses for grandparent names when you find the children's names in a baptismal register.

8. **The 1901 and 1911 census can work backward.** If any of the ancestor's siblings or parents were still alive in 1901 or 1911, their ages and relationships in those censuses provide direct evidence for the parent generation you are seeking.

9. **Session minutes complement the baptism register.** Presbyterian kirk session minutes record discipline cases (fornication, "irregular marriage," breach of sabbath) that sometimes document family relationships not otherwise recorded. They also record grants of certificates to members transferring to another congregation — these can trace migration within Ireland.

10. **Estate papers are under-used.** If the family were tenant farmers, the landlord's estate papers at PRONI (rent ledgers, lease books, ejectment notices) may contain their names for decades before any other record type. Identifying the townland (from Griffith's or the Tithe Books) identifies the landlord, and from there you can search the PRONI eCatalogue for that estate's archive.

11. **Emigration records require a two-sided search.** If any family member emigrated to North America (common from north Antrim after the 1840s), their US naturalization declaration may name the specific Irish county or parish. Canadian ship passenger records from Ulster ports (particularly Londonderry) are available on Findmypast.

12. **Adjoining parishes.** Billy civil parish borders Dunluce (to the west), Ballintoy (to the east), and Ramoan (to the northeast). A family on a parish boundary may have used congregations, schools, or civil registration districts in the neighbouring parish. Always check the registers of the churches immediately over the boundary. The Church of Ireland diocesan structure placed all these parishes within the Diocese of Connor, and the Presbyterian Route Presbytery covers all of north Antrim, so the same presbytery and the same diocesan archive cover the whole area — administrative continuity even across civil parish lines.

Billy civil parish in north Antrim is a well-documented corner of Ulster for the period 1780–1870, with the important caveat that Ireland suffered severe record losses in 1922. For a Presbyterian family, the Bushmills (Route) congregation register at PRONI in Belfast is the single most important source for baptisms and marriages before 1864, when civil registration began for all events. The Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) and Griffith's Valuation (c.1860) are the main census substitutes for the target years and are both freely available online; together they anchor the family's location in specific townlands, which unlocks access to every other record type.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
County Cork, within the province of Munster, was administered as part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland during this period. The county seat is Cork City. Key events of the 1830s–1840s include the Tithe Wars (1831–1836), the Poor Law Act (1838), and the onset of the Great Famine (1845–1852), which drove massive emigration chiefly via Cork/Cobh (Queenstown). The population was predominantly Gaelic Irish and Roman Catholic, with a smaller Anglo-Irish landowning class.

---

## ⚠️ Critical Record Loss: The 1922 Four Courts Fire
The single most important fact for Cork research is that the **1922 Four Courts fire** destroyed nearly all Irish national census returns prior to 1901 — including the **1841 and 1851 manuscripts**, which would have been the primary census sources for your ancestor's period. It also destroyed most original pre-1858 wills. You must rely on substitute sources.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(Core source for 1830s–1840s)*
- **Roman Catholic parish registers** are the only birth/marriage/death equivalent for Catholic families, since civil registration did not begin until 1864 (1845 for non-Catholic marriages only).
- RC registers typically record baptisms and marriages; burial entries are rare for this period.
- **Where:** National Library of Ireland (NLI) — digital images free online; some name-indexed at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie)
- **Survival:** Varies by parish. Many Cork RC parishes begin in the 1810s–1830s, so coverage of the target period is possible but not guaranteed.
- **Church of Ireland** (Anglican) registers record baptisms, marriages, and burials; held at the Representative Church Body Library (RCBL), Dublin, and partially microfilmed through FamilySearch.

### Census Substitutes *(replacing destroyed census records)*
| Record | Date Range | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tithe Applotment Books** | 1823–1837 | Named male occupiers of farmland by townland | Free at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) & FamilySearch |
| **Griffith's Valuation** | Early 1850s | Every householder in Ireland — name, address, valuation | Free at [AskAboutIreland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie) |
| **Poor Law rate books** | From 1838 | Ratepayers by Poor Law Union | National Archives of Ireland; Cork City & County Archives |

### Land Records
- **Tithe Applotment Books & Griffith's Valuation** (see above)
- **Registry of Deeds** (from 1708): Memorials (abstracts) of deeds, leases, and mortgages — searchable online at [irishdeeds.ie](https://www.irishdeeds.ie)
- **Estate/landlord records**: Tenant lists and rental books for Cork estates deposited at the NLI or National Archives of Ireland (NAI) — uneven coverage but can be highly specific.

### Probate Records
- Pre-1858 probate was handled by ecclesiastical courts; most original records destroyed in 1922.
- **Substitutes:** Printed abstract calendars; Betham abstracts at the Genealogical Office, Dublin; Index to Irish Wills.
- **Where:** National Archives of Ireland, Dublin.

### Military Records
- Many Irish men served in the British Army or East India Company forces during the 1830s–1840s.
- British Army service records and Kilmainham pension registers are at The National Archives (UK), Kew, and the National Archives of Ireland.
- Also available on Ancestry and FindMyPast (subscription).

### Poor Law & Workhouse Records *(from 1838)*
- Workhouse admission/discharge registers, relief lists, and minute books for Cork Poor Law Unions name the poorest families who appear nowhere else.
- **Where:** National Archives of Ireland; Cork City and County Archives. Not yet comprehensively online.

### National School Registers *(from 1831)*
- List pupils by name, age, religion, and father's occupation — valuable for family reconstruction.
- **Where:** National Archives of Ireland. Not comprehensively digitized.

### Emigration Records
- **Cork/Cobh (Queenstown)** was a primary port of emigration. Passenger arrival manifests at US ports are indexed free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry.
- US **naturalization papers** often name the specific Irish townland of origin — frequently the most precise location clue you'll find.
- Famine-era manifests often list complete family groups, including infants.

### Cemetery Records
- RC cemeteries generally did not maintain written burial registers in the 1830s–1840s.
- Workhouse burial records (from 1838) may document Famine-era deaths.
- Partial gravestone transcriptions at IrishGenealogy.ie and FindAGrave.

### Newspapers
- **Cork Examiner** (founded 1841): obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, shipping news. Available via Irish Newspaper Archives (subscription) and British Newspaper Archive (subscription).

---

## Repository Guide

### Online (Free)
- **[IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie)** — Tithe Applotment Books, church register indexes, civil registration from 1864
- **[NLI.ie](https://registers.nli.ie)** — RC parish register digital images to 1880
- **[AskAboutIreland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie)** — Griffith's Valuation
- **[FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)** — Irish RC registers, Tithe Applotment, emigration records, US arrivals

### Online (Subscription)
- **Ancestry.com** — US passenger arrivals, naturalization records, some British Army records
- **FindMyPast.com** — Irish church records, British passenger lists, military records
- **Irish Newspaper Archives (irishnewsarchive.com)** — Cork Examiner from 1841
- **British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk)** — Cork newspapers

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Census fragments, probate indexes, Poor Law records, school registers, Tithe originals |
| National Library of Ireland, Dublin | RC register microfilm, estate papers, newspapers |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland parish registers |
| Cork City and County Archives, Cork | Local government, estate papers, Cork-specific collections |
| The National Archives (UK), Kew | British Army records, British passenger departure records |

---

## Records NOT Online (Physical Access Required)
- Workhouse and Poor Law Union records (most Cork unions)
- Estate and landlord tenant lists
- RC burial registers (largely absent for this period)
- National school registers
- Grand Jury and county court records
- Militia and yeomanry records

---

## Research Tips

1. **Identify the townland first.** Irish records are organized at the townland — not county — level. Use Griffith's Valuation to find the surname and narrow to a specific townland and civil parish.

2. **Use the two-record starting sequence:**
   1. Search **Griffith's Valuation** (early 1850s) to locate the family's townland.
   2. Search the **Tithe Applotment Books** (1823–1837) to confirm the family's presence in the 1830s.
   3. Then find the **RC parish register** for that civil parish at the NLI or IrishGenealogy.ie.

3. **Civil vs. RC parish boundaries differ.** Always determine both the civil parish and the Roman Catholic parish — they frequently differ in name and extent, and church registers are filed under the RC parish.

4. **Poor Law records (from 1838) partially fill the census gap.** Rate books and workhouse records bridge the window between the Tithe Books and Griffith's Valuation.

5. **Search US records for Irish origins.** Passenger arrival manifests and naturalization papers often specify the Cork townland of origin — sometimes more precisely than any surviving Irish record.

6. **Irish naming conventions:** Children were commonly named for grandparents, so the same given names recur across generations. Married women were often known locally by their birth surname, so search both names.

7. **Search adjoining counties.** Families near Cork's borders (Kerry to the west, Limerick to the north-east, Waterford to the east) may have records in neighbouring counties' series.

---

**Bottom line:** The 1830s–1840s in County Cork is a challenging research window because the census records were destroyed and civil registration didn't yet exist. Your primary tools are Roman Catholic parish registers (free online at the NLI), the Tithe Applotment Books (free at IrishGenealogy.ie), and Griffith's Valuation (free at AskAboutIreland.ie). If your ancestor emigrated, US passenger manifests and naturalization records are often the best way to pin down the specific townland of origin in Cork.
