# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s-1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** County Cork has existed as a county within the province of Munster since 1606. During the 1830s-1840s it was administered as part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (union formed 1801).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Cork City
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Munster, Ireland
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this place and period. The county was among the most populous in Ireland before the Famine; the Great Famine (beginning 1845) caused severe population loss through death and emigration by the end of the target window.
- **Economy:** Predominantly small-tenant agriculture (tillage and cattle). Cork City was a significant port and commercial hub. The rural majority lived in acute poverty as tenant farmers on British-held estates. The Tithe Wars (1831-1836) — resistance to paying tithes to the Church of Ireland — were a defining event of the 1830s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Overwhelmingly Gaelic Irish; a smaller Anglo-Irish landowning class and English Protestant minority.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic; Church of Ireland (Anglican) among the landowning class and some town residents; small communities of Presbyterians and Methodists.
- **Key historical events:** Tithe Wars (1831-1836); Poor Law Act (1838) creating Poor Law Unions; onset of the Great Famine (1845-1852); mass emigration chiefly via Cork/Cobh (Queenstown).

## Boundary changes
- County Cork boundaries were stable throughout the 1830s-1840s target period. No subdivision changes affected record-keeping jurisdictions during these years.
- The Poor Law Act (1838) created Poor Law Unions that crossed county and civil parish boundaries for purposes of poor relief. Researchers searching workhouse or rate-book records must identify the specific Union (e.g., Cork, Bandon, Skibbereen, Kinsale, Fermoy, Mallow, Youghal, Kanturk, Millstreet, Macroom, Bantry, Castletown) that covered the townland in question.
- Ireland has two parallel geographic systems that do not align: **civil parishes** (the administrative unit for land and tax records) and **Roman Catholic parishes** (the ecclesiastical unit for church registers). These frequently differ in name and extent. Always establish both before searching church records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Civil (state) registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages did not begin at the national level until **1 January 1864**. Non-Catholic (mainly Church of Ireland) marriages were registered at the national level from **1845**. There are no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for Roman Catholic families during the entire 1830s-1840s target period. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **What exists for the target period:** Non-Catholic marriage registrations only from 1845. Nothing else.
- **Where held:** General Register Office, Werburgh Street, Dublin (post-1845 for non-Catholic marriages; post-1864 for all).
- **Gaps:** The entire 1830s-1840s is a civil registration gap for Catholic families.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Roman Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers are the only documentation of baptisms, marriages, and burials for this period. See Church Records below.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant); Church of Ireland (Anglican); Methodist; Presbyterian.
- **Record types:** RC registers record baptisms and marriages; burial entries in RC registers are rare for this period. Church of Ireland registers record baptisms (or christenings), marriages, and burials. Confirmations in RC registers are a separate event occurring years after baptism and constitute a distinct dated record series.
- **Where held:** The National Library of Ireland holds microfilm and digital images of Roman Catholic parish registers up to 1880, available free online. Church of Ireland registers are held at the Representative Church Body Library (RCBL), Dublin, and some remain in local custody. FamilySearch has microfilmed many Church of Ireland registers as well. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Survival:** Survival of RC parish registers varies widely by parish. The FamilySearch Wiki states that many Cork parishes begin in the 1810s-1830s, so some parishes have registers covering the target period and others do not begin until after it. Researchers must check the NLI's specific parish holdings before concluding records do not exist.
- **Language:** English for most entries; Latin formulas appear in RC registers for sacramental headings.
- **Digitization level:** RC registers at the NLI are available as free digital images online (browse-level at minimum; some are name-indexed through IrishGenealogy.ie). Church of Ireland registers are primarily microfilm or physical.

### Census records

- **National census:** Irish national censuses were taken in 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851, but the 1841 and 1851 returns were almost entirely destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire. The 1821 and 1831 returns also suffered major losses; only fragments survive for County Cork.
- **Census substitutes — Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837):** List male occupiers of tithe-liable agricultural land by name, townland, and land area. A critical census substitute for the 1830s. Landless labourers and most town dwellers are absent. Indexed and available online at IrishGenealogy.ie (free) and FamilySearch. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Census substitutes — Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork, early 1850s):** Lists every householder in Ireland — landholders, house occupiers, and tenants — giving name, address, and valuation. Published just after the target period, reflecting a post-Famine reduced population, but the FamilySearch Wiki describes it as the major substitute for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses. Available free online at AskAboutIreland.ie. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Other substitutes:** Poor Law rate books (from 1838) list ratepayers by Poor Law Union and can substitute for the missing 1841 census in the late 1830s-early 1840s.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, and inventories. Pre-1858 probate was handled by ecclesiastical courts — the Prerogative Court of Armagh (for estates over a certain value) and the Consistorial Court of Cork. From 1858 onward, civil probate registries (Principal Registry, Dublin; District Registry at Cork) took over.
- **Record loss:** The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most original pre-1858 wills and administration bonds. Surviving substitutes include printed abstract calendars, will extracts in the Betham Papers (Genealogical Office, Dublin), and the Index to Irish Wills (published; also partly available online at the National Archives of Ireland). (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland, Bishop Street, Dublin. Some surviving post-1858 will books are accessible online through the NAI catalog.
- **Research note:** For a testator dying in the 1830s-1840s: first search the surviving printed indexes to identify whether a will or administration was proved; then seek any surviving abstracts. Do not assume no probate occurred because original documents were destroyed.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** The Irish townland system: province > county > barony > civil parish > townland. Land was not surveyed on a rectangular grid.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** In this period, most land in County Cork was held under British landlord tenure. The Registry of Deeds, Dublin (established 1708), registered memorials (abstracts) of deeds, leases, and mortgages. Memorials are searchable online through the Registry of Deeds. The Landed Estates Court (from 1849) processed encumbered estate sales and its records are at the National Archives of Ireland.
- **Types:** Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837); Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s); Registry of Deeds memorials; estate records and rental books (where deposited); Grand Jury presentment books.
- **Estate records:** Many Cork landlord estates deposited rental lists, tenant maps, and estate correspondence at the National Library of Ireland or National Archives of Ireland. These name tenants and sometimes give family details not found elsewhere. Coverage is uneven — only estates whose papers were deposited and catalogued.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland; National Library of Ireland; Cork City and County Archives; Registry of Deeds online.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The target period falls after the Napoleonic Wars (ended 1815). Many Irish men served in the British Army throughout the 1830s-1840s; some served in the East India Company forces.
- **Record types:** British Army service records, muster rolls, Chelsea and Kilmainham pension records. The Kilmainham Hospital pensioners (Irish soldiers) are particularly relevant.
- **Where held:** The National Archives (UK), Kew, holds British Army service records. The National Archives of Ireland holds Kilmainham Hospital pension registers. Some British Army records from this period are available through FindMyPast and Ancestry (subscription).

### Cemetery records

- **Types:** Gravestone inscriptions; burial registers (where they exist — RC burial registers for the 1830s-1840s are largely absent).
- **Online coverage:** The Irish Gravestone Photographs Project and volunteer transcription projects on IrishGenealogy.ie cover some Cork cemeteries. FindAGrave (findagrave.com) indexes some Cork burials. Coverage is partial and incomplete for rural parishes in the target period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are at individual churches or Cork City and County Archives. Coverage is highly uneven.
- **Important note:** Roman Catholic cemeteries generally did not maintain written burial registers in the 1830s-1840s. Workhouse burial records (from 1838 for Cork unions) may document Famine-era deaths of the poorest families.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Cork Examiner (founded 1841; now the Irish Examiner) covers the latter part of the target period. The Cork Constitution was another major paper. Earlier Cork papers existed in the 1830s.
- **Where held:** The British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, subscription) holds digital copies. The Irish Newspaper Archives (irishnewsarchive.com, subscription) holds the Cork Examiner and other titles. Physical copies and microfilm at Cork City Library and the National Library of Ireland.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, estate sale announcements, and shipping news. A valuable source for middle-class and commercial families where church records are missing or sparse.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Cork (Cobh/Queenstown) was a primary port of emigration for Munster, particularly during the Famine (1845-1852), but departures were ongoing throughout the 1830s-1840s as well. Ships also departed from Cork to North America directly and via Liverpool.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at US ports are held at NARA and are indexed on FamilySearch (free), Ancestry.com, and other databases. British passenger departure lists (for Liverpool-departing ships) are at The National Archives (UK) and on FindMyPast. Departure records from Cork itself for this period are sparse; arrival records are the more complete source.
- **Content note:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that passenger manifests from Cork ports during the Famine list complete family groups, including infants and young children traveling with parents — not just heads of household. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Naturalization records:** Declarations of intention and naturalization petitions were filed in US courts (not at the port). These often state the county or townland of Irish origin and are held at the relevant US courthouse or state archives. These records are inland US documents; they are a critical source for pinpointing the Cork townland of origin.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837) function simultaneously as a tithe assessment and a land/census substitute (see Land Records and Census above). Poor Law rate books (from 1838) list ratepayers in each Poor Law Union.
- **Where held:** Tithe Applotment Books: National Archives of Ireland; IrishGenealogy.ie (free online). Poor Law rate books: National Archives of Ireland; some at Cork City and County Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Poor Law rate books name householders not otherwise documented and can serve as a census substitute for 1838-1851, partially bridging the gap left by destroyed census records.

### Other record types

- **Poor Law and workhouse records (from 1838):** Workhouse admission/discharge registers, relief lists, and minute books for Cork Poor Law Unions survive for some unions. These name the poorest families who appear in no other record type. Held at the National Archives of Ireland and Cork City and County Archives.
- **National school registers (from 1831):** Following the establishment of the National Board of Education in 1831, school registers list pupils by name, age, religion, and father's occupation — a valuable source for family reconstruction. Cork school registers are held at the National Archives of Ireland.
- **Estate and landlord records:** Tenant lists, maps, and correspondence held at the NLI and NAI where deposited. Uneven coverage but can be highly specific about townland residence and family circumstances.

## Records NOT online

- **Workhouse and Poor Law Union records:** Most Cork union records (relief lists, minute books, admission registers) are physical-only at the National Archives of Ireland or Cork City and County Archives, not comprehensively indexed online.
- **Estate and landlord papers:** Tenant lists and estate maps are physical-only at the NLI and NAI; there is no comprehensive online index to their contents.
- **RC burial registers:** Catholic burial records for this period are largely absent (cemeteries did not systematically register interments). Gravestone inscription projects cover only a fraction of burial sites.
- **Church of Ireland burial registers for Cork:** While some are microfilmed through FamilySearch, many remain in physical custody at the RCBL or local churches.
- **Grand Jury and county court records:** Physical custody at the National Archives of Ireland; not systematically digitized for this period.
- **Militia and yeomanry records:** Physical-only at the NAI.
- **National school registers:** At the National Archives of Ireland; not comprehensively digitized or indexed online.

---

## Known record losses

The **1922 Four Courts fire** (destruction of the Public Record Office of Ireland) is the central event shaping pre-1901 Irish genealogical research. The fire destroyed:
- Nearly all pre-1901 Irish national census returns. The 1841 and 1851 manuscripts — which would have been the primary census sources for the target period — are almost entirely gone. Fragments of the 1821 and 1831 returns survive for some Cork parishes. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- Original pre-1858 wills and administration bonds processed through Irish probate courts.
- Many other government records.

**Substitute sources compensating for census losses:** Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837), Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s), Poor Law rate books (from 1838), and national school registers (from 1831) together provide overlapping land and householder coverage. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))

**Substitute sources compensating for probate losses:** Printed abstract calendars and the Betham abstracts at the Genealogical Office, Dublin, capture some pre-fire will content. These survive for a portion of the original records.

No tool result stated a specific further loss particular to County Cork beyond the national 1922 fire.

---

## Research tips

- **Church records are the core source for the 1830s-1840s.** Because national civil registration did not begin until 1864 (1845 for non-Catholic marriages), Roman Catholic parish registers are the only civil-era equivalent for Catholic families. Identify the ancestor's specific civil parish, then determine which RC parish served that civil parish's townland — they frequently differ in name and boundary. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Identify the townland first.** Irish records are organized at the townland level, not by county. If you know only the county, start with Griffith's Valuation or the Tithe Applotment Books, searching by surname, to narrow the family to a specific townland and civil parish before seeking church records.
- **Use a two-record starting sequence.** First search Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s) to locate the family's townland and civil parish. Then search the Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837) to confirm the same family's presence in the 1830s. Then seek the RC parish register for that civil parish at the NLI or IrishGenealogy.ie. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Famine emigration records cross into US sources.** Passenger arrival manifests at US ports (indexed free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry) often record the port of departure (Cork) and sometimes the county or townland of origin. Naturalization papers filed in US courts frequently name the specific Irish townland of origin — these are often the most precise location clues you will find.
- **RC burial records are largely absent for the 1830s-1840s.** Most Catholic cemeteries in Cork did not maintain registers in this period. Search gravestone inscription projects (IrishGenealogy.ie, FindAGrave) and, from 1838 onward, workhouse burial registers if the individual may have died during or near the Famine.
- **Poor Law records begin 1838 and partially fill the census gap.** Rate books and workhouse records from Cork's Poor Law Unions begin in 1838 — exactly spanning the gap between the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation. These are held at the National Archives of Ireland and Cork City and County Archives, and are not yet comprehensively available online.
- **Irish naming conventions:** Irish families commonly named children after grandparents and other close relatives, which means the same given names recur across generations. A married woman in rural 19th-century Ireland was often known locally by her birth surname rather than her husband's surname — searching only the married name for those years may return nothing. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms both of these naming practices for Ireland. (Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Search adjoining counties.** Families near Cork's borders routinely generated records in neighbouring jurisdictions. County Kerry borders Cork to the west, County Limerick to the north-east, and County Waterford to the east. Records for families near these borders — Tithe books, Griffith's entries, church registers — may appear in the adjoining county's series. The County Cork home wiki page did not return a Neighbouring Counties table for this survey, so check each bordering county's series independently.
- **The Cork Examiner (founded 1841)** covers the latter part of the target period and is a valuable source for middle-class obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices. Available through the Irish Newspaper Archives (subscription).

---

County Cork in the 1830s-1840s is a challenging research period because the most important genealogical records — national censuses and civil birth/death/marriage certificates — were either destroyed or did not yet exist. The records that do survive and are most useful for this period are Roman Catholic parish registers (many beginning in the 1810s-1830s, held free online at the National Library of Ireland), the Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837, free online at IrishGenealogy.ie), and Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s, free at AskAboutIreland.ie). The single most important warning is that the 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed the 1841 and 1851 Irish census manuscripts, so there is no national census coverage for your ancestor's years in Cork — you must build the case from church, land, and tax records instead. If your ancestor emigrated during or just after the Famine, passenger arrival manifests at US ports and any US naturalization records are often the most specific source for pinning down the Cork townland of origin.

The logical next step is to identify the specific civil parish and townland your ancestor came from, then locate the relevant RC parish register at the National Library of Ireland, search the Tithe Applotment Books for the surname, and cross-reference with Griffith's Valuation — after which a research plan for the individual can be built.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Berkshire County was formed in **1761** and borders **Columbia County, New York** (to the west/southwest) and **Bennington County, Vermont** (to the north). A family near either state line may have generated records across the border. The county seat is **Pittsfield**.

---

## Births, Marriages & Deaths — What Exists and Where

### Civil (Town-Level) Vital Records

- **Before 1841:** There was **no statewide registration system** in Massachusetts. Every birth, marriage, and death record was created by — and remains with — the **individual town clerk**. You must identify the specific town first.
- **From 1841 onward:** Massachusetts launched the first unified statewide registration system. A parallel state-level series exists for 1841–1850 *in addition to* the town record.
- **Marriage intentions:** These were a **separate filing**, most commonly in the *bride's home town*, but also sometimes in the groom's town and their joint residence. A marriage may appear in up to three towns' records. Search all.

**FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) (id 2061550)

**Digitized Berkshire County volume:** DGS 004500891 (Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850, 512 images) — **0% indexed, browse-only** (no name search available).

> **Tip:** Start with the *published* **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** compilations instead. These name-indexed transcriptions exist for most Berkshire County towns, are far more accessible than the browse-only digitized volume, and are held at NEHGS and many public libraries.

---

### Church Records

- **Essential for 1820–1840:** Before statewide civil registration, the church register is often the *only* surviving record of a birth (baptism) or burial.
- A digitized volume for **Pittsfield Congregational Church Records, 1791–1850** (DGS 004500892, 274 images) exists on FamilySearch — also **0% indexed, browse-only**.
- Records of other denominations and other towns are not confirmed as digitized; contact NEHGS and denominational archives.

**FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) (id 1921657)

---

## Census Records

| Year | Coverage | Notes |
|------|----------|-------|
| 1820 | All households | Indexed |
| 1830 | All households | Indexed |
| 1840 | All households | Indexed |
| 1850 | All households + **Mortality Schedule** | Mortality Schedule records deaths in the year prior to enumeration |

Available indexed at both **FamilySearch** and **Ancestry.com**.

---

## Other Key Record Types

| Record Type | Repository | FamilySearch Collection |
|-------------|-----------|------------------------|
| Probate (wills, administrations, guardianships) | Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) (id 1678901) |
| Land/deeds | Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Not confirmed online — contact registry directly |
| Naturalization | Any court of record pre-1906 | [Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) (id 1459213) |
| Military (War of 1812, Mexican-American War) | NARA / Fold3 | [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/); [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |
| Passenger lists | FamilySearch | [Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) (id 1784312) |
| Cemetery records | Find A Grave | [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers | Newspapers.com | Marriage notices, obituaries, legal notices |

---

## Physical Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Individual town clerks** (each Berkshire County town) | Original vital records and marriage intentions |
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | Colonial/state records, militia rolls, early patents |
| **NEHGS, Boston** (also AmericanAncestors.org) | Published vital records compilations, local histories, manuscript collections — the primary specialist library for this research |
| **Local churches** | Registers not yet filmed or digitized |

---

## Cross-Border Warning

Because this family lived near *both* the New York and Vermont lines, **check Columbia County, NY and Bennington County, VT** systematically. Each state had its own vital registration timeline and record system. Events such as marriages, land transactions, or church memberships may have been recorded across the border.

---

## Recommended Starting Steps

1. **Identify the specific town** the family lived in within Berkshire County.
2. **Pull the published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** compilation — name-indexed and far more accessible than the browse-only FamilySearch volume.
3. **Search the FamilySearch Town Vital Records collection** (id 2061550) for that town.
4. **Search church records** — especially Congregational — for baptisms and burials, which may fill gaps where town records are missing.
5. **Check adjoining counties in New York and Vermont** for any events that crossed the state line.
6. **Consult NEHGS** (AmericanAncestors.org or in person in Boston) for local histories and finding aids not available digitally.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

> **Tool coverage note:** The FamilySearch place-authority tools did not resolve a place record for Ireland or County Antrim in this run, and `collections_search` / `volume_search` returned 0 results. All place-based tool calls fell back to a generic "Genealogy Records" page. The one exception was the **Ireland Naming Customs** wiki page, which returned full content and is cited below. Every section drawing on external knowledge is clearly marked as such; only the naming conventions section is directly sourced from a tool result.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, Barony of Dunluce Lower (later Dunluce Upper), County Antrim, Province of Ulster, Ireland
- **County seat:** Antrim town; the parish lies in north County Antrim near Bushmills and Ballycastle
- **Administrative context:** Under British rule — Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, then the United Kingdom after the Act of Union 1800
- **Economy:** Domestic linen weaving (Ulster linen trade), subsistence tenant farming, and coastal fishing; severely disrupted by the Great Famine (1845–1852)
- **Religious composition:** Predominantly Presbyterian (Scots plantation descent), with a Church of Ireland (Anglican) minority and a smaller Roman Catholic population. **Denomination is the single most important factor in record strategy.**

---

## Boundary Changes

| Change | Date | Effect on records |
|---|---|---|
| Act of Union | 1800 | Ireland joined Great Britain; civil administration remained county/barony/townland |
| Ballycastle Poor Law Union established | 1838 | Post-1838 poor relief and workhouse records file under Ballycastle Union, not the civil parish |
| Probate Act | 1858 | Probate jurisdiction shifted from ecclesiastical courts to civil district registries |

The civil parish of Billy itself was a **stable administrative unit** throughout 1780–1870. Barony boundaries did not affect record survival for this parish.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Pre-civil registration (before civil registration began):** Church records are the **only** source for baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- **Access gap:** The FamilySearch wiki tools did not return the Ireland Civil Registration page with specific start dates. Researchers should consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Vital_Records directly for current civil registration start dates and access points.
- **Note:** General Register Office (GRO), Belfast holds civil registration records for Northern Ireland.

### Church Records *(primary source for the entire 1780–1870 window)*

| Denomination | Record types | Main repository |
|---|---|---|
| Presbyterian | Baptisms, marriages, session books | PRONI (Belfast); Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland |
| Church of Ireland | Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry books | PRONI; Representative Church Body (RCB) Library, Dublin |
| Roman Catholic | Baptisms, marriages | PRONI; National Archives of Ireland (NAI) |

- **Language:** English throughout. Some Presbyterian session headings may use formal Latin.
- **Access gap:** No tool result confirmed which specific congregations served Billy civil parish. Consult PRONI's eCatalogue at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni and the FamilySearch Catalog for "Billy, Antrim, Ireland."

### Census and Census Substitutes

| Record | Coverage | Survivorship |
|---|---|---|
| 1821, 1831, 1841 censuses | All Ireland | Almost entirely destroyed |
| 1851 census | All Ireland | Very limited survival for Ulster |
| 1861, 1871 censuses | All Ireland | Administratively destroyed after statistical use |
| **Tithe Applotment Books** (c.1823–1837) | All townlands | Survive; widely transcribed |
| **Griffith's Primary Valuation** (1847–1864) | All occupiers and lessors | Survive; widely indexed |
| Valuation revision books (post-1864) | Annual updates to Griffith's | Survive at PRONI |

> **Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation effectively substitute for census records for this period.** They are the recommended first name search when civil or church records are absent.

### Probate Records

- **Pre-1858:** Jurisdiction held by the Prerogative Court of Armagh (larger estates) and the Consistorial Court of Connor (the diocese for County Antrim, smaller estates).
- **Critical loss:** The Public Record Office of Ireland in Dublin was destroyed by fire in 1922, destroying most centrally held wills and administrations. Surviving substitutes are will abstracts, indexes, and calendars held at PRONI and the NAI.

### Land Records

| Record | Date range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Tithe Applotment Books | c.1823–1837 | PRONI; NAI; various online databases |
| Griffith's Primary Valuation | 1847–1864 | NAI; PRONI; AskAboutIreland.ie |
| Registry of Deeds | From 1708 | Registry of Deeds, Dublin |
| Estate papers (rent rolls, eviction notices, tenancy correspondence) | Varies | PRONI holds many County Antrim estate collections |

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** United Irishmen rebellion (1798), Napoleonic Wars, mid-19th-century British campaigns
- **Record types:** British Army service records and pensions (The National Archives, Kew); County Antrim Yeomanry muster rolls
- **Access:** TNA Kew in person; some records via Ancestry/Findmypast under subscription; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery Records

- Presbyterian and Church of Ireland churchyard burial registers and headstones are the primary source.
- **Online search:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — search directly for Billy civil parish cemeteries; no specific pages were identified in this survey.
- Physical sexton records held by the relevant church or at PRONI.

### Poor Law Records

- **Ballycastle Poor Law Union** (est. 1838): workhouse admissions, outdoor relief lists, and assisted emigration records. These name the **poorest residents**, who may appear in no church register.
- Held at PRONI; digitization status not confirmed by tools in this run.

### Emigration Records

- **Context:** Large-scale Ulster Presbyterian emigration to North America began in the 18th century; the Great Famine (1845–1852) produced mass emigration.
- **Key ports:** Londonderry (Derry) and Belfast; Liverpool was a common transshipment point.
- **Record types:** US customs passenger manifests (post-1820); Poor Law Union assisted emigration lists; landlord-assisted emigration schemes (occasional lists survive).
- Always examine the full passenger manifest — infants and children traveling with parents are recorded.

### Newspaper Records

- Ulster newspapers carried obituaries, marriage notices, and post-Famine eviction notices.
- **Access:** British Newspaper Archive (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/); Irish Newspaper Archives (https://www.irishnewsarchive.com/). Specific north Antrim titles were not identified by tools in this run.

---

## Repository Guide

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Key holdings for Billy civil parish | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI** (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland), Belfast | Church registers, estate papers, Poor Law records, valuation books, Tithe Applotment | In person + online catalog: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| **National Archives of Ireland (NAI)**, Dublin | Griffith's Valuation, surviving census fragments, wills calendars | In person + online: https://www.nationalarchives.ie/ |
| **General Register Office (GRO)**, Belfast | Civil registration records (births, marriages, deaths) | In person; some online access |
| **The National Archives (TNA)**, Kew, England | British Army service records, pension records | In person; some via Ancestry/Findmypast |
| **RCB Library**, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers not held at PRONI | In person: https://www.ireland.anglican.org/about/rcb-library |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland**, Belfast | Presbyterian session books, congregational histories | In person |

### Online Starting Points

Since no specific FamilySearch collection IDs were returned for Ireland in this run, researchers should search directly:

- **FamilySearch Catalog:** https://www.familysearch.org/catalog/search → search "Billy, Antrim, Ireland"
- **FamilySearch Records:** https://www.familysearch.org/search/records → place "Antrim, Ireland"
- **PRONI eCatalogue:** https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/services/search-proni-online
- **County Antrim wiki page:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Antrim,_Ireland_Genealogy *(navigate directly — tools could not retrieve it in this run)*

---

## Known Record Losses

| Record series | Loss | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| 1821, 1831, 1841 census returns | Destroyed (various) | No household census survives for most of the period; use Tithe/Griffith substitutes |
| 1861, 1871 census returns | Administratively destroyed post-enumeration | No household census for 1861 or 1871 |
| Pre-1922 wills and administrations (PROI) | 1922 Four Courts fire, Dublin | Most original probate records gone; use surviving indexes and abstracts at PRONI/NAI |

---

## Naming Conventions *(from FamilySearch Ireland Naming Customs wiki page)*

*Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs — the one Ireland-specific wiki page fully returned by the tools in this run.*

### Surname variations
- Gaelic surnames were anglicized under English rule, producing multiple spellings: the same family may appear as **O'Flynn**, **Flynn**, and **Flinn** across different records.
- The prefixes *Mac* (son of) and *O* (grandson/descendant of) were frequently dropped and restored across the 19th century.
- Spelling was unstandardized; a single family's surname may appear several ways within one register.

### Given name variations
- Irish given names are Gaelic in origin and were anglicized. Per the wiki page, **Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah** are examples of variations of the same underlying name.
- Some given names were used for both males and females (Florence, Sydney, Evelyn).
- Nicknames may bear little resemblance to the formal name in a register.

### Traditional naming pattern *(as stated by the FamilySearch Ireland Naming Customs page)*

| Child | Usual namesake |
|---|---|
| 1st son | Father's father |
| 2nd son | Mother's father |
| 3rd son | Father |
| 4th son | Father's eldest brother |
| 1st daughter | Mother's mother |
| 2nd daughter | Father's mother |
| 3rd daughter | Mother |

> **The wiki page states explicitly:** *"The pattern is a clue, not a rule — it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity."*

---

## Research Strategy Summary

1. **Establish denomination first.** Presbyterian, Church of Ireland, and Roman Catholic families used separate registers held at different repositories. Do not assume one denomination's registers cover all families in the parish.
2. **Use Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation as census substitutes.** These are the primary name-indexed finding tools for 1780–1870 given the near-total loss of Irish census records.
3. **Search PRONI's online catalog and the FamilySearch Catalog directly** for Billy civil parish holdings — no specific collection IDs were returned by the tools in this run.
4. **For post-1838 poverty-level families,** check Ballycastle Poor Law Union records at PRONI before concluding a person is untraceable.
5. **For emigrant descendants,** emigration likely occurred through Londonderry or Belfast; trace the family in US/Canadian passenger manifests and, if post-1845, check Poor Law assisted emigration records.
6. **Apply surname spelling variants broadly** — the same family name may appear under multiple anglicizations. Search by soundex or wildcard where available.

### Church records

- **Denominations present in Billy civil parish:** Presbyterian (dominant), Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic (minority). No tool result in this run confirmed the names of specific congregations or their founding dates.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and session (kirk session) records for Presbyterians. The Church of Ireland kept vestry books, baptism registers, and burial registers. Roman Catholic registers typically record baptisms and marriages.
- **Where held:** PRONI (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Belfast) holds microfilm and original deposits of many County Antrim church registers. The Representative Church Body (RCB) Library in Dublin holds Church of Ireland registers not held locally. Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland holds Presbyterian session records. No `volume_search` or `collections_search` result confirmed which of these are digitized or indexed online for Billy civil parish specifically.
- **Language:** English. Presbyterian session records may use formal ecclesiastical Latin for some headings; the registers themselves are in English.

### Census records

- **Irish censuses relevant to this period:** Censuses of Ireland were taken in 1813, 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, and 1871. The 1821, 1831, and 1841 returns for most of Ireland were destroyed. The 1861 and 1871 returns were administratively destroyed after being used for statistical purposes. For the 1780–1870 window, survivorship of census returns is extremely limited.
- **Substitute enumerations:** Tithe Applotment Books (c.1823–1837) and Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864) are the main name-indexed substitutes for census records in this period. No tool result in this run confirmed specific collection IDs or access points for these for Billy civil parish.
- **Access gap:** `collections_search` and `volume_search` returned 0 results. No specific collection was returned by any tool.

### Probate and court records

- **Pre-1858 probate:** Before 1858, probate jurisdiction in Ireland lay with the Prerogative Court of Armagh (for estates over a threshold) and the Consistorial Court of Connor (the diocese covering County Antrim) for smaller estates. The 1858 Probate Act transferred jurisdiction to civil district probate registries.
- **Destruction of records:** The Public Record Office of Ireland in Dublin was destroyed by fire during the Four Courts attack in 1922. This destroyed the vast majority of pre-1922 wills, administrations, and other probate records that had been centralized there. No tool result in this run explicitly confirmed this loss for Billy civil parish specifically, but it is the reason surviving probate indexes and abstracts are the primary substitute.
- **Surviving substitutes:** Will abstracts and indexes in PRONI, the NAI (National Archives of Ireland), and printed calendars of wills and administrations from the 19th century are the main remaining access points.
- **Access gap:** No tool result returned specific collection IDs, indexed volumes, or digitization status for County Antrim probate records.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Ireland used a townland-based survey system. The Ordnance Survey townland index provides the granular mapping unit. The relevant land distribution authority during this period was the Crown (through the Landed Estates Court and its predecessors) and private landowners under the tenant-at-will system.
- **Key record sets:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books** (c.1823–1837): record tenant occupiers townland by townland across Ireland. Billy civil parish would have a Tithe Applotment Book.
  - **Griffith's Primary Valuation** (1847–1864): the national property survey listing every occupier and immediate lessor in each townland. This is the single most important finding tool for 19th-century Irish research.
  - **Registry of Deeds** (from 1708): Dublin-based central registry where voluntary registration of land transactions could be made.
- **Access gap:** No tool result returned collection IDs, digitization status, or repository details for these record sets for Billy civil parish specifically. Researchers should search the FamilySearch Catalog and the PRONI eCatalogue directly.

- **Relevant conflicts during 1780–1870:** United Irishmen rebellion (1798); Napoleonic Wars service (British Army); various mid-19th-century colonial campaigns.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** The Great Famine (1845–1852) drove massive emigration from County Antrim. Pre-Famine emigration to North America was also common from Ulster, beginning in the 18th century.

- **Record types:** Passenger manifests at the destination ports (e.g., US customs manifests, then post-1819 US passenger lists); assisted emigration records under the Ballycastle Poor Law Union (for those receiving workhouse assistance); landlord-assisted emigration schemes occasionally generated lists.

- **Poor Law records:** Ballycastle Poor Law Union (established 1838) records include workhouse admissions, outdoor relief lists, and assisted emigration records. ## Research tips

### Naming conventions — confirmed by tool result

The following comes from the **Ireland Naming Customs** page returned at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs:

- **Surname variations:** Irish surnames of Gaelic origin were anglicized under English rule, producing multiple forms of the same name (e.g., Houlihan/O'Houlihan may appear as Holland). The prefixes *Mac* (son of) and *O* (grandson or descendant of) were frequently dropped or restored, so the same family may appear as O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn across different records. Spelling was not standardized; a single family's surname may be recorded several ways within one parish register.
- **Given name variations:** Irish given names are Gaelic in origin and were anglicized. Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah, for example, are stated by the page to be variations of the same name. Some given names were used for both males and females (Florence, Sydney, Evelyn). Some given names have nicknames that little resemble the formal name.
- **Traditional naming pattern:** According to the FamilySearch Ireland Naming Customs page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs), a traditional pattern was often used until the later 19th century:
  - First son: usually named for the father's father
  - Second son: usually named for the mother's father
  - Third son: usually named for the father
  - Fourth son: usually named for the father's eldest brother
  - First daughter: usually named for the mother's mother
  - Second daughter: usually named for the father's mother
  - Third daughter: usually named for the mother
  - The FamilySearch wiki page states explicitly: "The pattern is a clue, not a rule — it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity."

### General research strategy given tool coverage gaps

- Because `place_search` did not resolve a standardPlace for Ireland in this run, and because `collections_search` and `volume_search` returned 0 results, the practical starting point for online research is a direct FamilySearch Catalog search for "Billy, Antrim, Ireland" and a direct FamilySearch Records search for "Antrim" as place — not any collection ID this guide can supply.
- The two substitute-census sources — Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Primary Valuation — are the recommended first search for any person in Billy civil parish during 1780–1870. Both have been widely transcribed and are available in part through PRONI online, the NAI, and various genealogical databases; search each by name and townland.
- Because church registers are the primary source for vital events before civil registration, and because three distinct denominations (Presbyterian, Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic) served the Billy civil parish population, researchers should not assume one denomination's registers cover all families. Confirm the family's denomination before selecting a register series to search.
- The denomination split also matters for emigration: Ulster Presbyterians emigrated to North America in large numbers from the 18th century onward; the relevant emigrant reception records may be in US, Canadian, or Australian archives, not just Irish ones.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 (place_search dateRange "+1811/")
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed in any tool result returned in this survey. (All FamilySearch Wiki pages for Schuylkill County and Pennsylvania returned generic fallback content.)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this jurisdiction and period.
- **Economy:** No tool data returned.
- **Ethnic composition:** Church Records volume 007936751 (1842–1895) includes German-language records (languages: en, de), confirming at least one German-speaking congregation operated in the county during the target period.
- **Religious denominations:** At least one congregation produced German-language church records during 1842–1895 (volume 007936751). No other denomination-specific tool data was returned.
- **Key historical events:** No tool data returned. The Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and the Civil War (1861–1865) fall within the period and generated military records relevant to Schuylkill County residents.

## Boundary changes
Schuylkill County has been in continuous existence since 1811 (place_search dateRange "+1811/"). place_search_all returned no alternate jurisdictional representations for the county, indicating no boundary-change splits are recorded for the 1840–1880 period. Records throughout the target window were created and are held under the single "Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States" jurisdiction.

## Available record types

For each record type, the jurisdictional level (county, state, federal) is given as returned by tool results.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records and related Pennsylvania-specific pages returned only generic content — no specific registration dates for Pennsylvania were provided by any tool in this survey. Collection 2255317 ("Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968") begins in 1906, establishing that statewide death registration at the state level did not begin before that date. Collection 1921317 ("Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950") begins in 1885, establishing that county-level marriage registration did not begin before that date. No birth registration collection overlapping 1840–1880 was returned. The FamilySearch Wiki does not confirm any earlier registration level from tool results in this run.
- **What exists for 1840–1880:** No civil birth or death registration collection covering 1840–1880 was returned by any tool. Marriage: collections 1571957 ("Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950", 312,045 indexed records + 156,023 images) and 1502909 ("Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900", 198,765 indexed records, no images) both overlap the target period. FamilySearch volume 007936753 (Marriage Records 1870–1910, 94 images) covers the last decade of the target period but is browse-only.
- **Where held:** County-level marriage records: Schuylkill County courthouse and FamilySearch (collections above). State-level death certificates (post-1906): Pennsylvania Department of Health / State Archives.
- **Gaps:** No indexed civil birth or death records for 1840–1880 were returned by any tool. The county marriage volume (007936753) covers only 1870–1910 and is browse-only.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials — see Church Records below); federal census mortality schedules (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) recording deaths in the year preceding each census enumeration.

### Church records
- **FamilySearch volume 007936751:** Church Records for Schuylkill County, 1842–1895. 187 images. 0% name-indexed, no full-text search — **browse-only**. Languages: English and German. Researchers must be prepared to read German-language ecclesiastical script.
- **Collections_search note:** "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) appeared in collections_search but is explicitly labeled a **"synthetic test fixture"** in its collection title. It cannot be treated as a real FamilySearch collection and must not be used as a research source without independent verification at FamilySearch.org.
- **What to expect in church registers:** Baptisms (recording birth date/place and parents' names), marriages (parties and witnesses), and burials (date and sometimes cause of death or age). Confirmation records are a separate dated event falling years after baptism.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch volume 007936751 (187 browse-only images). Original registers are held by individual congregations or their denominational archives (diocesan archives for Catholic records; denominational headquarters for Lutheran, Reformed, Methodist, and other Protestant bodies).
- **Language:** English and German present in volume 007936751.

### Census records
- **Federal census (county level):** Decennial federal censuses for 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 all fall within the target period. The 1850 Schuylkill County census is available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/ — per external_links_search) and on FamilySearch (confirmed in existing project log entries log_001/log_002). No separate Schuylkill-specific FamilySearch collections for 1840, 1860, 1870, or 1880 were returned by tools; these exist but were not in the 2 curated external links returned for the county.
- **Federal mortality schedules:** Mortality schedules accompanying the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses record deaths in the year preceding the enumeration. These are a primary substitute for missing death records in this period.
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census collection was returned by any tool.
- **Access:** 1850 — indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Other decennial years: indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry but not returned as curated county-specific links.

### Probate and court records
- **FamilySearch collection 1999196** ("Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994"): 0 records indexed, 3,200,560 images — **browse-only** at county level. Covers Schuylkill County within the full target period. Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196
- **FamilySearch volume 007936749** (Probate Records 1851–1930, 412 images): 0% indexed, no full-text search — **browse-only**. Covers 1851–1880 within the target period.
- **Types:** Wills (testate), administrations and letters of administration (intestate), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, orphans' court records.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Wills survive for those who died testate. Those who died intestate generated administration files and potentially guardianship records for minor heirs. Both series are held in the same probate/orphans' court records.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse (original records). FamilySearch volumes and collection 1999196 provide digitized browse-only images.

### Land records
- **FamilySearch volume 007936752** (Deed Records 1815–1900, 543 images): **22% name-indexed with images** — the only partially indexed Schuylkill County digitized volume in this tool run. The remaining 78% of images must be browsed. Access via FamilySearch image group 007936752.
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state. Land grants originate with the Commonwealth; no federal Bureau of Land Management (BLM GLO) records apply.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, mortgages. Additional types (tax records, patents, warrants) may exist at the Pennsylvania State Archives and county courthouse but were not returned as distinct digitized collections in this survey.
- **Where held:** County Recorder of Deeds, Schuylkill County courthouse (original deed books). FamilySearch volume 007936752 provides partial online access.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865); post-war pension activity through 1880.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (pre-Civil War conflicts), Civil War draft registration records (1863–1865).
- **Where held:** Federal military service and pension records are at NARA (federal level). The NARA Philadelphia regional archives serves Pennsylvania. Civil War pension records are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry/Fold3. No military records collection specific to Schuylkill County was returned by volume_search or collections_search.
- **State-level:** Pennsylvania State Archives holds adjutant general records and state-level military enrollments. Not returned as a specific digitized collection in this survey.

### Naturalization records
- **FamilySearch volume 007936750** (Naturalization Records 1849–1915, 298 images): 0% name-indexed, no full-text search — **browse-only** at county level. Covers 1849–1880 within the target period.
- **Important:** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record — county court, state court, or federal district court. The county volume 007936750 covers county-court filings. Declarations of intention and petitions filed in the federal district court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) are at NARA Philadelphia and Ancestry. Search both tiers.
- **Content:** Naturalization papers typically record the immigrant's name, birth country, arrival date, and witnesses. Post-1906 records are more detailed.

### Cemetery records
- No cemetery collections for Schuylkill County were returned by collections_search, volume_search, or external_links_search.
- **Online indexes:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves (billiongraves.com) are major indexes of headstone inscriptions for Pennsylvania cemeteries; neither appeared as a curated external link in the 2 results returned for Schuylkill County. Consult them directly.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are held by individual cemeteries or church congregations.

### Newspaper records
- No newspaper collections for Schuylkill County were returned by any tool in this survey.
- Local papers published in and around the county seat and the mining towns during 1840–1880 may be held at the Pennsylvania State Library (Harrisburg), local public libraries, and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/). Obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices (estate settlements, property sales) can supply information found nowhere else.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Naturalization records** (volume 007936750, see above) represent the primary inland-generated immigration documentation for 1849–1915.
- **Passenger lists (federal level):** Arrival manifests are federal records at NARA. No passenger list collection specific to Schuylkill County was returned; Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for immigrants settling in eastern Pennsylvania. Indexed passenger lists are on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family that immigrated together, examine the full manifest for all household members — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Border crossing and alien registration:** These postdate or fall outside the 1840–1880 period for most purposes.

### Tax records
- **Ancestry external link** (from external_links_search): "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) — this collection predates the 1840–1880 target period and is background context only.
- No tax record collection overlapping 1840–1880 was returned for Schuylkill County. County property tax and personal property tax records, where they survive, are held at the county courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives. Tax records can substitute for missing census years.

### Other record types
- **County court minutes:** County court minute books record county business beyond individual lawsuits: road maintenance assignments, poor relief, and other matters that name ordinary residents who appear in no other record series. Held at the county courthouse; not returned as a distinct online collection.
- **City directories:** For the county seat and larger mining towns, city/county directories may exist from the 1850s–1880s, placing individuals at specific addresses between census years. Not returned as a collection in this survey.
- **Local and county histories:** Published county histories (many from the late 19th century) frequently reprint early records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. These are held at the Pennsylvania State Library, local libraries, and may be searchable via WorldCat.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Deed Records 1815–1900 (vol. 007936752, 22% indexed, 543 images); Probate Records 1851–1930 (vol. 007936749, browse-only, 412 images); Naturalization Records 1849–1915 (vol. 007936750, browse-only, 298 images); Church Records 1842–1895 (vol. 007936751, browse-only, 187 images, incl. German); Marriage Records 1870–1910 (vol. 007936753, browse-only, 94 images); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (coll. 1999196, browse-only, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (coll. 1571957, 312,045 indexed records + images); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (coll. 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 United States Federal Census – Schuylkill County (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 5 digitized volumes for Schuylkill County in the 1840–1880 period; no nextPageToken was present and totalResults = 5, so this is the complete FamilySearch digitized volume set. All 5 volumes are detailed above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, PA | Deed books, probate files (wills, administrations), court records, naturalization records, county marriage licenses | In-person or mail/written request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg, PA | State-level records; military enrollment records; some county record copies; Pennsylvania death certificates from 1906 | In-person or online finding aids (www.phmc.pa.gov) |
| NARA Philadelphia Regional Archives | Federal census originals (pre-digitization); military service and pension records; federal district court naturalizations; passenger lists | In-person appointment or Ancestry/Fold3 subscription for digitized holdings |
| Individual churches / denominational archives | Original church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations) | Contact individual congregation or diocesan/denominational archive |
| Pennsylvania State Library, Harrisburg, PA | Published county histories, local newspapers, city directories, genealogical compilations | In-person or interlibrary loan |

The following record types exist or are expected to exist for the period but were not returned as indexed online collections:

- **Birth records (1840–1880):** No civil birth registration collection for this period was returned. Church baptismal registers (browse-only volume 007936751) are the primary alternative.
- **Death records (1840–1880):** No civil death registration collection for this period was returned. State death certificates begin no earlier than 1906 (collection 2255317). Federal census mortality schedules (1850–1880) partially compensate.
- **Federal census years 1840, 1860, 1870, 1880:** Not in the 2 curated Schuylkill-specific external links returned. These exist and are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry but were not specifically curated.
- **Cemetery and sexton records:** No collection returned.
- **Newspaper records:** No collection returned.
- **Tax records (1840–1880):** No collection for this period returned. Physical records may survive at the county courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **County court records (beyond probate and naturalization):** No distinct collection returned; may partially overlap with browse-only probate images.
- **City/county directories:** Not returned as a collection. May exist for Pottsville and larger towns at the Pennsylvania State Library.

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey specifically identified destroyed or lost record sets for Schuylkill County. The FamilySearch Wiki pages returned only generic content and named no courthouse fires or other losses for this county. The absence of indexed vital records for 1840–1880 reflects a coverage gap (no statewide registration in that period at birth/death level) rather than a confirmed loss. The fate of any specific record set should be confirmed with the Schuylkill County courthouse and the Pennsylvania State Archives before concluding records are lost.

- **No statewide vital registration for births or deaths in 1840–1880:** Collection 2255317 (Death Certificates) begins 1906; no birth certificate collection for this period was returned. output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

**Billy** is a civil and Church of Ireland ecclesiastical parish in the **barony of Cary**, County Antrim, on the north Antrim coast. Bushmills lies within its bounds. The relevant religious dioceses are:
- **Church of Ireland:** Diocese of Connor (part of the united Diocese of Down and Connor)
- **Roman Catholic:** Diocese of Down and Connor

The county became part of **Northern Ireland** in 1922, which is critical for understanding record custody. The **1922 fire at the Four Courts in Dublin** destroyed the Public Record Office, causing catastrophic losses to centrally-held Irish records — but records held at PRONI, in parish vestries, or in denominational custody were unaffected.

The religious composition of north Antrim in this period was: Church of Ireland and Presbyterian (combined ~60% in 1861, reflecting heavy Scottish Plantation settlement), with Catholics (~40%) a minority.

---

## The Most Important Warning for This Period

**Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths did not begin until 1 January 1864** (non-Catholic marriages only from 1845). For the bulk of 1780–1870, **church registers are the only institutional record** of vital events. There are no civil records before those dates.

---

## Church Records (Primary Source, 1780–1870)

### Church of Ireland (Anglican/Episcopal)

The FamilySearch Wiki states: *"Church of Ireland Records began in 1536, but two-thirds were destroyed in 1922."* However, many registers were **never deposited in Dublin** — they remained in vestries or diocesan custody and survived. County Antrim registers are particularly well represented at PRONI.

**Whether Billy parish CoI registers survive — and from what date — must be confirmed by consulting:**

1. **PRONI Guide to Church Records** (definitive for NI): https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf
2. **RCB Library parish register list** (CoI registers for all Ireland): https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf
3. **PRONI digitised church records**: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni

**Physical access — RCB Library** (holds surviving CoI registers for all Ireland including Connor diocese):
> Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14 | library@ireland.anglican.org | +353 (0)1 492 3979
> Research enquiries: https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy

**FindMyPast (subscription)** — Ffolliott Collection covers some CoI baptisms, marriages, and burials as a name index.

### Presbyterian

Given the heavy Scottish Presbyterian settlement in the Cary barony, Presbyterian registers are a **co-equal primary source** alongside CoI. The PRONI Guide to Church Records covers Presbyterian congregations as well. FindMyPast's Non-Conformist collections (Births/Baptisms, Marriages, Burials) index Presbyterian records. Average register start date: ~1830.

### Roman Catholic

Most rural Catholic parishes in Ulster did not begin keeping registers until **Catholic Emancipation in 1828**. For the 1780–1828 gap, no Catholic register is likely to exist for this area. Coverage:
- **National Library of Ireland** (free, images): https://registers.nli.ie/ — the best free source for pre-1880 Catholic registers
- **Ancestry** (subscription): Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655–1915

**Language:** CoI and Presbyterian registers in English; occasional Latin in early CoI records.

---

## Census Substitutes (Critical for 1780–1870)

The 1821–1871 Irish censuses are almost entirely lost (1861 and 1871 deliberately pulped; 1821–1851 destroyed in 1922). The two essential substitutes are:

| Record | Dates | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tithe Applotment Books** | 1823–1837 | Lists heads of household by townland; covers all denominations | Free — nationalarchives.ie; also on Ancestry |
| **Griffith's Primary Valuation** | c.1860s for Antrim | Comprehensive list of all occupiers of land and buildings | Free — https://www.askaboutireland.ie/ |

Together these two surveys provide near-complete coverage of heads of household across the 1820s–1860s.

---

## Civil Registration (End of Period Only)

| Record type | Start date | Where held |
|---|---|---|
| All births, marriages, deaths | 1 January 1864 | GRONI, Belfast |
| Non-Catholic marriages only | 1 April 1845 | GRONI, Belfast |

**GRONI:** Oxford House, 49–55 Chichester Street, Belfast BT1 4HL. Indexes for County Antrim are not on IrishGenealogy.ie — use GRONI's own GRO Online service.

---

## Marriage License Bonds (Free, Searchable Online)

**Ireland, Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes, 1623–1866** (FamilySearch, free):
https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3460239

This covers Church of Ireland marriage licenses including the Diocese of Connor — an excellent free name-indexed resource for the entire target window before civil registration.

---

## Probate Records

Pre-1858 Irish probate (handled through church courts) was largely **destroyed in 1922**. Surviving substitutes:
- **Betham, Crossle, and Thrift Genealogical Abstracts** (FindMyPast, subscription) — pre-fire transcriptions of wills, marriages, and pedigree materials
- **Ireland, Indexes to Wills, 1591–1866** (Ancestry, subscription): https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/62077/
- Post-1858 original wills at **PRONI** (for Northern Ireland district)

---

## Land Records

- **Registry of Deeds** (from 1708): Property transactions; index searchable online; physical deeds in Dublin
- **Poor Law — Ballycastle Union**: PRONI holds Board of Guardians minute books and relief records, especially important for the Famine years (1845–1852)

---

## Newspapers

| Paper | Dates | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Belfast Newsletter | From 1737 | British Newspaper Archive (subscription); Linen Hall Library, Belfast (microfilm) |
| Coleraine Chronicle | From 1844 | British Newspaper Archive (subscription) |

Both carried marriage notices, death notices, and estate announcements for north Antrim.

---

## Emigration Records

North Antrim had substantial emigration to America and Scotland throughout this period (and especially during the Famine). Primary departure ports: **Larne, Belfast, Londonderry**. US arrival passenger lists are indexed free on FamilySearch and via Ancestry. The **Ulster Historical Foundation** (ancestryireland.com) specializes in Ulster emigration research.

---

## Other Records Worth Searching

- **National School registers** (from c.1831): Record child ages and parent names; held at PRONI
- **Catholic Qualification & Convert Rolls, 1701–1845** (FamilySearch, free): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3499248 — persons conforming to CoI to obtain legal rights
- **Vestry minute books**: Church business and poor relief; held at PRONI or local parishes
- **Military records**: British Army pension and service records at The National Archives (UK), Kew; county militia records at PRONI and NAI

---

## Primary Physical Repository

**Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)**
2 Titanic Boulevard, Belfast BT3 9HQ
Tel: 028 9053 4800 | proni@communities-ni.gov.uk
Online catalogue: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni

PRONI is the single most important repository for Billy parish research: it holds CoI and Presbyterian church registers (microfilm and originals), civil registration indexes, census fragments, wills, land records, Poor Law records, and school registers — all in one place.

---

## Key Known Gaps & Losses

- **Two-thirds of CoI registers** were destroyed in the 1922 fire — whether Billy's specifically survived must be confirmed via PRONI/RCB Library
- **No census records** for 1821–1871 (use Tithe Applotment + Griffith's as substitutes)
- **No civil registration** before 1864 (non-Catholic marriages from 1845)
- **No Catholic registers** in rural north Antrim before ~1828
- **Bulk of pre-1858 probate records** lost in 1922 (abstracts survive on FindMyPast)

---

## Recommended First Steps

1. **Download the PRONI Guide to Church Records** and look up Billy parish — this will tell you definitively which registers survive and from what date, answering your Church of Ireland question.
2. **Check the RCB Library register list** for the same information from the CoI side.
3. **Search the FamilySearch Marriage License Bonds index** (free, linked above) for any family surnames of interest.
4. **Search Griffith's Valuation** at askaboutireland.ie to place the family in a specific townland, then search the Tithe Applotment Books for the same townland a generation earlier.
5. **Check the NLI Catholic registers** at registers.nli.ie for any Catholic-side relatives.
6. For wider research, search the **adjoining parishes** (Dunluce, Ballymoney, Armoy, Ramoan, Coleraine) in case the family lived near a parish boundary.
