entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** One of the original Thirteen Colonies; a royal colony from the early 1600s; declared a Commonwealth in 1776; admitted to the Union in 1788
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital through 1780), then Richmond (state capital from 1780 onward)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (pre-1776); independent Commonwealth of Virginia (post-1776)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place tools for this specific period. Virginia was one of the most populous colonies.
- **Economy:** Tobacco agriculture dominated tidewater counties; wheat farming expanded in the Piedmont and Shenandoah Valley; iron manufacturing, maritime trade, and frontier settlement were active
- **Ethnic composition:** English majority in tidewater counties; Scots-Irish and German settlers concentrated in the Shenandoah Valley and Piedmont; enslaved Africans constituting a large share of the population; some Native American communities on the western frontier
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (Church of England), the established church until the Revolution; Presbyterian congregations in the Piedmont and Shenandoah Valley; rapidly growing Baptist and Methodist congregations; Quaker meetings in scattered areas
- **Key historical events:** Virginia contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony (per Wikipedia summary). Major engagements were fought on Virginia soil; the war ended with the British surrender at Yorktown, Virginia, in October 1781. Virginia also administered vast western territories (present-day Kentucky and West Virginia) during this period.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia in 1775-1783 encompassed far more territory than the modern state. It included all of present-day West Virginia and the area that became Kentucky (formed as Kentucky County, Virginia in 1776; became a separate state in 1792).
- Virginia also claimed the Northwest Territory (present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin), which it ceded to the federal government in 1784.
- Ancestors living in what is now West Virginia or Kentucky in 1775-1783 will have their records in Virginia county series.
- Virginia's county structure was expanding during this period; new counties were carved regularly from existing ones. Always verify which county a place belonged to at the exact event date before searching.

## Available record types

Note on jurisdictional level: Virginia maintained county-level record-keeping throughout this period. Records are created and filed by county, not statewide. Identifying the county where a family lived is a prerequisite for most searches.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content for this survey and did not state a Virginia-specific civil registration start date. Virginia had no statewide civil registration system during 1775-1783. No civil birth or death certificates were issued at any level.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage bonds and marriage licenses survive from the 1700s in many Virginia counties; these are the closest analog to civil vital registration during this period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285); Library of Virginia; individual county courthouses
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration at any level during 1775-1783
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the primary source for births (as baptisms) and deaths (as burials) — see Church Records below

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican (Church of England / Protestant Episcopal after the Revolution) was the established church and kept the most systematic registers; Presbyterian congregations in the Piedmont and Shenandoah Valley; Baptist and Methodist meetings (records more scattered); Quaker monthly meetings
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; vestry books (which also recorded poor relief, apprenticeship bindings, and levy assessments naming ordinary residents)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230); Episcopal Diocesan archives; Presbyterian Church USA archives; Library of Virginia
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814, per the FamilySearch Wiki page "Virginia Military Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The first surviving Virginia federal census is 1800.
- **State enumeration substitute:** Virginia county tax lists from 1782 onward are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census, per the same FamilySearch Wiki source. FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Virginia state enumerations and tax lists 1782-1799 (DGS 005301449, 87 images); this volume is **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — it can be searched by text string but browsing requires going image by image.
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianships, administrator bonds, letters of administration — all at the county level. County court order books record road assignments, poor relief, oaths of loyalty, and local assessments that name ordinary residents who never appear in any other series.
- **Date range:** Virginia county courts operated from the colonial period; probate records survive in many counties from the mid-1700s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567). FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Augusta County court order books 1775-1795 (DGS 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed — **indexed + images** for that county). Original records at individual county courthouses; many transferred to the Library of Virginia.
- **Wartime note:** Men who died in military service often had estates probated during or immediately after the war; wartime probate records may name widows, minor children, and sureties and can establish family relationships

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds; Virginia is a state-land state (not a federal public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Virginia State Land Office held authority for colonial grants and post-independence patents. The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Land and Property page returned only generic content and did not identify the specific office for this period. Post-Revolution bounty land grants for military service were administered separately (see Military Records below).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records, military bounty land warrants
- **Date range:** Colonial grants survive from the 1600s; county deed books from the 1700s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285); Library of Virginia for original patents; county courthouses for deed books

### Military records
This is the primary record class for the stated research focus.

- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War, 1775-1783
- **Record types:**
  - **Continental Line service records and muster rolls:** At the National Archives, Record Group 93, per the FamilySearch Wiki "Virginia Military Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
  - **Virginia militia records:** At the Library of Virginia, Richmond, per the same source
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files:** At the National Archives, Record Group 15. These are among the richest genealogical sources for this period — pension applications often include sworn affidavits from veterans or widows naming family members, dates of birth, marriage, and death. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
  - **Virginia State Navy records:** Published; cited in the FamilySearch Wiki
  - **Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (digitized):** FamilySearch has a volume of 341 images covering 1779-1800 (DGS 005301447, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — **browse-only images**, must be examined image by image)
  - **Post-war bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their land claims, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Dedicated FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)
- **Online access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for service and pension records; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds originals

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online cemetery index; coverage of 18th-century burials is uneven — many Revolutionary-era graves are unmarked or in private family burial grounds
- **Physical records:** Anglican vestry books sometimes recorded burials; sexton records for this period are rare. Many burial grounds from this period are undocumented.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia had active colonial and early Revolutionary-era newspapers (Virginia Gazette, published in Williamsburg from 1736, with multiple competing editions during the Revolution). These carried estate notices, marriage announcements, loyalist proclamations, and advertisements relating to military service.
- **Where held:** Chronicling America (Library of Congress digital newspaper archive); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/)
- **Content value:** Estate and probate notices, marriage announcements, military service-related notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant patterns:** Virginia in 1775-1783 received primarily internal migrants (settlers moving into the Shenandoah Valley from Pennsylvania; Scots-Irish and German immigrants arriving via Philadelphia). International migration was disrupted by the war. Loyalists emigrated from Virginia during and after the war.
- **Record types:** Virginia land grant records sometimes note origins; county court order books recorded oaths of allegiance (a wartime loyalty requirement). Passenger lists before 1820 are sparse for any port.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal-era records; Library of Virginia for colonial- and Revolutionary-era arrivals; FamilySearch collection 2134567 (county court records) for loyalty oaths
- **Content note:** When researching families with immigrant origins, examine full manifests for all family members — passenger lists record every person aboard including children.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property tax lists and county land tax lists, created annually at the county level
- **Date range:** Virginia's systematic annual tax list series begins in 1782 (the year the General Assembly established systematic county taxation after the Revolution)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723); Library of Virginia holds originals; many counties' lists microfilmed. DGS 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists 1782-1799, 87 images) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed.
- **Substitute value:** The 1782 tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census. A man who appears on the 1782 list but not on a later year's list may have died, moved, or entered military service; tracking his presence across yearly lists can bracket a death or departure date.

### Other record types
- **Vestry books and overseers of the poor:** Anglican vestries functioned as civil administrative bodies in colonial and early state Virginia; their records name paupers, apprentices, and recipients of poor relief who often appear in no other series. Held primarily at the Library of Virginia and local Episcopal churches.
- **Loyalist and confiscated estates records:** Virginia confiscated the estates of Loyalists who sided with Britain; these records (at the Library of Virginia) name families on both sides of the political divide and can document relationships
- **Oaths of allegiance:** County courts administered loyalty oaths during the Revolution; these appear in court order books (FamilySearch collection 2134567) and name residents who swore allegiance or refused

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, muster rolls | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA | Continental Line service records (RG 93), pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15) | In-person / online request — https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census collection (post-1790 Virginia; 1790 destroyed) | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search above was filtered to Military record types only and returned the complete set of 3 digitized volumes (totalResults: 3, no further pages). Other record types (church, land, probate, court) will have additional digitized volumes not examined here; a complete volume survey would require separate queries per record-type group.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, county court records, land patents, tax lists, vestry books, church records, loyalist estate records | In-person; many records microfilmed and on FamilySearch |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington DC / College Park MD | Continental Line service records (RG 93), pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15) | In-person; online via Fold3 |
| Individual county courthouses | Deed books, will books, marriage bonds, court order books | In-person or mail; many older records transferred to Library of Virginia |
| Episcopal Diocesan archives (Virginia) | Surviving Anglican/Episcopal vestry books and parish registers | Contact the diocese |
| Presbyterian Church USA archives | Presbytery and session records for Virginia congregations | Contact the denomination |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized or indexed online; many require in-person access or correspondence with the Library of Virginia
- Vestry books and overseers of the poor records (primarily at the Library of Virginia) are not comprehensively digitized
- Confiscated loyalist estates records are primarily accessible at the Library of Virginia
- Most Virginia county court order books for 1775-1783 are not fully indexed online (the Augusta County volume on FamilySearch is 61% indexed; other counties' books vary)
- The Revolutionary War land bounty warrant volume on FamilySearch (DGS 005301447) is browse-only — 341 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable

## Known record losses
- The 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814, per the FamilySearch Wiki "Virginia Military Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The 1782 county tax lists are the primary substitute.
- Virginia "burned counties" — localities whose courthouse records were largely destroyed by fire or Civil War damage — are a known research hazard. No tool result in this survey identified specific burned-county losses for the 1775-1783 period, but researchers should verify record survival for their specific county before concluding records do not exist. The Library of Virginia can advise on surviving holdings by county.

## Research tips
- **Start with the pension file, not just the service record.** Pension application files (NARA RG 15, accessible on Fold3) often contain sworn affidavits from the veteran or his widow giving dates and places of birth, marriage, and death, plus names of children. They are far richer genealogically than muster rolls. Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Virginia Military Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Use the 1782 tax lists as your census substitute.** The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed (see above). Annual county personal property tax lists starting in 1782 are available in FamilySearch collection 1456723. Tracking a man's presence across yearly lists can bracket a death, move, or period of military absence.
- **Distinguish Continental Line from militia.** Virginia contributed soldiers to both the Continental Army (NARA RG 93) and the county militia (Library of Virginia). Search both — a man might appear in one record series but not the other.
- **Check the Virginia Military District of Ohio.** Veterans who received bounty land may have surveyed land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio (south-central Ohio) even if they never relocated. Warrant and survey records link a veteran's name to his claimed acreage; per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Identify the specific county first.** Virginia's records are filed at the county level. Determining which county the family lived in during 1775-1783 — and verifying the county's formation date — is a prerequisite before searching any county-level series.
- **Check for Kentucky and West Virginia ancestors.** If an ancestor lived in what is now Kentucky or West Virginia during 1775-1783, their records will be in Virginia county series (Kentucky County, Virginia records; western Virginia county records). Kentucky became a separate state in 1792.
- **Examine vestry books alongside civil court records.** Anglican vestries functioned as civil administrative bodies in Virginia; their records name people who do not appear in secular court records, including recipients of poor relief, apprenticed children, and foundlings.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page for Virginia Military Records** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) is the primary research strategy source returned by this survey — all four wiki_place_page sections returned only generic content rather than Virginia-specific guidance. Use the direct wiki URL for jurisdiction-specific strategy.

- **What exists:** County-level marriage bonds and marriage licenses survive from the 1700s in many Virginia counties; these are the closest analog to civil vital registration during this period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285); Library of Virginia; individual county courthouses
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration at any level during 1775-1783
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the primary source for births (as baptisms) and deaths (as burials) — see Church Records below

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican (Church of England / Protestant Episcopal after the Revolution) was the established church and kept the most systematic registers; Presbyterian congregations in the Piedmont and Shenandoah Valley; Baptist and Methodist meetings (records more scattered); Quaker monthly meetings
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; vestry books (which also recorded poor relief, apprenticeship bindings, and levy assessments naming ordinary residents)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230); Episcopal Diocesan archives; Presbyterian Church USA archives; Library of Virginia
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814, per the FamilySearch Wiki page "Virginia Military Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The first surviving Virginia federal census is 1800.
- **State enumeration substitute:** Virginia county tax lists from 1782 onward are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census, per the same FamilySearch Wiki source. FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Virginia state enumerations and tax lists 1782-1799 (DGS 005301449, 87 images); this volume is **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — it can be searched by text string but browsing requires going image by image.
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianships, administrator bonds, letters of administration — all at the county level. County court order books record road assignments, poor relief, oaths of loyalty, and local assessments that name ordinary residents who never appear in any other series.
- **Date range:** Virginia county courts operated from the colonial period; probate records survive in many counties from the mid-1700s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567). FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Augusta County court order books 1775-1795 (DGS 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed — **indexed + images** for that county). Original records at individual county courthouses; many transferred to the Library of Virginia.
- **Wartime note:** Men who died in military service often had estates probated during or immediately after the war; wartime probate records may name widows, minor children, and sureties and can establish family relationships

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds; Virginia is a state-land state (not a federal public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Virginia State Land Office held authority for colonial grants and post-independence patents. The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Land and Property page returned only generic content and did not identify the specific office for this period. Post-Revolution bounty land grants for military service were administered separately (see Military Records below).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records, military bounty land warrants
- **Date range:** Colonial grants survive from the 1600s; county deed books from the 1700s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285); Library of Virginia for original patents; county courthouses for deed books

### Military records
This is the primary record class for the stated research focus.

- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War, 1775-1783
- **Record types:**
  - **Continental Line service records and muster rolls:** At the National Archives, Record Group 93, per the FamilySearch Wiki "Virginia Military Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
  - **Virginia militia records:** At the Library of Virginia, Richmond, per the same source
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files:** At the National Archives, Record Group 15. These are among the richest genealogical sources for this period — pension applications often include sworn affidavits from veterans or widows naming family members, dates of birth, marriage, and death. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
  - **Virginia State Navy records:** Published; cited in the FamilySearch Wiki
  - **Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (digitized):** FamilySearch has a volume of 341 images covering 1779-1800 (DGS 005301447, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — **browse-only images**, must be examined image by image)
  - **Post-war bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their land claims, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Dedicated FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)
- **Online access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for service and pension records; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds originals

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online cemetery index; coverage of 18th-century burials is uneven — many Revolutionary-era graves are unmarked or in private family burial grounds
- **Physical records:** Anglican vestry books sometimes recorded burials; sexton records for this period are rare. Many burial grounds from this period are undocumented.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia had active colonial and early Revolutionary-era newspapers (Virginia Gazette, published in Williamsburg from 1736, with multiple competing editions during the Revolution). These carried estate notices, marriage announcements, loyalist proclamations, and advertisements relating to military service.
- **Where held:** Chronicling America (Library of Congress digital newspaper archive); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/)
- **Content value:** Estate and probate notices, marriage announcements, military service-related notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant patterns:** Virginia in 1775-1783 received primarily internal migrants (settlers moving into the Shenandoah Valley from Pennsylvania; Scots-Irish and German immigrants arriving via Philadelphia). International migration was disrupted by the war. Loyalists emigrated from Virginia during and after the war.
- **Record types:** Virginia land grant records sometimes note origins; county court order books recorded oaths of allegiance (a wartime loyalty requirement). Passenger lists before 1820 are sparse for any port.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal-era records; Library of Virginia for colonial- and Revolutionary-era arrivals; FamilySearch collection 2134567 (county court records) for loyalty oaths
- **Content note:** When researching families with immigrant origins, examine full manifests for all family members — passenger lists record every person aboard including children.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property tax lists and county land tax lists, created annually at the county level
- **Date range:** Virginia's systematic annual tax list series begins in 1782 (the year the General Assembly established systematic county taxation after the Revolution)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723); Library of Virginia holds originals; many counties' lists microfilmed. DGS 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists 1782-1799, 87 images) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed.
- **Substitute value:** The 1782 tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census. A man who appears on the 1782 list but not on a later year's list may have died, moved, or entered military service; tracking his presence across yearly lists can bracket a death or departure date.

### Other record types
- **Vestry books and overseers of the poor:** Anglican vestries functioned as civil administrative bodies in colonial and early state Virginia; their records name paupers, apprentices, and recipients of poor relief who often appear in no other series. Held primarily at the Library of Virginia and local Episcopal churches.
- **Loyalist and confiscated estates records:** Virginia confiscated the estates of Loyalists who sided with Britain; these records (at the Library of Virginia) name families on both sides of the political divide and can document relationships
- **Oaths of allegiance:** County courts administered loyalty oaths during the Revolution; these appear in court order books (FamilySearch collection 2134567) and name residents who swore allegiance or refused

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, muster rolls | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA | Continental Line service records (RG 93), pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15) | In-person / online request — https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census collection (post-1790 Virginia; 1790 destroyed) | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search above was filtered to Military record types only and returned the complete set of 3 digitized volumes (totalResults: 3, no further pages). Other record types (church, land, probate, court) will have additional digitized volumes not examined here; a complete volume survey would require separate queries per record-type group.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, county court records, land patents, tax lists, vestry books, church records, loyalist estate records | In-person; many records microfilmed and on FamilySearch |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington DC / College Park MD | Continental Line service records (RG 93), pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15) | In-person; online via Fold3 |
| Individual county courthouses | Deed books, will books, marriage bonds, court order books | In-person or mail; many older records transferred to Library of Virginia |
| Episcopal Diocesan archives (Virginia) | Surviving Anglican/Episcopal vestry books and parish registers | Contact the diocese |
| Presbyterian Church USA archives | Presbytery and session records for Virginia congregations | Contact the denomination |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized or indexed online; many require in-person access or correspondence with the Library of Virginia
- Vestry books and overseers of the poor records (primarily at the Library of Virginia) are not comprehensively digitized
- Confiscated loyalist estates records are primarily accessible at the Library of Virginia
- Most Virginia county court order books for 1775-1783 are not fully indexed online (the Augusta County volume on FamilySearch is 61% indexed; other counties' books vary)
- The Revolutionary War land bounty warrant volume on FamilySearch (DGS 005301447) is browse-only — 341 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable

## Known record losses
- The 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814, per the FamilySearch Wiki "Virginia Military Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The 1782 county tax lists are the primary substitute.
- Virginia "burned counties" — localities whose courthouse records were largely destroyed by fire or Civil War damage — are a known research hazard. No tool result in this survey identified specific burned-county losses for the 1775-1783 period, but researchers should verify record survival for their specific county before concluding records do not exist. The Library of Virginia can advise on surviving holdings by county.

## Research tips
- **Start with the pension file, not just the service record.** Pension application files (NARA RG 15, accessible on Fold3) often contain sworn affidavits from the veteran or his widow giving dates and places of birth, marriage, and death, plus names of children. They are far richer genealogically than muster rolls. Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Virginia Military Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Use the 1782 tax lists as your census substitute.** The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed (see above). Annual county personal property tax lists starting in 1782 are available in FamilySearch collection 1456723. Tracking a man's presence across yearly lists can bracket a death, move, or period of military absence.
- **Distinguish Continental Line from militia.** Virginia contributed soldiers to both the Continental Army (NARA RG 93) and the county militia (Library of Virginia). Search both — a man might appear in one record series but not the other.
- **Check the Virginia Military District of Ohio.** Veterans who received bounty land may have surveyed land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio (south-central Ohio) even if they never relocated. Warrant and survey records link a veteran's name to his claimed acreage; per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Identify the specific county first.** Virginia's records are filed at the county level. Determining which county the family lived in during 1775-1783 — and verifying the county's formation date — is a prerequisite before searching any county-level series.
- **Check for Kentucky and West Virginia ancestors.** If an ancestor lived in what is now Kentucky or West Virginia during 1775-1783, their records will be in Virginia county series (Kentucky County, Virginia records; western Virginia county records). Kentucky became a separate state in 1792.
- **Examine vestry books alongside civil court records.** Anglican vestries functioned as civil administrative bodies in Virginia; their records name people who do not appear in secular court records, including recipients of poor relief, apprenticed children, and foundlings.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page for Virginia Military Records** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) is the primary research strategy source returned by this survey — all four wiki_place_page sections returned only generic content rather than Virginia-specific guidance. Use the direct wiki URL for jurisdiction-specific strategy.

Here is what the locality guide found for New Orleans in the early 1800s:

---

**Researching Ancestors in New Orleans, Early 1800s**

Researching ancestors in New Orleans during the early 1800s means working in one of the most disaster-shaped archival landscapes in the United States.

### What Survived the Fires

Devastating fires in **1788 and 1794** destroyed much of colonial New Orleans and many records, but significant material survived:

- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, with gaps from the fires) remain the primary vital records source for the period, since Louisiana had no comprehensive statewide civil registration during the early 1800s.

### Notarial Records — The Key Substitute for Missing Civil Records

Louisiana's civil-law system (Napoleonic Code, not English common law) made notaries the hub of legal life. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over 30 million pages of acts from 1734. Only a single browse-only volume of 167 images covering 1803–1820 is digitized on FamilySearch — the vast majority requires an in-person or mail request to New Orleans.

### Critical Terminology Warning

Searching for common terms will miss records in Louisiana:
- **"Wills" and "probate"** → search instead for **"successions"**
- **"Guardianship"** → search instead for **"tutorship"**
- All records before 1812 are under **Orleans Territory**, held at the **Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge**, not at the local courthouse.

### Key Record Sets to Search

| Collection | Coverage | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Church Records (FamilySearch) | 1718–1925 | FamilySearch |
| St. Louis Cathedral Registers | 1731–present (gaps) | Diocese / FamilySearch |
| Probate/Successions | 1756–1984 | FamilySearch |
| Federal Census Records | 1810–1850 | FamilySearch / Ancestry |
| Notarial Archives | 1734–present | New Orleans Notarial Archives (mostly undigitized) |

### Next Steps

A research plan targeting your specific ancestors would draw on these surviving series — especially the sacramental registers, the FamilySearch Louisiana Church Records and Successions collections, and the notarial archives for any property or family-contract records.

Louisiana is a civil-law state (Napoleonic Code) — search for 'successions' not 'wills/probate', 'tutorships' not 'guardianships', and 'interdictions' for court-ordered incompetency. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)

Notarial acts are central to Louisiana genealogy: the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734; the single FamilySearch volume (004990115, 1803-1820, 167 images) must be browsed image by image in French and English — it is not name-indexed.

Records created before Louisiana statehood (1812) are filed under Orleans Territory and held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge, not at the Orleans Parish courthouse. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
Louisiana uses 'parishes' not 'counties' as its civil jurisdiction — the correct search term is Orleans Parish, not Orleans County.
Records from the Spanish colonial period (1763-1800) may be in Spanish; records from the French colonial era and early American period may be in French — plan for bilingual records.

New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the early US; if an ancestor arrived here, search NARA and Ancestry passenger lists. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any Louisiana court of record.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded in 1718 by the French. It passed to Spanish control in 1763, briefly reverted to France, and became part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. The Orleans Territory was organized 1803–1812; Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)
- **Civil jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish is Louisiana's civil jurisdiction (equivalent to a county) covering New Orleans. Louisiana uses "parishes" not "counties."
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans serves as the seat of Orleans Parish.

---

Researching ancestors in New Orleans during the early 1800s means working in one of the most disaster-shaped archival landscapes in the United States. Devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of colonial New Orleans and many records, but significant material survived: sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, with gaps from the fires) remain the primary vital records source for the period, since Louisiana had no comprehensive statewide civil registration during the early 1800s. | Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (from 1731, with gaps) | In-person or by request |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) and court records | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Local history, newspapers, maps | In-person |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | Local history, newspapers | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The vast majority of notarial acts: the New Orleans Notarial Archives holds 30 million pages from 1734; only 167 images covering 1803–1820 are on FamilySearch, and those are browse-only.
- Pre-1803 French and Spanish colonial records, except as partially captured in the FamilySearch "Louisiana, Church Records" collection.
- Full sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral beyond what is in FamilySearch collection 1612905.
- Tax records from the territorial and early statehood period.
- Many records relating to enslaved persons and free people of color that exist only in notarial and church archives.

## Known record losses
Per the Wikipedia result (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) and FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters): devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of colonial New Orleans and many of the earliest records. Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings. Despite these losses, the wiki_search result reports that St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive from 1731 (with gaps), notarial records survive at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center from 1734, and Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body) records survive. No tool result pinpoints the destruction of any specific post-1800 record set; empty search results for any particular collection represent a digitization gap, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- Despite the catastrophic fires of 1788 and 1794, significant records survive: St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 with gaps), notarial records, and Cabildo records. Begin research with these surviving series. ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))
- Louisiana is a civil-law state. Use "successions" when searching for probate/will records, "tutorships" for guardianship records, and "interdictions" for court-ordered incompetency filings. ([Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))
- Notarial acts are central to Louisiana genealogy in a way they are not elsewhere in the US. Before searching court records, search the notarial archives — they may document property transfers, family contracts, manumissions, and estate matters. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734. ([New Orleans Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))
- Records created before 1812 (Louisiana statehood) are filed under Orleans Territory and held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge. ([Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))
- Records from the Spanish colonial period (1763–1800) may be in Spanish; records from the French colonial and early American eras may be in French. The single FamilySearch notarial volume (004990115) is in both French and English and must be read in the original languages.
- Louisiana uses "parishes" not "counties" — search for "Orleans Parish," never "Orleans County."
- New Orleans was one of the most active ports of entry in the early US. Search NARA and Ancestry for passenger arrival manifests. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any Louisiana court of record.
- The 1 digitized FamilySearch volume of notarial acts (004990115, covering 1803–1820, 167 images) is browse-only — not name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Budget time for careful page-by-page examination.
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, and Naming Customs all returned only generic fallback content when fetched during this survey. Specific start dates, record levels, and naming conventions for Louisiana were not available from the retrieved pages. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for current detail.
- An empty online search result for early New Orleans records is most likely a digitization gap, not evidence the record does not exist — the New Orleans Notarial Archives alone holds 30 million largely undigitized pages.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**. Here is what the research found:

---

Boston in the 1840s was one of the five main U.S. ports of entry, receiving tens of thousands of Irish immigrants during the Great Famine years. The most important record for tracing arrivals is the **customs passenger list for the Port of Boston** (National Archives Record Group 36), which covers 1820 through 1891 and is available through FamilySearch (collection 1784312) and Ancestry. One digitized volume covering 1840–1850 exists on FamilySearch and is full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed, so it must largely be browsed or searched by document text rather than a standard name index. Critically, 1840s lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not the specific Irish county or townland — so they confirm arrival but rarely give a precise place of origin.

**Catholic parish registers** at the Archdiocese of Boston (especially the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's) are the essential companion source for baptisms, marriages, and burials of arriving families.

The single most distinctive resource for this period is the **Missing Persons notices** published in *The Pilot*, a Boston Irish Catholic newspaper, where newly arrived immigrants advertised for relatives who had come before them. Boston College Burns Library maintains a partially indexed database of these notices.

**Naturalization records** are scattered across any court that operated in any state where the immigrant later settled — not just Massachusetts courts — so a search limited to Boston courts will miss filings made after a move to Pennsylvania or elsewhere.

---

**Recommended next step:** Build a research plan targeting the most specific combination of passenger lists, the 1850 census, and Boston Catholic parish registers to pin down the family before any move inland.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Port of Boston, Massachusetts (1840–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston was founded in 1630 and incorporated as a city in 1822.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston is the county seat of Suffolk County.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this place. Wikipedia notes that by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting rapid immigrant-driven population growth during the Great Famine years.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, commerce, and manufacturing. Boston was one of the five major U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s, receiving tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants. (wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American Protestant majority with a rapidly growing Irish Catholic immigrant community. By 1850, more than a quarter of Boston residents were Irish-born. Immigrants settled concentrated in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods. (Wikipedia tool result)
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (Puritan), Episcopal, and a growing Catholic community served especially by the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's parish. (wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)
- **Key historical events:** The Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) drove mass emigration through the Port of Boston; the period also saw the Mexican-American War (1846–1848), which generated military records for Boston-area men.

## Boundary changes
- Boston remained within Suffolk County throughout the 1840s and 1850s with no boundary changes affecting record custody.
- The place_search_all tool returned no historical boundary change data for this place.
- No boundary split or record-custody transfer is reported by any tool result for this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts Vital Records did not resolve to its specific content in this survey (it returned only the generic Genealogy Records page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records). The FamilySearch Wiki does not state a specific start date or registration level from the sources returned here. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection 2061550) indicates town-level recording extending back to the colonial period; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records for the specific date and level.
- **What exists:** Town-level birth, marriage, and death records in FamilySearch collection 2061550.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550); town clerks' offices hold originals.
- **Gaps:** Newly arrived immigrant families may not appear in civil vital records if events occurred before registration was in practice or if the family quickly moved on from Boston.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — at the Archdiocese of Boston archives and FamilySearch collection 1921657.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's) serving Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward; Congregationalist; Episcopal. (wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Boston archives holds Catholic parish registers. FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) covers the period.
- **Language:** English; Catholic sacramental entries may include Latin.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 (head of household only); 1850 (all household members named, with birthplace recorded — the critical anchor for 1840s arrivals); 1860. Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding the census.
- **State census:** Massachusetts did not take a regular state census during this period; confirm with the Massachusetts State Archives.
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed with images at FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Passenger lists (immigration arrival records) — PRIMARY SOURCE
- **Types:** Customs passenger lists maintained at the Port of Boston (pre-1891); held in NARA Record Group 36. (wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Date range:** 1820–1891, covered by FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection 1784312, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312). Also indexed on Ancestry.
- **Content of 1840s lists:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only — NOT the specific town or village of origin. (wiki_search result)
- **Digitization:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images) covering Boston passenger lists 1840–1850. This volume is 3% name-indexed but is full-text searchable — researchers can search document text for names. It is not fully indexed for record_search; expect to browse or use full-text search tools.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest page for all family members — do not rely on a single index hit.
- **Where held (originals):** National Archives at Boston, Waltham, Massachusetts; NARA Record Group 36. (wiki_search result)

### Naturalization records
- **Critical rule:** Before 1906, any court of record could perform naturalizations. A Boston arrival might have naturalized in Massachusetts courts or in the courts of any subsequent state of residence (e.g., Pennsylvania). Search all.
- **Process in the 1840s:** Declaration of Intention ("first papers") filed upon arrival; Petition for Naturalization ("second papers") filed after the required waiting period.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (collection 1459213, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213).
- **Where held:** NARA (federal courts in Boston); Massachusetts State Archives (state courts); Suffolk County courthouse; and courts in subsequent states of residence.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, equity proceedings at the Suffolk County level. Court minute books may name ordinary residents in road maintenance, poor relief, and other county business.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901).
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Probate Court; Massachusetts State Archives; FamilySearch collection 1678901.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is a state-land state).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, recorded at the county level.
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts Land and Property did not resolve to specific content in this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Land_and_Property directly.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865, just outside the target window but affecting 1840s arrivals).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations at NARA; state adjutant general records at the Massachusetts State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 online (https://www.fold3.com/).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/); BillionGraves.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at Catholic cemeteries; Holy Cross Cemetery (Malden) and St. Augustine's (South Boston) served the Irish Catholic community in this period.

### Newspaper records
- **The Pilot (Boston):** Published Missing Persons notices placed by recently arrived Irish immigrants seeking relatives who had emigrated before them. This is the single most important supplemental newspaper source for 1840s Irish immigration research through Boston. (Wikipedia tool result) Boston College's Burns Library has a partially indexed database of these notices.
- **Other papers:** Boston Daily Atlas, Boston Herald (local news, obituaries, legal notices).
- **Where held:** Boston Public Library (physical and microfilm); Newspapers.com online (https://www.newspapers.com/).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of Boston (primary for this guide). Other Atlantic ports — New York (Castle Garden), Philadelphia, Baltimore — also received Irish immigrants during the same period; search those if no Boston arrival is found.
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists (covered above); declarations of intention; petitions for naturalization.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); FamilySearch collection 1784312; Ancestry.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Boston city property and poll tax records.
- **Where held:** City of Boston Archives; some transcribed by local historical societies.
- **Substitute value:** City tax lists can place an immigrant in Boston in specific years between the 1840 and 1850 census, confirming presence before the 1850 enumeration.

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Boston city directories place a resident at a specific address and occupation year by year between censuses. For immigrants who settled in Boston before moving elsewhere, directory entries can narrow the window of residence. Boston Public Library holds these.
- **Poor relief and almshouse records:** A significant proportion of newly arrived Famine immigrants were destitute. Overseers of the Poor records and almshouse registers at the City of Boston Archives may name individuals not found in other records.
- **Alien registration:** No federal alien registration existed in the 1840s; naturalizations are the primary government record of immigrant status.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Passenger Lists 1820–1891 (1784312); Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (1921657); Naturalization Records 1790–1906 (1459213); Probate Records 1635–1991 (1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | Passenger lists; federal census | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) | Historical newspapers including Boston papers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Federal records: NARA RG 36 (passenger lists); federal court naturalizations | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210) for the Migration/Naturalization/Emigration record-type groups, covering 1840–1850. This is not confirmed to be the complete digitized set; additional volumes may exist under other record-type groups or for adjacent years.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA | NARA RG 36: Port of Boston customs passenger lists; federal court naturalization records | In-person / written request |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | State court naturalization records; vital records; state enumerations | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) for parishes serving Irish immigrants from the 1840s | Contact in advance; access may be restricted |
| Boston Public Library | City directories; Boston newspapers; local history collections; The Pilot | In-person |
| Boston College Burns Library | Indexed database of The Pilot Missing Persons notices | In-person / online (partial) |

This is not confirmed to be the complete digitized set; additional volumes may exist under other record-type groups or for adjacent years.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA | NARA RG 36: Port of Boston customs passenger lists; federal court naturalization records | In-person / written request |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | State court naturalization records; vital records; state enumerations | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) for parishes serving Irish immigrants from the 1840s | Contact in advance; access may be restricted |
| Boston Public Library | City directories; Boston newspapers; local history collections; The Pilot | In-person |
| Boston College Burns Library | Indexed database of The Pilot Missing Persons notices | In-person / online (partial) |
| Suffolk County Probate Court | Probate files from 1636 | In-person / written request |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds | Land deeds and mortgages | In-person / online |
| City of Boston Archives | City tax records; overseers of the poor; almshouse registers | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online
- Complete run of The Pilot Missing Persons notices — Boston College has indexed a portion but not all issues are digitized
- Archdiocese of Boston Catholic parish registers — many are not digitized; in-person or written access required
- Boston city tax records and overseers-of-the-poor records — largely physical only
- Suffolk County court minute books recording routine county business
- City of Boston almshouse and poor relief records

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey states that a specific Boston record set was destroyed or lost for this period. The National Archives at Boston (Waltham) holds the original Port of Boston customs passenger lists per the wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston). Researchers should confirm current NARA holdings before planning a visit.

## Research tips
- **The Pilot Missing Persons notices are the most important supplemental source for 1840s Irish arrivals.** Per the Wikipedia tool result, this Boston Irish Catholic newspaper published notices placed by immigrants seeking family members who had emigrated before them. Boston College Burns Library maintains a partially indexed database. Search this resource before concluding an immigrant cannot be traced.
- **1840s customs passenger lists contain minimal information** — name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin only, not town or village. Per the wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston), to find the specific origin townland or parish, researchers must work backward from later census entries or from church records at the destination.
- **Passenger manifests list all family members including infants.** When researching a family, examine the full manifest page for siblings and parents traveling together, not just the individual's index entry.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record.** A Boston arrival who subsequently moved to Pennsylvania may have naturalized in a Pennsylvania county court. Do not limit the search to Massachusetts courts.
- **The 1850 federal census is the critical anchor.** It is the first census to name all household members and record birthplace. Establish the family group here before searching backward for the passenger list.
- **Search Boston Catholic parish records even for families who moved on quickly.** A family that passed through Boston and settled in Pennsylvania may have had a baptism or marriage recorded at a Boston Catholic parish during a brief stay before relocating.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki place pages for Massachusetts and Boston returned only generic content in this survey.** Consult the following pages directly for more complete guidance: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration.

The region you are researching was called **Indian Territory** in the mid-1800s — a federal designation, not a standard state or territory with county courts and civil registration. The **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) each governed themselves separately, so records are organized by tribal nation rather than by county.

### Key Record Collections

- **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (FamilySearch) — 567,890 records, fully indexed with images; this is the core collection for your target period.
- **Tribal Enrollment Cards for Indian Territory, 1840–1870** (DGS 002298871, FamilySearch) — 940 images, 99% name-indexed, free to access.
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — The landmark enrollment, falling near the end of your period but essential as a gateway: find an ancestor there, then trace backward through earlier rolls.
- **Rejected Dawes Applicant Case Files** (NARA Fort Worth) — Appeal files containing sworn family testimony, often more genealogically detailed than the rolls themselves.
- **"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (FamilySearch collection 1654321) — Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionary records; for the 1830s–1850s before consistent rolls, these are frequently the only sources naming individuals and family relationships.

### Critical Warnings

- Oklahoma had **no civil vital registration** before statehood in 1907.
- **Freedmen** (formerly enslaved tribal members) appear on entirely **separate Freedmen rolls**, not on the blood-quantum tribal rolls — if your ancestor may have been Freedmen, search those specifically.

### Next Steps

Narrow your research to the **specific tribe** your ancestor belonged to, then build a research plan targeting:
1. That tribe's own rolls and council records
2. The eastern origin state's **removal records** (tracking families relocated via the Trail of Tears era)
3. NARA Fort Worth holdings for that tribal nation

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma — Native American Tribal Research (1830–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory was established by the Indian Removal Act of 1830 as a federal designation for land set aside for relocated tribes. Oklahoma Territory was organized in 1890 from the western (unassigned) lands. Both merged to form the State of Oklahoma in 1907.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Indian Territory had no county system during the mid-1800s. Tribal capitals served as administrative centers: Tahlequah (Cherokee Nation), Tishomingo (Chickasaw Nation), Doaksville / later Tuskahoma (Choctaw Nation), Okmulgee (Creek / Muscogee Nation), Wewoka (Seminole Nation).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government (Bureau of Indian Affairs); the Five Civilized Tribes exercised internal self-governance within their respective national boundaries.
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool. Wikipedia confirms that mass relocations under the Indian Removal Act began in 1830, including the Cherokee Trail of Tears (1838–1839) and equivalent forced removals for the Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole nations.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, cattle ranching, small-scale trade; enslaved labor on some tribal lands before the Civil War; cattle drive economy from the 1860s onward.
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole); Freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members); smaller Plains tribes in western portions (Osage, Comanche, Kiowa, others); growing Anglo-American presence from the 1880s onward.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records).
- **Key historical events:** Indian Removal Act (1830); Trail of Tears relocations (1830s–1840s); Five Civilized Tribes divided in Civil War allegiance (1861–1865); Reconstruction treaties (1866); Dawes Commission established (1893); Dawes Rolls compiled (1898–1914); Oklahoma statehood (1907).

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1890:** The entire region was designated Indian Territory — a federal designation without standard territorial civil government. The Five Civilized Tribes governed their own districts internally, each with its own national boundaries.
- **1890:** Oklahoma Territory was organized from the western unassigned lands, introducing standard territorial civil government in the west. Indian Territory remained in the east under tribal governance.
- **1907:** Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged to form the State of Oklahoma. Records created before 1907 in Indian Territory are federal and tribal records held primarily at NARA — not Oklahoma state records.
- Because Indian Territory had no county system during the mid-1800s, records are organized by tribal nation, not by county. Searching requires knowing or discovering the specific tribe first.

## Available record types

Record-keeping in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s was primarily federal (through the BIA) and tribal (through each nation's own government), with no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths. The holding level varies: tribal records are held at the tribe's own archives or at NARA; federal agency records are at NARA.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma state-level civil registration began with statehood in 1907. The collections_search result shows county marriage recording beginning around 1890 in Oklahoma Territory (western portion). For Indian Territory during the mid-1800s, there was no civil vital registration at any level.
- **What exists:** No state or territorial vital records exist for the 1830–1890 target period. Pre-statehood vital events are documented in church/missionary registers, tribal records, and BIA agency records.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Department of Health for post-1907 records; NARA for pre-statehood federal records.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1830–1890 period lacks civil vital registration for Indian Territory. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Oklahoma-specific Vital Records page; the fetch resolved to generic content.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal rolls, annuity payment lists, church and missionary registers, BIA agency correspondence.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries established congregations in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records).
- **Record types:** Registers of converts, school enrollment lists, community membership lists, baptism and burial registers.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321, "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (123,456 records, 61,728 images); denominational archives; NARA.
- **Language:** English (missionaries wrote in English); some materials exist in the Cherokee syllabary for Cherokee Nation records.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1654321).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Federal census schedules did not enumerate Indian Territory in 1830–1850. From 1860 onward, some Indian Territory schedules were included. The 1880 federal census includes Indian Territory; the 1890 census was largely destroyed (see Known Record Losses). The 1900 federal census includes full Indian Territory coverage.
- **Tribal / BIA rolls:** The BIA conducted annual Indian census rolls from 1885 onward. Earlier rolls in the target period include the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852), per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 records, 283,945 images) — directly covers the target period.
- **Access:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch, free).

### Tribal rolls and enrollment records
This is the primary and most distinctive record class for Native American research in this region:
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** The most widely used enrollment records for the Five Civilized Tribes; list name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation. Held at NARA Fort Worth; indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls).
- **Pre-Dawes rolls (mid-1800s focus):** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851); Drennen Roll (1852). Additional rolls exist for each tribe through the 1830s–1890s. The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (1987432) covers this span.
- **Digitized volume:** DGS 002298871 — Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, United States, 1840–1870; 940 images; 99% name-indexed; full-text searchable. Access level: **indexed + images** (FamilySearch).
- **Freedmen rolls:** The Dawes Commission enrolled Freedmen on separate rolls. Search these in parallel when an ancestor may have been enslaved by a tribal member.
- **Rejection and appeal files:** Dawes Commission rejection files at NARA Fort Worth contain family affidavits and testimony — often the richest genealogical documents available for this population.
- **Where held:** NARA Southwest Region (Fort Worth, TX) for Dawes Commission records; FamilySearch and Ancestry for online indexed access.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts handled probate and civil matters within Indian Territory; U.S. Courts for Indian Territory (established by the Curtis Act of 1898) handled cases involving non-citizens.
- **Date range:** Tribal court records vary by tribe's establishment date; U.S. Court records begin 1898.
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth holds U.S. Court for Indian Territory records; tribal archives and Oklahoma Historical Society hold tribal court records.
- **Access:** Primarily physical or microfilm; limited digitization.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory lands were tribal communal lands — not distributed under the federal rectangular survey system until the Dawes allotment process (1898–1907). The BLM General Land Office records do not apply to Indian Territory communal lands.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Dawes Commission administered allotment; allotment records and patents are held at NARA Fort Worth. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Oklahoma-specific Land and Property page.
- **Types:** Allotment applications, allotment patents, tribal land permits, leases, deeds (post-allotment); annuity payment rolls (which function as population registers tied to land rights).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 records, 117,283 images) — indexed + images (FamilySearch, free).
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth; Oklahoma Historical Society; Bureau of Indian Affairs records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Five Civilized Tribes were divided in Civil War allegiance (1861–1865); both Union and Confederate service records exist for tribal members. Some tribal members served in earlier U.S. campaigns.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files at NARA; tribal warrior records in tribal archives; Indian Home Guard records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and Fort Worth); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to service records and pension files.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Tribal cemeteries, mission school cemeteries, and family burial grounds throughout former Indian Territory.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage; Oklahoma Historical Society cemetery surveys.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for the mid-1800s; headstone surveys by local historical societies provide partial coverage.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Cherokee Advocate (published from 1844 in English and Cherokee syllabary) is the most notable; other tribal papers existed.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; Library of Congress Chronicling America project (partial digitization).
- **Content value:** Tribal government announcements, legal notices, obituaries, community news.

### Immigration and removal records
- **Context:** For this population, "immigration" means the forced relocation from eastern states under the Indian Removal Act (1830). Removal records are key documents for tracing families back to their eastern origins.
- **Record types:** Removal muster rolls, emigration pay vouchers, enrollment lists compiled before and during removal.
- **Where held:** NARA; Smithsonian National Anthropological Archives; state archives in the eastern removal states (Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, North Carolina).
- **Content note:** Removal muster rolls list entire family groups including children and the elderly; examine the full roll for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tribal governments collected their own taxes and fees; annuity payment rolls serve as population and property registers tied to federal treaty obligations.
- **Date range:** Varies by tribe; generally available from each tribe's establishment in Indian Territory.
- **Where held:** NARA; tribal archives; Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Substitute value:** Annuity rolls can substitute for missing census coverage in the pre-1880 period.

### Missionary and agency records
