  - DGS 008120443 (Naturalization Records, 1790–1915, 351 images, English/German) — 15% name-indexed; the remainder must be browsed.
- **Pennsylvania Probate Records collection** (FamilySearch 1999196, 1683–1994): 3,200,560 browse-only images; 0 indexed records — must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (original records); FamilySearch has digitized volumes (browse-only); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds some transferred records.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization were filed in any court of record. The Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, the National Archives at Philadelphia (which holds U.S. District Court records), and city courts all hold relevant files. The wiki_search result from the Allegheny County Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records) names the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia as the main repositories.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land grants from the Pennsylvania Land Office, not the federal BLM).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, and tax records held at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds. Pennsylvania land patents held by the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Date range:** County deed records from 1788 onward.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (original deed books); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for colonial-era grants and warrants. The specific FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property did not return place-specific content in this survey.
- **Note:** For working-class mill families, land records are less central than for agricultural populations, but homeownership in Pittsburgh's mill neighborhoods did occur and deeds can confirm residence and family relationships.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861–1865) immediately preceded the target period; many 1870–1900 Pittsburgh residents were veterans. The Spanish-American War (1898) falls at the period's end.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files (at NARA); pension files are especially rich for family data. Civil War draft registration records. Spanish-American War service records.
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA), Washington, D.C. and regional centers. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized military records (subscription). Pennsylvania State Archives holds state-level adjutant general records.
- **Note:** A Civil War pension file for a mill worker who served in the war will name his wife, children, and sometimes his own parents — making pension files among the most information-dense records for this generation.

### Cemetery records
- **Where held:** The Allegheny County area has numerous cemeteries, including Allegheny Cemetery, St. Mary's Cemetery, and many denominational burial grounds. Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides indexed headstone transcriptions for many of these.
- **Sexton records:** Physical sexton registers exist at individual cemeteries and vary in survival.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had multiple daily newspapers in the 1870–1900 period, including the Pittsburgh Gazette, the Pittsburgh Post, and the Pittsburgh Dispatch. These carried death notices, marriage announcements, and — critically for the steel industry — strike coverage naming individual workers.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers are available on Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) and through the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's microfilm holdings.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, labor dispute coverage, legal notices, and immigrants' naturalization announcements all appear in the local press.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most European immigrants arrived through the Port of New York (Ellis Island open from 1892; Castle Garden before that), with some through Philadelphia and Baltimore.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (pre-1892 manifests list fewer details; post-1892 manifests list hometown of origin in Europe, nearest relative in the country of origin, and contact in the U.S.). Naturalization declarations and petitions (filed in Allegheny County or federal courts).
- **Where held:** NARA holds passenger lists; Ancestry and FamilySearch have indexed and digitized many. The National Archives at Philadelphia holds U.S. District Court naturalization records for this region.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members — the family group may be listed across consecutive lines.
- **Note:** The wiki_search result from the Allegheny County Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records) identifies naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia as the main repositories for this region.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County tax records from 1788 onward.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists for years between censuses can confirm where a person lived and provide economic context about their household.

### Occupational and industrial records
This is the category most distinctive to Pittsburgh's late-1800s steel district.
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary. The wiki_search result from the Allegheny County Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) identifies the Senator John Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives as the main repositories for surviving company records.
- **Union membership lists:** Steel workers were organized in the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers (AAISW) during this period. Union records, where they survive, list members by name. The Heinz History Center holds some labor records.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s onward. The wiki_search result from the Allegheny County Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) specifically notes that directories list occupations. Annual directories 1870–1900 identify individuals by name, address, and employer.
- **State factory inspector reports:** The Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics was established in 1872 and published annual reports that sometimes named individual employees in specific plants. These are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.
- **Homestead Strike records (1892):** Court records, newspaper coverage, and labor commission testimony from the 1892 Homestead Strike name hundreds of workers by name. These are held at the Allegheny County courthouse (court records) and are partially available through newspaper archives.

### Online repositories

| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 indexed records); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 index only); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M indexed records); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (15% indexed, browse remainder) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Federal census 1870, 1880, 1900 (indexed + images); passenger lists; naturalization records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Pittsburgh-area historical newspapers 1870–1900 | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery headstone transcriptions | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh | Industrial and immigration records; company employment records; labor union records | In-person; contact the library for finding aids |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives | Steel company and labor records | In-person; inquire directly |
| Allegheny County Courthouse, Pittsburgh | Deeds, probate records, court records, naturalization petitions, marriage licenses | In-person; some records transferred to state archives |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1810s; local history collection | In-person; some materials digitized |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State-level records; Bureau of Industrial Statistics factory inspector reports; land patents; transferred county records | In-person; mail requests available for some record types |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region 3) | U.S. District Court records including naturalization petitions; federal records for Pennsylvania | In-person; online ordering for some record types |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) for parishes that have deposited records | In-person by appointment |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment records for Pittsburgh steel mills (fragmentary; physical only at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives)
- Union membership lists for the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers (fragmentary; physical at Heinz History Center)
- Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics factory inspector reports (physical at Pennsylvania State Archives)
- Allegheny County deed books and property tax lists for 1870–1900 (physical at Allegheny County Courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives; not indexed online as of this survey)
- Pittsburgh city directories for 1870–1900 (physical at Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; not fully digitized or indexed online)
- Individual Catholic parish registers not yet microfilmed or deposited with the diocese
- Sexton records for individual cemeteries

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally by a fire in 1921. Surviving fragments do not include Pennsylvania. For the year 1890, substitute sources are city directories, state and local tax lists, and the 1900 census.
- No tool result in this survey reported destruction of Allegheny County courthouse records. If a specific record set has been confirmed destroyed, the Pennsylvania State Archives or the Heinz History Center can advise.

## Research tips
- **Identify the ethnic parish first.** Pittsburgh's immigrant communities formed ethnically specific Catholic parishes. The wiki_search results from the Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records) state that Catholic parish registers are often the best source for immigrant family data. Knowing whether an ancestor was Polish, Slovak, Croatian, or Italian determines which parish — and therefore which register — to search.
- **Use the federal census as an occupational anchor.** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses list occupation for every individual. A worker enumerated as a 'puddler,' 'roller,' or 'laborer' at a steel mill in a specific Pittsburgh ward can be linked to company and union records at the Heinz History Center. The wiki_search results from the Allegheny County Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) specifically recommend census schedules for this purpose.
- **Layer city directories across census years.** Annual Pittsburgh city directories from the Carnegie Library list occupations and home addresses. Working backward and forward from a census year with directories fills in the years between censuses and can reveal changes in employer or address that signal a move to a different mill or neighborhood.
- **For pre-1906 deaths, go to church records.** Pennsylvania statewide death registration began in 1906 (evidenced by the FamilySearch Death Certificates collection starting that year). For deaths 1870–1905, church burial registers and newspaper death notices are the primary documentary sources.
- **Search for naturalization in multiple courts.** Before 1906, any court of record could naturalize an immigrant. Allegheny County workers may have filed declarations in the Court of Common Pleas, in federal district court, or in city courts. The wiki_search result from the Allegheny County Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records) names the Allegheny County courthouse and National Archives at Philadelphia as the principal repositories.
- **Check the City of Allegheny separately.** The neighboring City of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh, annexed in 1907) was a distinct municipality with its own records through 1906. If your ancestor lived across the river, search Allegheny city records, not Pittsburgh records, for the pre-1907 period.
- **Search adjoining counties for satellite mill towns.** Mill operations extended into Westmoreland County (east), Washington County (southwest), and Beaver County (northwest). Families near those borders may have generated records in those counties. Each county had its own recording system; search them independently.
- **Pension files are rich for Civil War veterans.** Many Pittsburgh steel workers in the 1870–1900 period were Civil War veterans. A pension file names the veteran's wife, children, and sometimes parents — making it one of the most genealogically detailed record types for this generation.

subagents.description: Locality guide for Philadelphia 1793 yellow fever epidemic records

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide produced for your research:

---

## Philadelphia County & City, Pennsylvania — Yellow Fever Epidemic, 1793
*(Survey window: c. 1780–1810)*

### Why Church Registers Are the Starting Point

Pennsylvania had **no civil vital registration in 1793** — statewide death recording did not begin until 1906. That means church burial registers are the **only vital-record source** for the roughly 5,000 people (one-tenth of Philadelphia's population) who died in the epidemic. Fortunately, several distinctive documentary trails supplement them.

---

### Key Records & Repositories

**1. Mathew Carey's Published Pamphlet**
Carey's *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793, with multiple editions) includes named lists of the dead. It is available in digitized form and is often the fastest way to confirm whether an ancestor died in the outbreak.

**2. Committee for the Relief of the Sick and Distressed**
This emergency committee operated Bush Hill hospital and provided aid to victims' families. Its records — relief lists, ledgers, and correspondence — survive at:
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** — Philadelphia, PA
- **Philadelphia City Archives**

These are among the most specific sources for identifying affected families.

**3. Bush Hill Hospital Records**
Records from the makeshift epidemic hospital survive in fragmentary form at HSP and the City Archives.

**4. Church Burial Registers**
Multiple denominations kept burial records. Key congregations with surviving registers include:
- Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal)
- St. Peter's Church
- Philadelphia Monthly Meeting (Quakers) — one Yearly Meeting minutes volume is digitized on FamilySearch but must be browsed image by image (not indexed)
- German Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic, and Presbyterian congregations

Most originals are held at **HSP**, individual churches, or the **Presbyterian Historical Society**.

**5. Federal Censuses — 1790 & 1800**
These bracket the epidemic and can reveal household disappearances. A head of household present in 1790 but absent in 1800 with no other explanation is circumstantial evidence of epidemic death.

**6. Philadelphia Orphans' Court — Guardianship Filings, 1793–1795**
Children orphaned by the epidemic appear in guardianship petitions. These are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and can directly tie a child to a parent killed in 1793.

**7. City Directories & Tax Lists**
Philadelphia directories (published annually from the 1790s) and ward tax lists can show a name disappearing between the 1792 and 1794 volumes — a strong indirect indicator of epidemic death when no church record survives.

**8. Probate Records**
FamilySearch holds browse-only Philadelphia probate images (**collection 1999196**, ~3.2 million images, not yet indexed). Wills and administrations filed in late 1793 and 1794 often name epidemic decedents. Physical research at the **Philadelphia Register of Wills / City Archives** may be needed for systematic access.

**9. FamilySearch Indexed Collections**
FamilySearch holds indexed Philadelphia marriage collections for this period. Use them to establish a pre-epidemic family unit.

---

### Physical Research Is Likely Necessary

For deep investigation of a specific family's experience during the epidemic, on-site research at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** and **Philadelphia City Archives** is strongly recommended. Both institutions hold undigitized manuscript sources — committee records, church vestry minutes, hospital registers — that are not available online.

---

### Recommended Next Step

Use this guide as the foundation for a **targeted research plan**: identify which church your family attended, then prioritize that congregation's burial register, followed by the Committee for Relief records and Orphans' Court guardianship filings for the 1793–1795 window.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, with focus on the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682 as one of Pennsylvania's three original counties. The city of Philadelphia was founded the same year by William Penn.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, making Philadelphia the largest city in the United States and the nation's capital at the time of the epidemic (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). The city proper was smaller than the county; thousands lived in surrounding townships.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port, mercantile trade, shipping, crafts, printing, and early manufacturing. The city hosted the federal government (1790–1800) and was a hub of commerce and immigration.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers (founding population), Germans, Welsh, Scots-Irish, Irish, Swedish (long-established along the Delaware), and a significant free Black population. The epidemic disproportionately impacted poorer neighborhoods.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Quaker (Society of Friends), Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), Dutch Reformed, and others. Each maintained its own registers.
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November): approximately 5,000 deaths — roughly one-tenth of the population. Thousands fled the city. Mayor Matthew Clarkson and physician Benjamin Rush coordinated relief. The city organized the Committee for the Relief of the Sick and Distressed. Bush Hill estate was converted to a public hospital. The epidemic generated a distinctive documentary record with no parallel in other years.

## Boundary Changes

- Philadelphia County and Philadelphia City coexisted as separate jurisdictions within the same territory from 1682 onward. In 1793, the city proper occupied a relatively small grid between the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers; the county encompassed surrounding townships (Northern Liberties, Southwark, Kingsessing, Germantown, etc.).
- The Act of Consolidation (1854) merged city and county into a single unified jurisdiction. Records created before 1854 under city authority versus county authority are held separately and should be searched as distinct record sets.
- For the 1780–1810 period, determine whether an ancestor lived within the city limits or in a surrounding township before deciding which set of administrative records applies.

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had NO statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793. Statewide registration began only in 1906 (FamilySearch wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records). No civil death certificates exist for epidemic victims.
- **What exists for 1780–1810:** No government-issued birth, marriage, or death records. Church registers are the sole vital record source for this period.
- **Where held:** Church archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, denominational archives, FamilySearch microfilm. Many registers have been transcribed and published.
- **Gaps:** Philadelphia's earliest civil registration attempts were scattered and incomplete. For 1793 specifically, the epidemic's disruption to normal record-keeping may have caused gaps even in church registers — some burials occurred before clergy could record them.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (primary), Mathew Carey's published lists of the dead, Committee for Relief records, newspaper death notices, probate filings.

### Epidemic-Specific Records (1793)

These record classes are unique to the 1793 outbreak and are the most direct sources for tracing affected families:

- **Mathew Carey's published account:** "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia" (1793) includes lists of the dead by name. This is a published source available through major libraries and some digitized collections. It is the closest available approximation to a death register for the epidemic period. Per FamilySearch wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793
- **Committee for the Relief of the Sick and Distressed:** This committee kept minutes and relief records naming epidemic victims and their families. Manuscript sources held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives. Per FamilySearch wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** The Bush Hill estate served as the public hospital during the epidemic. Per FamilySearch wiki, these records are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793
- **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's records and accounts:** Detailed administrative records of the city's epidemic response.
- **Benjamin Rush's papers:** Dr. Rush treated hundreds of patients. His papers at the Library Company of Philadelphia and other repositories may name individual patients.

### Church Records

- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal, Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Quaker, Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei), and others. Most established congregations predate 1793.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Church burial registers for August–November 1793 will show a dramatic spike — the epidemic period produces identifiable clusters.
- **Key congregations named in the FamilySearch wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793):**
  - Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal) — registers transcribed and published
  - Gloria Dei / Old Swedes' (Swedish Lutheran) — one of the oldest surviving records in the region
  - Other Philadelphia churches with burial registers covering the epidemic period
- **Where held:** Individual parish archives, denominational archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, and FamilySearch microfilm. Many colonial and early national church registers have been transcribed and published. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (per FamilySearch wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** One volume of Quaker Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group 001188322, covering 1750–1800, 145 images) is available on FamilySearch. It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image. This is minutes, not a membership or burial register.
- **Language:** Most records are in English. German Lutheran and Reformed records may be in German. Swedish records (Gloria Dei) are partly in Swedish and Latin. Researchers must read the original language.

### Census Records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census (first enumeration) and the 1800 census bracket the epidemic and establish household composition before and after. Both are indexed. Philadelphia County is included in both.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a separate state census in this period. No intercensal enumeration is known for 1793–1799.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists (see below) serve as a proxy for census records between federal enumerations.
- **Access:** The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and other platforms.

### Probate and Court Records

- **Types:** Wills, letters testamentary, letters of administration, inventories of estate, guardianships, orphans' court proceedings.
- **Relevance to the epidemic:** The epidemic generated a surge in probate filings in late 1793 and 1794. Persons who died intestate (without a will) left administration filings; persons who made wills under the pressure of illness may have dated wills to the epidemic months. Guardianship petitions were filed for orphaned children — a major byproduct of the epidemic's mortality.
- **Date range:** Philadelphia Orphans' Court and Register of Wills records begin with county formation in 1682.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection ID 1999196, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196). This collection holds 3,200,560 images and is browse-only — 0 records are name-indexed. Researchers must browse images directly.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia Register of Wills / Orphans' Court. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds older series. The Philadelphia City Archives holds supplementary administrative records.

### Land Records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was granted by the Penn proprietors, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land grants and patents were issued by the Penn proprietors (pre-Revolution) and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (post-Revolution). The Pennsylvania State Archives holds patent records.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, ground rents. Ground rent (the Penn family's preferred land-tenure instrument) was common in Philadelphia and generates a distinctive record class.
- **Date range:** Deed books begin with county formation in 1682.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds (county level) for deeds and mortgages; Pennsylvania State Archives for patents and grants. Some deed books have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783), Quasi-War (1798–1800), and War of 1812 (1812–1815) all touch the target period. Philadelphia was the seat of federal government through 1800 and a major military logistics center.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA); Pennsylvania militia records (Pennsylvania State Archives); bounty land warrants; War of 1812 service records and pension files (NARA and Fold3).
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) for federal service records and pension files (https://www.archives.gov/); Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia and pension records; Fold3 for digitized military records (https://www.fold3.com/).

### Cemetery Records

- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Churchyard, St. Peter's Churchyard, Friends (Quaker) burial grounds, and numerous denominational churchyards. The epidemic required rapid burial — some victims were interred in hastily prepared sites.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Philadelphia-area cemeteries. Coverage is uneven for 1793 burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual churches or their archives. Many have been transcribed and published by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Newspaper Records

- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had multiple active newspapers in 1793, including the Federal Gazette, Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, and the General Advertiser. These covered the epidemic extensively, published lists of the dead, ran notices of families who had fled, and carried legal notices of estate settlements.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Library of Congress Chronicling America project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Readex/America's Historical Newspapers for earlier newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, sheriff's sales of decedents' property, and notices of estate administration are genealogically rich for the epidemic period.

### Immigration/Emigration Records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of immigration throughout this period. The Port of Philadelphia (Delaware River) received substantial arrivals.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (pre-1820 lists are fragmentary; the 1820 Steerage Act created more systematic lists), naturalization records (filed in any court of record before 1906), and ship manifests.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Pennsylvania State Archives; Ancestry and FamilySearch for digitized lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax Records

- **Types:** Pennsylvania county tax lists (taxables lists), which name heads of household and list taxable property. These serve as a substitute for census records in non-census years.
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County tax records predate 1793 and continue through the period. They can establish an ancestor's presence in the county before and after the epidemic, and a disappearance from the tax lists after 1793 may indicate death.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; Pennsylvania State Archives. Some series have been microfilmed.
- **Substitute value:** Because no state census exists for the 1793–1799 intercensal period, tax records are the primary tool for locating individuals in those years.

### Other Record Types

- **City directories:** Philadelphia directories were published from the 1780s onward, listing residents by name, occupation, and address. They are invaluable for locating individuals between census years and can reveal when a person disappeared from the city record.
- **Guardianship and orphans' court records:** The epidemic left many children orphaned. The Philadelphia Orphans' Court records naming guardianship appointments in 1793–1795 are a key source for tracing families split by the epidemic.
- **Poor relief records:** The city's Committee for the Relief of the Sick and Distressed distributed aid to epidemic survivors. These records name recipients and may identify widows and orphans not documented elsewhere.
- **Hospital records:** Bush Hill hospital served epidemic patients. Records are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives per the FamilySearch wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (coll. 1999196, 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (coll. 1571957, 312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (coll. 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1790 and 1800 Philadelphia (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records for Philadelphia-area churchyards (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers including Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser and General Advertiser (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including Revolutionary War and War of 1812 pension files for Pennsylvania residents (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including naturalization papers, passenger lists, military service and pension files (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free / fee for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia and the 1780–1810 period (the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes). The collections_search returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections; 3 overlap the target date range and are listed above. One collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, labeled in the tool result as a synthetic test fixture) was excluded as a non-genuine record set. The survey does not represent a complete catalog of all Philadelphia records held by FamilySearch — additional volumes and microfilm may be available through the FamilySearch Catalog.

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Manuscript sources for the 1793 epidemic, Committee for Relief records, Bush Hill hospital records, church registers, city directories, newspapers | In-person / some digitized; contact HSP directly |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Official city records, Committee for Relief records, administrative records of the epidemic response | In-person / mail request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State-level records, patent and land records, Pennsylvania militia records | In-person / some online |
| Philadelphia Register of Wills / Orphans' Court | Probate files, wills, administrations, guardianship records from 1682 onward | In-person / some on FamilySearch |
| Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds | Deed books from 1682 onward, mortgages, ground rent records | In-person / some microfilmed |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes and transcriptions of Philadelphia church records, published family histories | In-person / library access |
| Individual church archives | Original parish registers for Christ Church, Gloria Dei, St. Peter's, and other congregations | Contact each church or diocese |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Benjamin Rush's papers, city directories, early newspapers | In-person |

## Records NOT Online

- Committee for the Relief of the Sick and Distressed minutes and relief distribution records (manuscript, held at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives)
- Bush Hill hospital patient records (manuscript, held at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives)
- Philadelphia Orphans' Court guardianship case files for 1793–1795 (Philadelphia Register of Wills; the FamilySearch probate collection has browse-only images but is not name-indexed for this period)
- Most individual Philadelphia church burial registers for 1793 — many are on FamilySearch microfilm but not indexed; some published transcriptions exist through the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania
- Philadelphia County tax lists for 1793–1799 (Pennsylvania State Archives and Philadelphia City Archives; not digitized or indexed for this period)
- City directories for 1780–1810 (available on microfilm or in research libraries; not in a freely searchable online database for this period)
- Benjamin Rush patient papers and correspondence (Library Company of Philadelphia)

## Known Record Losses

No tool result in this survey states that a specific Philadelphia record set for 1780–1810 was destroyed or lost. The epidemic's disruption to normal record-keeping may have caused gaps in church burial registers for August–November 1793, but the FamilySearch wiki does not document a specific loss. Researchers who find a gap in a particular church register should consult the repository holding the originals before concluding records are lost.

## Research Tips

- **Start with Mathew Carey's 1793 pamphlet and the Committee records.** For epidemic-affected families, these published and manuscript sources are the closest thing to a death register and should be checked before, or alongside, church burial records. Per the FamilySearch wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)), the pamphlet lists names of the dead, and the Committee records name relief recipients and their families.
- **Church burial registers are the vital records.** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration in 1793. For any birth, marriage, or death in this period, the church register is the only governmental-equivalent record. Per the FamilySearch wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)), the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many of these registers, and many colonial registers have been transcribed and published.
- **Check the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses together.** A household present in 1790 but reorganized or absent in 1800 may reflect epidemic mortality. A widow now heading a household, or children enumerated with a different family, can indicate a 1793 death.
- **Orphans' Court filings, 1793–1795, are a targeted search.** Guardianship petitions for children orphaned by the epidemic would have been filed in the Philadelphia Orphans' Court in the months following the outbreak. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (FamilySearch collection 1999196, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) has 3.2 million images covering 1683–1994, but they are browse-only — plan to work through the relevant volumes for 1793–1795.
- **Tax lists fill the gap between 1790 and 1800 censuses.** Because no Pennsylvania state census exists for this period, county tax lists are the primary tool for locating individuals in non-census years. A person who disappears from the tax rolls after 1793 is a candidate for an epidemic death.
- **Search surrounding counties for families who fled.** Wikipedia documents that thousands left Philadelphia during the epidemic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). Bucks County (north), Montgomery County (northwest), Delaware County (southwest), and Chester County (west) were the primary receiving areas. Families who fled may have generated records — boarding notices, church memberships, land transactions — in those jurisdictions during August–November 1793.
- **Ground rent records are distinctive to Philadelphia.** The Penn family's preferred land tenure created a class of ground rent instruments that do not exist in most other jurisdictions. When searching land records, look for ground rent assignments and reversions as well as conventional deeds.
- **City directories name residents by address and occupation.** Philadelphia directories were published from the 1780s onward. They can establish the exact street address of an ancestor, confirm an occupation, and reveal a year of disappearance from the city's population.
- **The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania returned only generic content** during this survey — the constructed-URL wiki_read calls did not resolve to specific Pennsylvania pages. Researchers should consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for additional jurisdiction-specific guidance.

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census (first enumeration) and the 1800 census bracket the epidemic and establish household composition before and after. Both are indexed. Philadelphia County is included in both.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a separate state census in this period. No intercensal enumeration is known for 1793–1799.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists (see below) serve as a proxy for census records between federal enumerations.
- **Access:** The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and other platforms.

### Probate and Court Records

- **Types:** Wills, letters testamentary, letters of administration, inventories of estate, guardianships, orphans' court proceedings.
- **Relevance to the epidemic:** The epidemic generated a surge in probate filings in late 1793 and 1794. Persons who died intestate (without a will) left administration filings; persons who made wills under the pressure of illness may have dated wills to the epidemic months. Guardianship petitions were filed for orphaned children — a major byproduct of the epidemic's mortality.
- **Date range:** Philadelphia Orphans' Court and Register of Wills records begin with county formation in 1682.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection ID 1999196, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196). This collection holds 3,200,560 images and is browse-only — 0 records are name-indexed. Researchers must browse images directly.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia Register of Wills / Orphans' Court. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds older series. The Philadelphia City Archives holds supplementary administrative records.

### Land Records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was granted by the Penn proprietors, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land grants and patents were issued by the Penn proprietors (pre-Revolution) and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (post-Revolution). The Pennsylvania State Archives holds patent records.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, ground rents. Ground rent (the Penn family's preferred land-tenure instrument) was common in Philadelphia and generates a distinctive record class.
- **Date range:** Deed books begin with county formation in 1682.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds (county level) for deeds and mortgages; Pennsylvania State Archives for patents and grants. Some deed books have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783), Quasi-War (1798–1800), and War of 1812 (1812–1815) all touch the target period. Philadelphia was the seat of federal government through 1800 and a major military logistics center.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA); Pennsylvania militia records (Pennsylvania State Archives); bounty land warrants; War of 1812 service records and pension files (NARA and Fold3).
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) for federal service records and pension files (https://www.archives.gov/); Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia and pension records; Fold3 for digitized military records (https://www.fold3.com/).

### Cemetery Records

- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Churchyard, St. Peter's Churchyard, Friends (Quaker) burial grounds, and numerous denominational churchyards. The epidemic required rapid burial — some victims were interred in hastily prepared sites.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Philadelphia-area cemeteries. Coverage is uneven for 1793 burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual churches or their archives. Many have been transcribed and published by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Newspaper Records

- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had multiple active newspapers in 1793, including the Federal Gazette, Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, and the General Advertiser. These covered the epidemic extensively, published lists of the dead, ran notices of families who had fled, and carried legal notices of estate settlements.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Library of Congress Chronicling America project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Readex/America's Historical Newspapers for earlier newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, sheriff's sales of decedents' property, and notices of estate administration are genealogically rich for the epidemic period.

### Immigration/Emigration Records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of immigration throughout this period. The Port of Philadelphia (Delaware River) received substantial arrivals.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (pre-1820 lists are fragmentary; the 1820 Steerage Act created more systematic lists), naturalization records (filed in any court of record before 1906), and ship manifests.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Pennsylvania State Archives; Ancestry and FamilySearch for digitized lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax Records

- **Types:** Pennsylvania county tax lists (taxables lists), which name heads of household and list taxable property. These serve as a substitute for census records in non-census years.
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County tax records predate 1793 and continue through the period. They can establish an ancestor's presence in the county before and after the epidemic, and a disappearance from the tax lists after 1793 may indicate death.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; Pennsylvania State Archives. Some series have been microfilmed.
- **Substitute value:** Because no state census exists for the 1793–1799 intercensal period, tax records are the primary tool for locating individuals in those years.

### Other Record Types

- **City directories:** Philadelphia directories were published from the 1780s onward, listing residents by name, occupation, and address. They are invaluable for locating individuals between census years and can reveal when a person disappeared from the city record.
- **Guardianship and orphans' court records:** The epidemic left many children orphaned. The Philadelphia Orphans' Court records naming guardianship appointments in 1793–1795 are a key source for tracing families split by the epidemic.
- **Poor relief records:** The city's Committee for the Relief of the Sick and Distressed distributed aid to epidemic survivors. These records name recipients and may identify widows and orphans not documented elsewhere.
- **Hospital records:** Bush Hill hospital served epidemic patients. Records are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives per the FamilySearch wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (coll. 1999196, 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (coll. 1571957, 312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (coll. 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1790 and 1800 Philadelphia (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records for Philadelphia-area churchyards (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers including Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser and General Advertiser (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including Revolutionary War and War of 1812 pension files for Pennsylvania residents (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including naturalization papers, passenger lists, military service and pension files (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free / fee for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia and the 1780–1810 period (the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes). The collections_search returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections; 3 overlap the target date range and are listed above. One collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, labeled in the tool result as a synthetic test fixture) was excluded as a non-genuine record set. The survey does not represent a complete catalog of all Philadelphia records held by FamilySearch — additional volumes and microfilm may be available through the FamilySearch Catalog.

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Manuscript sources for the 1793 epidemic, Committee for Relief records, Bush Hill hospital records, church registers, city directories, newspapers | In-person / some digitized; contact HSP directly |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Official city records, Committee for Relief records, administrative records of the epidemic response | In-person / mail request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State-level records, patent and land records, Pennsylvania militia records | In-person / some online |
| Philadelphia Register of Wills / Orphans' Court | Probate files, wills, administrations, guardianship records from 1682 onward | In-person / some on FamilySearch |
| Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds | Deed books from 1682 onward, mortgages, ground rent records | In-person / some microfilmed |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes and transcriptions of Philadelphia church records, published family histories | In-person / library access |
| Individual church archives | Original parish registers for Christ Church, Gloria Dei, St. Peter's, and other congregations | Contact each church or diocese |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Benjamin Rush's papers, city directories, early newspapers | In-person |

## Records NOT Online

- Committee for the Relief of the Sick and Distressed minutes and relief distribution records (manuscript, held at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives)
- Bush Hill hospital patient records (manuscript, held at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives)
- Philadelphia Orphans' Court guardianship case files for 1793–1795 (Philadelphia Register of Wills; the FamilySearch probate collection has browse-only images but is not name-indexed for this period)
- Most individual Philadelphia church burial registers for 1793 — many are on FamilySearch microfilm but not indexed; some published transcriptions exist through the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania
- Philadelphia County tax lists for 1793–1799 (Pennsylvania State Archives and Philadelphia City Archives; not digitized or indexed for this period)
- City directories for 1780–1810 (available on microfilm or in research libraries; not in a freely searchable online database for this period)
- Benjamin Rush patient papers and correspondence (Library Company of Philadelphia)

## Known Record Losses

No tool result in this survey states that a specific Philadelphia record set for 1780–1810 was destroyed or lost. The epidemic's disruption to normal record-keeping may have caused gaps in church burial registers for August–November 1793, but the FamilySearch wiki does not document a specific loss. Researchers who find a gap in a particular church register should consult the repository holding the originals before concluding records are lost.

## Research Tips

- **Start with Mathew Carey's 1793 pamphlet and the Committee records.** For epidemic-affected families, these published and manuscript sources are the closest thing to a death register and should be checked before, or alongside, church burial records. Per the FamilySearch wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)), the pamphlet lists names of the dead, and the Committee records name relief recipients and their families.
- **Church burial registers are the vital records.** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration in 1793. For any birth, marriage, or death in this period, the church register is the only governmental-equivalent record. Per the FamilySearch wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)), the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many of these registers, and many colonial registers have been transcribed and published.
- **Check the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses together.** A household present in 1790 but reorganized or absent in 1800 may reflect epidemic mortality. A widow now heading a household, or children enumerated with a different family, can indicate a 1793 death.
- **Orphans' Court filings, 1793–1795, are a targeted search.** Guardianship petitions for children orphaned by the epidemic would have been filed in the Philadelphia Orphans' Court in the months following the outbreak. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (FamilySearch collection 1999196, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) has 3.2 million images covering 1683–1994, but they are browse-only — plan to work through the relevant volumes for 1793–1795.
- **Tax lists fill the gap between 1790 and 1800 censuses.** Because no Pennsylvania state census exists for this period, county tax lists are the primary tool for locating individuals in non-census years. A person who disappears from the tax rolls after 1793 is a candidate for an epidemic death.
- **Search surrounding counties for families who fled.** Wikipedia documents that thousands left Philadelphia during the epidemic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). Bucks County (north), Montgomery County (northwest), Delaware County (southwest), and Chester County (west) were the primary receiving areas. Families who fled may have generated records — boarding notices, church memberships, land transactions — in those jurisdictions during August–November 1793.
- **Ground rent records are distinctive to Philadelphia.** The Penn family's preferred land tenure created a class of ground rent instruments that do not exist in most other jurisdictions. When searching land records, look for ground rent assignments and reversions as well as conventional deeds.
- **City directories name residents by address and occupation.** Philadelphia directories were published from the 1780s onward. They can establish the exact street address of an ancestor, confirm an occupation, and reveal a year of disappearance from the city's population.
- **The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania returned only generic content** during this survey — the constructed-URL wiki_read calls did not resolve to specific Pennsylvania pages. Researchers should consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for additional jurisdiction-specific guidance.

subagents.description: Locality guide for Chicago Great Fire 1871 records

output.text_response:
Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Chicago in 1871 presents a unique genealogical challenge because the **Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) burned down the Cook County Courthouse and destroyed virtually every official record** the city had created before that date: deed books, probate files, civil birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls are all presumed gone.

## What Survived and Where to Look

**Federal Records (escaped the fire — filed in Washington)**
- **1870 U.S. Federal Census** — the originals were held federally, so they survived intact. This is your primary snapshot of Chicago families just before the fire.

**Substitutes for Destroyed Records**
- **Burnt Record Act (1872) deed-reconstruction series** — partially searchable on FamilySearch; landowners could file affidavits to reconstruct property ownership.
- **City directories (1840s onward)** — held at the **Newberry Library**; can establish residence and occupation year by year.
- **Newspaper archives** — obituaries, fire-victim lists, and relief notices fill gaps left by destroyed civil records.
- **Church registers** — many parishes reconstructed their registers after the fire; some pre-fire originals survived because they were kept at the church, not the courthouse.

**Post-Fire Records (much richer)**
FamilySearch holds indexed collections for Cook County beginning in 1871:
- Birth certificates
- Death records
- Marriage records
- ~285,000 church records spanning 1833–1925

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** | City directories, maps, newspapers, local histories |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Insurance records (substitute for destroyed property docs), fire-relief lists |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD)** | Post-fire court records, naturalization records |
| **FamilySearch** | Indexed Cook County vitals (post-1871), church records, Burnt Record Act deeds |

## Important Caution

Pre-fire **civil vital records do not exist** — searching for them will always return nothing. Church registers and newspapers must fill that gap instead. Any family traced in Chicago before October 1871 will need to rely on the 1870 census, city directories, and surviving church records as the core evidence base.

---

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this survey. Wikipedia records that over 100,000 Chicago residents were left homeless by the October 1871 fire, indicating a large urban population by that date.
- **Economy:** Major trade, manufacturing, and transportation hub. Chicago was a significant railroad and Great Lakes port city by 1871.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant communities are evidenced by the surviving church records spanning multiple denominations; the wiki_search notes Catholic, German, Scandinavian, and other immigrant groups.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Archdiocese of Chicago records confirmed); multiple Protestant denominations including Lutheran, Methodist, and others (FamilySearch Church Records collection 1803978 spans 1833-1925).
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8-10, 1871, burned approximately 3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, and left more than 100,000 residents homeless. It destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and with it the city's pre-fire official records (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).

## Boundary changes
- No boundary change data was returned by place_search_all (it returned an empty result set). The earliest Cook County collection in collections_search begins in 1833, which is consistent with county organization in the early 1830s.
- The 1871 fire is the single most important event defining what records survive: it functions as a hard break in the documentary record, not a boundary change but a loss event that divides pre-fire and post-fire research into two separate strategies.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date (county level):** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories) states that the Cook County Clerk's office holds vital records from 1871 onward. All three civil vital collections returned by collections_search begin in 1871, consistent with that date. The Illinois Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content and did not confirm a statewide registration date.
- **What exists:** Birth Certificates 1871-1940 (1,450,000 records, FamilySearch collection 2024189, indexed); Death Records 1871-1947 (980,000 records, FamilySearch collection 1913456, indexed); Marriage Records 1871-1920 (620,000 records, FamilySearch collection 1756321, indexed). All are county-level records.
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals); FamilySearch (indexed digital collections, free).
- **Gaps:** No civil vital records survive for Chicago before October 1871. Pre-fire birth, marriage, and death events are documented only through church records, newspaper notices, and city directories.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records; city directories; newspaper marriage/obituary notices.

### Church records
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 1803978 — Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833-1925 (285,000 records, indexed + images). The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Survival note:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) states that many church registers were destroyed in the 1871 fire, but parishes that survived or were re-established hold registers from their re-establishment date. The pre-fire portion of collection 1803978 (1833-1871) represents church registers that did survive.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (Catholic); FamilySearch (collection 1803978); individual surviving parish offices.
- **Language:** Varies by denomination. Catholic records are frequently in Latin; German Lutheran records are in German. The Illinois Church Records wiki page returned only generic content and did not confirm language details for specific Chicago denominations.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because the original schedules were filed in Washington, not at the Cook County Courthouse (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The 1850, 1860, and 1870 censuses all predate or coincide with the fire period and survive. The 1880 census postdates the fire.
- **State census:** The Illinois wiki_place_page returned only generic content; no Illinois-specific state census dates were confirmed by a tool result in this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850-1885) record deaths in the year preceding the census and are a potential substitute for missing death records.
- **Access:** Federal census schedules are indexed on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch; free on FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) states that pre-fire probate files were destroyed in the 1871 fire.
- **Digitized volume — Pre-fire reconstructed copies:** FamilySearch DGS 009982110 — Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865-1871, 38 images. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
- **Post-fire:** Court records post-1871 are held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Note:** Naturalization records (pre-1906) could have been filed in any court of record, including Cook County Circuit Court. Post-fire naturalization records are held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal-land state using the rectangular (township-range) survey system.
- **Pre-fire deeds:** Destroyed in the 1871 fire (Wikipedia). The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds.
- **Digitized reconstruction series:** FamilySearch DGS 009982111 — Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871-1880, 112 images, 41% name-indexed (partially searchable by name). The remaining 59% must be browsed image by image. Not full-text searchable.
- **Insurance records substitute:** Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum are described by both Wikipedia and the FamilySearch Wiki as a critical substitute for pre-fire property ownership records.
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (originals post-fire); FamilySearch (DGS 009982111, partially indexed); Chicago History Museum (insurance/property substitute records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861-1865) immediately preceded the fire period. Veterans living in Chicago in 1871 can be traced through pension files and service records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for service records and pension files; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Illinois State Archives for state adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/).
- **Physical records:** The Newberry Library may hold sexton records for older Chicago cemeteries; this was not confirmed by a specific tool result in this survey.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago had active newspapers well before 1871. Historical newspapers are accessible through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Value for fire research:** Newspapers carried fire victim lists, relief-fund recipient lists, missing-persons notices, insurance claim announcements, and property re-registration notices in October-November 1871. These named many individuals not recorded anywhere else in the post-fire chaos.
- **Where held:** Newberry Library (physical newspaper archives); Newspapers.com (digital subscription).

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago's immigrant population arrived primarily through the port of New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island); some arrived via Great Lakes ports.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA; naturalization records (pre-1906 filed in any court of record including Cook County Circuit Court). Declarations of intention, naturalizations, and alien registrations were generated within the city.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry (passenger lists); FamilySearch. Post-fire naturalization records are held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire:** Tax rolls were destroyed in the 1871 fire (Wikipedia).
- **Post-fire:** Cook County tax records were re-established post-fire. The FamilySearch wiki returned only generic content and did not confirm specific post-fire Cook County tax record holdings or dates.
- **Substitute value:** Pre-fire tax records do not survive for Chicago. City directories substitute as the primary source for locating individuals in the years before the fire.

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). These are among the most important pre-fire sources still available.
- **Insurance company records:** Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum — critical for tracing pre-fire property owners (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki).
- **Relief records:** Post-fire relief organizations compiled lists of homeless and displaced residents; these may name families not captured in any other surviving record.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Cook County Birth Certificates 1871-1940 (1,450,000 records, col. 2024189); Death Records 1871-1947 (980,000 records, col. 1913456); Marriage Records 1871-1920 (620,000 records, col. 1756321); Church Records 1833-1925 (285,000 records, col. 1803978); Post-fire Property Re-recordings DGS 009982111 (112 images, 41% indexed); Pre-fire Court Records DGS 009982110 (38 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 for Chicago) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Chicago newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, passenger lists, military records | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Cook County, 1840-1900; both are detailed above and the returned page was the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library, Chicago | City directories (1840s onward), maps, manuscripts, newspapers | In-person / online catalog |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust insurance records, photographs, personal papers | In-person / by appointment |
| Illinois Regional Archives Depository, Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County court and naturalization records post-1871 | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | In-person / written request |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Civil vital records from 1871 onward | In-person / online request |
| Illinois State Archives, Springfield | State-level records, military adjutant general records | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-fire city directories (1840s-1870) are held physically at the Newberry Library; digital availability is not confirmed by a tool result.
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records at the Chicago History Museum are not confirmed to be available online.
- Pre-fire church registers that survived individual parish fires are held at the Archdiocesan Archives and local parishes and are not fully digitized.
- Illinois Regional Archives Depository holdings (post-fire court and naturalization records) are not confirmed to be online by a tool result in this survey.
- Post-fire Cook County tax records were not found in collections_search or volume_search and are likely physical only.

## Known record losses
The Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire) states that the fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) confirms that probate files and many church registers were also destroyed. This is the defining record-loss event for Chicago genealogy: all civil vital records, deed books, probate files, court records, and tax rolls created before October 10, 1871 should be presumed destroyed unless a specific surviving copy is identified.

Substitute sources that partially compensate:
- 1870 federal census (survived; originals in Washington, D.C.)
- City directories 1840s onward (survived; Newberry Library)
- Burnt Record Act (1872) deed reconstruction series (FamilySearch DGS 009982111, 41% indexed; Chicago Title and Trust records at Chicago History Museum)
- Surviving or re-established church registers (Archdiocesan Archives; FamilySearch collection 1803978, 285,000 records, 1833-1925)
- Newspaper missing-persons notices and victim lists from October-November 1871
- Mortality schedules (1850-1885) for the census years before the fire

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1870 census:** This is the last complete population snapshot before the fire and survived because the originals were in Washington. It is the most reliable pre-fire source for placing a Chicago family (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Use city directories in sequence:** Newberry Library holds Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward. Comparing directories from 1870, 1871, and 1872 shows whether a family remained in Chicago after the fire, disappeared, or reappeared at a new address.
- **For property research, use the Burnt Record Act reconstruction series:** FamilySearch DGS 009982111 (1871-1880, 41% indexed) is partially searchable by name. For the 59% not yet indexed, browse image by image. Also check Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum.
- **Treat 1871 as a registration start date, not a gap:** Civil vital registration at Cook County effectively began after the fire. The Birth, Death, and Marriage collections all start at 1871 (collections_search). Do not search for pre-fire civil vital records — none survived.
- **Check October-November 1871 newspapers:** Post-fire newspapers carried victim lists, relief-fund recipient lists, missing-persons notices, and property re-registration announcements. These name many individuals not recorded anywhere else. Access via Newspapers.com and the Newberry Library.
- **For Catholic families:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. Many parishes kept registers that survived or were reconstructed shortly after the fire. Contact the Archives directly.
- **For pre-fire court and probate records:** The only digitized pre-fire court material is FamilySearch DGS 009982110 — 38 images of reconstructed copies, 0% indexed, browse-only. Probate files from before the fire should be presumed lost per the FamilySearch Wiki.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Cook County Illinois Genealogy** are the most current curated guide to this jurisdiction — consult them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy for updates beyond what this survey captured.

- City directories 1840s onward (survived; Newberry Library)
- Burnt Record Act (1872) deed reconstruction series (FamilySearch DGS 009982111, 41% indexed; Chicago Title and Trust records at Chicago History Museum)
- Surviving or re-established church registers (Archdiocesan Archives; FamilySearch collection 1803978, 285,000 records, 1833-1925)
- Newspaper missing-persons notices and victim lists from October-November 1871
- Mortality schedules (1850-1885) for the census years before the fire

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1870 census:** This is the last complete population snapshot before the fire and survived because the originals were in Washington. It is the most reliable pre-fire source for placing a Chicago family (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Use city directories in sequence:** Newberry Library holds Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward. Comparing directories from 1870, 1871, and 1872 shows whether a family remained in Chicago after the fire, disappeared, or reappeared at a new address.
- **For property research, use the Burnt Record Act reconstruction series:** FamilySearch DGS 009982111 (1871-1880, 41% indexed) is partially searchable by name. For the 59% not yet indexed, browse image by image. Also check Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum.
- **Treat 1871 as a registration start date, not a gap:** Civil vital registration at Cook County effectively began after the fire. The Birth, Death, and Marriage collections all start at 1871 (collections_search). Do not search for pre-fire civil vital records — none survived.
- **Check October-November 1871 newspapers:** Post-fire newspapers carried victim lists, relief-fund recipient lists, missing-persons notices, and property re-registration announcements. These name many individuals not recorded anywhere else. Access via Newspapers.com and the Newberry Library.
- **For Catholic families:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. Many parishes kept registers that survived or were reconstructed shortly after the fire. Contact the Archives directly.
- **For pre-fire court and probate records:** The only digitized pre-fire court material is FamilySearch DGS 009982110 — 38 images of reconstructed copies, 0% indexed, browse-only. Probate files from before the fire should be presumed lost per the FamilySearch Wiki.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Cook County Illinois Genealogy** are the most current curated guide to this jurisdiction — consult them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy for updates beyond what this survey captured.
