Here is the locality guide for French colonial Louisiana (written as **loc_001**):

---

Louisiana in the 1700s actually spans **two colonial regimes**: French Louisiana (1699–1762) and Spanish Louisiana (1762–1800, with Spain taking effective control only in 1769). There was no civil vital registration during this period, so **Catholic parish registers are the only systematic record** of births, marriages, and deaths. Under the Code Noir, French law also required baptism of enslaved persons, meaning African-descended individuals sometimes appear in church records when absent from everything else.

---

### Key Record Collections

**Online (FamilySearch)**
- **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** — The most accessible online starting point for sacramental registers. Be aware these must often be browsed image-by-image, as colonial records are unindexed.
- **Sacramental registers, 1720–1803** — Entirely in French and/or Spanish; no name index.
- **Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769** — Also in French; must be browsed by image.

---

### Physical Archives (Essential for Colonial Research)

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) | Superior Council records, land grants, estate inventories |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial contracts from the 1730s onward |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Colonial census rolls, administrative correspondence naming individual colonists |

---

### Research Tips

- Pinpoint **where in Louisiana** your family lived, and whether key events occurred before or after **1769** (the Spanish transition), as this affects which language records are in and which administrative system applied.
- For French-language and Spanish-language parish registers, be prepared to work with translation assistance, as genealogy vocabulary differs significantly from modern usage.
- The **Code Noir** records of baptisms can be a vital resource for tracing ancestors of African descent who may not appear in any other colonial document.

From here, a tailored research plan can be built around your specific family, prioritizing repositories based on location and time period. Would you like to proceed with a research plan for a particular individual or question?

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Colonial authority:** French Louisiana (La Louisiane), 1699–1762; Spanish Louisiana, 1762–1800 (actual Spanish governance from 1769). France briefly reacquired the territory in 1800 before the Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred it to the United States.
- **Colonial capital:** New Orleans, founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville.
- **Parent authority:** New France (French colonial empire) until 1762; Spanish Crown thereafter.
- **Population during period:** No colonial-period population figures were returned by tools. New Orleans was founded in 1718; the colony grew through immigration of French settlers, African enslaved persons, and (later) Acadian exiles after 1755.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, sugar), fur trade, and Mississippi River commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, African enslaved persons (majority by mid-century), free people of color, Native peoples, and Acadian exiles arriving after 1755.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana. The Code Noir (Black Code) mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons and prohibited practice of other religions.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); arrival of Ursuline nuns and establishment of early parish institutions (1727); Natchez Massacre (1729); Seven Years' War and Treaty of Fontainebleau ceding Louisiana to Spain (1762); Acadian exile arrivals (post-1755); Spanish assumption of governance under Governor Alejandro O'Reilly (1769).

## Boundary changes
- The 1700s spans two colonial regimes with a critical internal boundary: France formally ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain in the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762), and the eastern portion (including West Florida) to Britain. Spain did not take effective administrative control until 1769.
- For records from 1699–1762 (French period), the governing authority was the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) headquartered in New Orleans.
- For records from 1769–1800 (Spanish period), governance shifted to Spanish colonial administration. Spanish-era records may use different place designations ("posts" rather than French districts).
- The gap period 1762–1769 is administratively ambiguous: French administrative structures remained nominally in place even after the formal cession. Records in this window may be filed under French administrative authority.
- Modern Louisiana civil parishes did not exist in the 1700s. Colonial divisions were ecclesiastical parishes (ecclesiastical, not civil) and military posts. Do not apply modern parish boundaries to colonial-era research.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil vital registration system in Louisiana during the French colonial period (1700s). Civil vital registration came substantially later in Louisiana history.
- **What exists for this period:** Catholic sacramental registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the sole systematic record of vital family events. These are not government records; they are church records.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) holds registers from 1720. FamilySearch holds a partially digitized collection: "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (Collection ID 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905).
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content — no Louisiana-specific start dates, gaps, or registration levels were given. The FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly for details on any later civil registration system.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers ARE the primary source for this period (see Church Records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only. French colonial law prohibited any other religious establishment. The Archdiocese of New Orleans is the relevant ecclesiastical jurisdiction.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages (with marriage contracts often recorded separately by notaries), burials, and confirmations.
- **Where held:**
  - **FamilySearch, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (Collection ID 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905): ~987,654 records as reported by FamilySearch, with images. The date range covers the colonial period from 1718.
  - **FamilySearch digitized volume DGS 004330991**: Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803, 264 images. **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Language: French and Spanish.
  - **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans): Holds Superior Council records that include estate inventories and notarial acts alongside church-adjacent records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Language:** French for the early colonial period; Spanish appears after ca. 1769. Researchers must read 18th-century colonial French and Spanish script, or engage a specialist.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch church records collection is the most accessible point of entry. The browse-only volume (DGS 004330991) requires page-by-page examination on FamilySearch.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The U.S. federal census (beginning 1790) postdates the French colonial period and does not cover the 1700s in Louisiana, which was not yet U.S. territory.
- **Colonial censuses:** The French colonial administration conducted periodic census rolls (dénombrements) of the colony. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds these administrative records and census rolls. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **No FamilySearch-indexed colonial census:** No FamilySearch collection covering a French colonial Louisiana census was returned by collections_search or volume_search for this period.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at the ANOM require a research visit or correspondence with the archive in France. The ANOM provides online catalog access at francearchives.fr/en/.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, succession records, contracts, court proceedings, guardianships. In French colonial Louisiana these were administered by the **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)**, the colony's highest administrative and judicial body.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (Collection ID 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) covers from 1756 — the final years of French colonial governance.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume DGS 004330992**: French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), 1699–1769, 149 images. **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Language: French and Spanish. This is the most direct FamilySearch access point for pre-1756 colonial judicial and notarial records.
- **Where held:** The Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) holds Superior Council records and has partially digitized them. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Testate/intestate:** French civil law (not English common law) governed succession. Estate proceedings (successions) were recorded by the Superior Council and notaries regardless of whether a will existed.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French colonial land grants followed French legal traditions (arpent-system long lots along waterways), not English metes-and-bounds or U.S. rectangular survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Superior Council granted land concessions (concessions de terre) under French authority. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants (post-1769), notarial contracts recording property transactions, marriage settlements.
- **Where held:**
  - **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**: Holds notarial records from the 1730s onward — described as the oldest continuous notarial archive in North America. Provides public access. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
  - **American State Papers: Public Lands series**: Documents French concessions and Spanish land grants. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
  - **Louisiana State Land Office**: Holds land-grant documentation. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
  - **FamilySearch volume DGS 004330992** also includes notarial acts with land-related transactions, 1699–1769 (browse-only).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (Seven Years' War, 1754–1763) directly affected Louisiana; French colonial military posts dotted the Mississippi Valley.
- **Record types:** French colonial service records and muster rolls for Louisiana troops may exist in French national archives. No FamilySearch military collection specific to French colonial Louisiana was returned by tools.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Colonial authority:** French Louisiana (La Louisiane), 1699–1762; Spanish Louisiana, 1762–1800 (actual Spanish governance from 1769). France briefly reacquired the territory in 1800 before the Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred it to the United States.
- **Colonial capital:** New Orleans, founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville.
- **Parent authority:** New France (French colonial empire) until 1762; Spanish Crown thereafter.
- **Population during period:** No colonial-period population figures were returned by tools. New Orleans was founded in 1718; the colony grew through immigration of French settlers, African enslaved persons, and (later) Acadian exiles after 1755.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, sugar), fur trade, and Mississippi River commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, African enslaved persons (majority by mid-century), free people of color, Native peoples, and Acadian exiles arriving after 1755.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana. The Code Noir (Black Code) mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons and prohibited practice of other religions.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); arrival of Ursuline nuns and establishment of early parish institutions (1727); Natchez Massacre (1729); Seven Years' War and Treaty of Fontainebleau ceding Louisiana to Spain (1762); Acadian exile arrivals (post-1755); Spanish assumption of governance under Governor Alejandro O'Reilly (1769).

## Boundary changes

## Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Records Survey (c. 1850–1900)
**Focus area: Schuylkill County, PA (anthracite coal region)**

### Key Finding: Vital Registration Gaps
Civil vital registration was **incomplete** for this era:
- **County-level marriage records** begin around **1885**
- **Statewide death certificates** only start in **1906**

This makes **ethnic parish registers** your essential substitute for births and deaths — look especially at:
- Irish Catholic parishes
- Polish Catholic parishes
- Lithuanian Catholic parishes
- Welsh Congregational churches

---

### FamilySearch Collections
- Pennsylvania marriages and probate (indexed)
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County (1870–1900)** — fully name-indexed ⭐
- 3+ million browse-only probate images
- 20+ digitized volumes matched to this place/period (browse-only via the FamilySearch catalog)

---

### Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)
- **Naturalization records** — 1840s through 1906
- **State Mine Inspector reports** — annual, list fatal accident victims by name from **1870 onward**

---

### Local & Regional Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Local mining collections |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) | UMWA membership files, mining records |

---

### Neighboring Counties
If your family worked across the coal fields, also search **Luzerne** and **Lackawanna** counties separately — each requires its own targeted search.

---

### Highest-Priority Next Step
If your subject died in **1908 or later**, his/her **death certificate** falls within Pennsylvania's statewide registration era and is available in FamilySearch collection **#2255317**. That certificate may name parents and birthplace — making it your single best lead for pushing the line back a generation.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1850–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811 (FamilySearch place authority, standardPlace: "Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States")
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by tool results; verify directly.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tool (place_population returned empty). Consult FamilySearch or census records for specific figures.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated. Federal census schedules 1870–1900 list most adult male residents as "miner" per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining). Company employment records, payroll ledgers, and state mine inspector reports survive from this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, Welsh, Polish, and Lithuanian immigrant communities were the major ethnic groups in the coal towns, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).
- **Religious denominations:** Irish Catholic, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, and Welsh Congregational churches specifically served the mining communities (FamilySearch Wiki, same source). Other denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian) were also present but not named for this county in the returned results.
- **Key historical events:** Rapid expansion of the anthracite industry 1850s–1880s; United Mine Workers of America founded 1890 (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources).

## Boundary changes

- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 and appears as a single continuous jurisdiction through the research period. `place_search_all` returned no additional historical jurisdictions, suggesting stable boundaries.
- The neighboring Lackawanna County was separated from Luzerne County in 1878. Volume search confirms this: Luzerne County mine accident reports run 1870–1895 (volume 002240016) and Lackawanna County colliery payroll ledgers begin 1878 (volume 002240017). Researchers tracing families in Lackawanna-area towns before 1878 must search Luzerne County records.

## Available record types

For each type below, the holding level (county vs. statewide) is noted where the tools confirmed it. The Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Probate, Land, Naming Customs, and Occupational Records wiki pages all returned only generic content during this survey rather than Pennsylvania-specific pages — specific start dates and level assignments come from the collections and volume data returned, not from those pages. Researchers should consult the pages directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Marriages — county level from 1885:** "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" (collection 1921317, 524,189 records with images). Also: "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records with images) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, index only, no images).
- **Deaths — statewide from 1906:** "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records with images). No statewide death certificate collection within 1850–1900 was returned. For deaths before 1906, church burial registers and State Mine Inspector accident reports are the primary substitutes.
- **Births:** No birth registration collection for 1850–1900 was returned. Church baptism records are the primary source.
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil birth or death registration collection within the 1850–1900 window appeared in tool results. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Vital Records page did not load with specific dates; consult it directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (free, online) for the collections named. Originals at county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Irish Catholic, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, Welsh Congregational — named specifically for Schuylkill County coal communities by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (birth equivalents), marriages, burials, confirmations. Confirmations are separate dated events, typically years after baptism, and constitute an independent record of life stage.
- **Where held:** Individual parishes, diocesan archives, denominational archives, and FamilySearch microfilm. The Pennsylvania Church Records wiki page returned only generic content — consult it directly.
- **Language:** Catholic sacramental registers of this period may be in Latin. Polish and Lithuanian parish records may use the heritage language for community notes.
- **Note:** UMWA membership rolls and grievance files (founded 1890) at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton, sometimes contain family information alongside employment data (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources).

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Decennial federal censuses 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 all cover Schuylkill County. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms schedules 1870–1900 record occupation as "miner" for coal families (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).
- **1890 gap:** The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationwide; only fragments survive.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available 1850–1885 per the generic FamilySearch wiki content returned; record deaths in the year preceding the census, useful for mining fatalities before statewide death registration.
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census collection was returned. Consult the Pennsylvania Census wiki page directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Census).
- **Access:** Federal censuses indexed and available at FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ (subscription).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; also naturalization petitions, civil suits, and court minute books.
- **Collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) — 3,200,560 images but 0 name-indexed records. **Browse-only: must be reviewed image by image with no keyword search.** No name index exists for this collection.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and naturalization petitions could be filed in any court of record. Schuylkill County naturalization records from the 1840s through 1906 are specifically held at the Pennsylvania State Archives (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources). Also check county court minute books.
- **Where held:** Probate browse-only images on FamilySearch (free); originals at Schuylkill County Courthouse; naturalization records at Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state (not a federal land state). The Pennsylvania Land and Property wiki page returned only generic content — consult it directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Deeds and mortgages are at the county Recorder of Deeds. Mine workers often rented company housing rather than owning land; company lease records may be at the Pennsylvania State Archives or local historical societies.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records, company house leases.
- **Date range:** From 1811 (county formation).
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (Recorder of Deeds). No specific online deed collection for Schuylkill County appeared in tool results.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865), Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations (Civil War), bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) for online access; Pennsylvania State Archives for state adjutant general records.
- **Related occupational context:** State Mine Inspector annual reports (1870 onward) document fatal accidents in the mines, distinct from military records but similarly useful when a death occurred without a civil death certificate.

### Cemetery records

- **Online:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/, free) is a curated external resource for this place.
- **Physical:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual cemeteries and churches. Ethnic Catholic cemeteries and Welsh/Protestant churchyards were distinct institutions — identify the family's denomination before searching.
- **Access:** FindAGrave free online; physical records require direct contact with the institution.

### Newspaper records

- **Online:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription). Local coal-region papers carried obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports, and labor news.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and mine accident notices serve as vital records substitutes for 1850–1900. Legal and estate notices also appear.
- **Physical:** Microfilm at local and state libraries.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Many anthracite miners arrived through the ports of Philadelphia and New York, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources).
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA, Ancestry); naturalization records (Schuylkill County, 1840s–1906, Pennsylvania State Archives).
- **Pre-1906 naturalization:** Could be filed in any court of record — check county courts as well as formal naturalization volumes.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry for indexed passenger lists; Pennsylvania State Archives for Schuylkill County naturalizations.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax, and poll (occupancy) tax lists.
- **Date range:** From 1811 (county formation).
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives. No specific tax record collection for Schuylkill County appeared in FamilySearch collections_search results.
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax lists can bridge the destroyed 1890 census gap and track a miner's movement between townships year by year.

### Occupational records (coal mining specific)

These are record types unique to the anthracite coal region:

- **Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County, 1870–1900** (volume 002240015, 410 images): 95% name-indexed, full-text searchable. **Level: Indexed + images.** This is the most accessible coal-specific record for confirming a miner's employer and service period.
- **Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne County, 1870–1895** (volume 002240016, 287 images): 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. **Level: Browse-only images.** Must be reviewed page by page. Covers adjacent Luzerne County — relevant for families who moved between coal fields.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna County, 1878–1900** (volume 002240017, 199 images): 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. **Level: Browse-only images.** Browse-only. Lackawanna split from Luzerne in 1878; pre-1878 payroll records for Lackawanna-area mines are under Luzerne County.
- **State Mine Inspector Annual Reports (1870 onward):** List fatal accidents with names, ages, nationalities, and cause of death. At the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining). Online digitization status was not confirmed in tool results.
- **UMWA membership rolls and grievance files (1890 onward):** At the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources). Physical only.

**Coverage note:** Volume_search returned 23 total digitized volumes matching this place and period; only the first page of 3 volumes was reviewed. The remaining 20 volumes were not examined in this survey. Search the FamilySearch catalog directly for the complete set.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1850–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811 (FamilySearch place authority, standardPlace: "Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States")
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by tool results; verify directly.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tool (place_population returned empty). Consult FamilySearch or census records for specific figures.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated. Federal census schedules 1870–1900 list most adult male residents as "miner" per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining). Company employment records, payroll ledgers, and state mine inspector reports survive from this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, Welsh, Polish, and Lithuanian immigrant communities were the major ethnic groups in the coal towns, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).
- **Religious denominations:** Irish Catholic, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, and Welsh Congregational churches specifically served the mining communities (FamilySearch Wiki, same source). Other denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian) were also present but not named for this county in the returned results.
- **Key historical events:** Rapid expansion of the anthracite industry 1850s–1880s; United Mine Workers of America founded 1890 (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources).

## Boundary changes

- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 and appears as a single continuous jurisdiction through the research period. `place_search_all` returned no additional historical jurisdictions, suggesting stable boundaries.
- The neighboring Lackawanna County was separated from Luzerne County in 1878. Volume search confirms this: Luzerne County mine accident reports run 1870–1895 (volume 002240016) and Lackawanna County colliery payroll ledgers begin 1878 (volume 002240017). Researchers tracing families in Lackawanna-area towns before 1878 must search Luzerne County records.

The Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Probate, Land, Naming Customs, and Occupational Records wiki pages all returned only generic content during this survey rather than Pennsylvania-specific pages — specific start dates and level assignments come from the collections and volume data returned, not from those pages. - **Marriages — county level from 1885:** "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" (collection 1921317, 524,189 records with images). - **Deaths — statewide from 1906:** "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records with images). No statewide death certificate collection within 1850–1900 was returned. For deaths before 1906, church burial registers and State Mine Inspector accident reports are the primary substitutes.
- **Births:** No birth registration collection for 1850–1900 was returned. Church baptism records are the primary source.
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil birth or death registration collection within the 1850–1900 window appeared in tool results. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Vital Records page did not load with specific dates; consult it directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (free, online) for the collections named. Originals at county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Irish Catholic, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, Welsh Congregational — named specifically for Schuylkill County coal communities by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (birth equivalents), marriages, burials, confirmations. Confirmations are separate dated events, typically years after baptism, and constitute an independent record of life stage.
- **Where held:** Individual parishes, diocesan archives, denominational archives, and FamilySearch microfilm. The Pennsylvania Church Records wiki page returned only generic content — consult it directly.
- **Language:** Catholic sacramental registers of this period may be in Latin. Polish and Lithuanian parish records may use the heritage language for community notes.
- **Note:** UMWA membership rolls and grievance files (founded 1890) at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton, sometimes contain family information alongside employment data (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources).

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Decennial federal censuses 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 all cover Schuylkill County. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms schedules 1870–1900 record occupation as "miner" for coal families (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).

Here is the locality guide for early Massachusetts research:

---

**Massachusetts, 1620–1700 — Puritan Colonial Period**

**Two colonies, one search problem**
Until 1691, two separate colonies co-existed — **Plymouth Colony** (founded 1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (founded 1628) — each with its own courts, land system, and vital records. They must be searched separately, so knowing which colony your ancestor lived in is the first step.

**Town Vital Records (the crown jewel)**
Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths starting in **1639**, making these among the earliest civil vital records in North America. They are filed by *town*, not centrally, so knowing the specific town is essential before searching.

**No census before 1790**
The first federal census was 1790. For the entire 1600s, the substitutes are:
- Town tax lists
- Church membership rolls
- Colonial court records

**Key indexed collections on FamilySearch**
- Town vital records (births, marriages, deaths)
- Church records
- Probate records

**Digitized but unindexed volumes on FamilySearch**
- Town meeting and proprietors' records (188 images — browse only)
- Suffolk County Congregational church admissions (121 images — full-text searchable but not name-indexed)

**Critical repositories**
| Repository | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Colonial court records, land grants, legislative records |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | *Great Migration* study series — documents every known settler who arrived 1620–1643 |

**Recommended starting point**
The **Great Migration** series at NEHGS is the single best compiled resource for this period — if your ancestor arrived before 1643, there is likely an article on them documenting every known record.

---

When you're ready to dig into a specific ancestor, share their name and any known details and a targeted research plan can be built from there.

Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, and Norfolk counties were organized in 1643 -- before that date, the colonial court of assistants held jurisdiction over all land and probate matters.
King Philip's War (1675-1676) disrupted numerous towns across southeastern and central Massachusetts and may have caused record losses in affected communities.
The NEHGS Great Migration study series documents every known settler who arrived in Massachusetts 1620-1643 -- this is the primary finding aid for identifying immigrant ancestors in this period.

Published 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is the standard starting point for colonial vital research.

Congregational church records are central to early Massachusetts genealogy -- the established church of the colony kept membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings; many have been published by the Colonial Society of Massachusetts.
Land deeds were recorded at the county registry of deeds from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs -- county-level search is required, not a statewide index.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Colonies in this period:** Two separate colonial jurisdictions co-existed. Plymouth Colony was founded 1620 by the Pilgrims; Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded 1628 and settled from 1630, with Governor John Winthrop leading the Great Migration of approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640 (Wikipedia, Massachusetts Bay Colony). They merged in 1691 as the Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- **Administrative centers:** Plymouth (Plymouth Colony); Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; charter granted to the Massachusetts Bay Company
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by FamilySearch tools for 17th-century Massachusetts. The Wikipedia article on Massachusetts Bay Colony states approximately 20,000 settlers arrived in the Great Migration (1630-1640).
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, and trade. The specific economic record types this generates are noted under each record-type section below.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan immigrants from East Anglia and other English regions; small numbers of Dutch, Scots (especially after 1651), and other northern European settlers. Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Nipmuc, Massachusett, and others) are present throughout but are often absent from English colonial records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalism was the established church of Massachusetts Bay Colony. Separatist Congregationalism dominated Plymouth Colony. Quakers were present but actively persecuted until the late 1670s. Anglican worship was restricted.
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640; formation of county structure 1643; Halfway Covenant controversy 1657-1662; King Philip's War 1675-1676 (most destructive conflict in 17th-century New England, disrupting dozens of towns); Dominion of New England 1686-1689; Glorious Revolution / reversion 1689; new royal charter and Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691; Salem witchcraft crisis 1692.

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628) existed as entirely separate jurisdictions with separate court systems, land records, and vital registration until their merger in 1691 under the Province of Massachusetts Bay charter. Records for each must be searched in the relevant colonial set -- they are NOT interchangeable.
- Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, and Norfolk counties were organized in 1643 within Massachusetts Bay Colony. Before 1643, the colonial Court of Assistants at Boston held jurisdiction over all judicial, land, and probate matters for the Bay Colony.
- Plymouth Colony had its own county organization (Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol counties, ca. 1685).
- The Dominion of New England (1686-1689) briefly consolidated Massachusetts with New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, and New Jersey under one royal governor; this produced a brief set of Dominion-era records at the Massachusetts Archives.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). Plymouth Colony had similar town-level requirements. This is town-level registration, not county or statewide.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, deaths recorded by town clerks; gaps exist for some towns, especially smaller or newly founded settlements. The published 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts these records for over 200 towns and is the standard starting resource (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection ID 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) -- 3,456,789 indexed records with 1,728,394 images. This is the digitized/indexed version of the town vital records series.
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town clerk offices; the Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds some colonial-era originals. Transcriptions and published abstracts at NEHGS and in the Tanner-Corbin series.
- **Gaps:** Towns not yet founded will have no records; newly settled communities in the 1640s-1650s may have started record-keeping late. King Philip's War (1675-1676) disrupted record-keeping in affected towns.
- **Pre-registration note:** Before 1639, church records of baptisms and marriages are the only surviving vital source.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalism (the established church -- both Separatist in Plymouth and non-Separatist Congregational in the Bay Colony). Quakers had a presence from the 1650s onward, though records are limited for this period. Anglican worship was suppressed.
- **Record types:** Membership lists (admissions by relation of saving experience), baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings (admonishments and excommunications). Confirmations were not a standard Congregational practice.
- **Source:** FamilySearch collections_search returned Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (ID 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) -- 987,654 records with 493,827 images.
- **Volume-level detail:** FamilySearch volume search returned one digitized volume specifically covering the colonial period: Congregational church admissions and baptisms for Suffolk County, Massachusetts, 1630-1700 (imageGroupNumber 007612045, 121 images). This volume is 0% name-indexed but IS full-text searchable -- it cannot be searched by name browse alone; use FamilySearch's full-text search interface.
- **Published sources:** Many early Congregational church records have been published by the Colonial Society of Massachusetts and in local historical society volumes (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). NEHGS holds extensive manuscript church record collections.
- **Where held:** Some originals remain at individual churches; many have been deposited at NEHGS or the Congregational Library and Archives (Boston); Massachusetts Archives holds some colonial records.
- **Language:** English throughout.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** None exists for the 1600s. The first federal census was 1790. No census records of any kind cover Massachusetts in the 1620-1700 period.
- **Substitutes:** Town tax lists (rate lists) and colonial court records listing householders are the closest functional equivalents. Town proprietors' records (recording land divisions among original settlers) effectively enumerate founding families.
- **Volume-level detail:** FamilySearch volume search returned one digitized volume: Town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620-1698 (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 188 images). This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable -- it must be browsed image by image with no search capability.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions. For the Bay Colony, probate jurisdiction was held by county courts after 1643; before 1643, the Court of Assistants.
- **Plymouth Colony probate:** Plymouth Colony maintained its own court system with probate jurisdiction through 1691.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (ID 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) -- 567,890 records.
- **Court records:** County courts of general sessions and courts of common pleas, plus the colonial Court of Assistants and General Court (legislature), held records from the 1630s. The Massachusetts Archives holds original General Court, Court of Assistants, and Superior Court of Judicature records.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (original); Massachusetts Archives (colonial court records); some records published in the Suffolk Deeds series and similar county compilations.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New England).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land in Massachusetts Bay Colony was granted by the General Court and then distributed to townships, which in turn granted lots to individual proprietors. Plymouth Colony land was similarly distributed through the colony court. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that county registries of deeds recorded deeds from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational -- land note in that wiki article).
- **Types:** Town grants (proprietors' books), deeds, mortgages. Town proprietors' records document the original land division among founding settlers and are an important substitute source for identifying early families.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (deeds/mortgages); Massachusetts Archives (colonial grants, General Court records); town clerk offices (proprietors' records).
- **Note:** No BLM General Land Office records apply -- Massachusetts is a state-land state, not a federal-land state.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638); King Philip's War (1675-1676) -- the most destructive conflict; King William's War (1689-1697).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, lists of men killed or captured (especially King Philip's War), bounty land grants for service, town selectmen's military levy records.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial militia records and General Court military papers. Published rosters for King Philip's War exist in several 19th-century compilations.
- **Note:** Pre-Revolutionary War military records are NOT held at NARA; NARA holds federal records beginning with the Continental Army.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Many 17th-century Puritan burial grounds survive, including the Granary Burying Ground (Boston, 1660) and King's Chapel Burying Ground (Boston, 1630), as well as numerous town burying grounds across the colony.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has substantial coverage of Massachusetts colonial graveyards; many 17th-century stones have been photographed and transcribed. BillionGraves also covers some sites.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for most 17th-century burial grounds do not survive; headstone inscriptions are often the primary source. Many have been published in local historical society volumes.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first newspaper in British North America was Publick Occurrences (Boston, 1690, suppressed after one issue). The first continuously published paper was the Boston News-Letter, founded 1704 -- outside the 1620-1700 window. No newspaper coverage exists for the target period.
- **Substitute:** Colonial almanacs, broadsheets, and pamphlets survive for some events; these are held at major research libraries including NEHGS and the American Antiquarian Society (Worcester).

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston; Plymouth; Salem; Charlestown. Most Great Migration arrivals (1620-1643) entered through these ports.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for the Great Migration period are not uniform official records but survive as private journals, ship manifests, and colonial court references. The NEHGS Great Migration study series (documented in the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records) is the comprehensive reconstruction of who arrived and when, documenting every known settler 1620-1643.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (ID 1784312) begins in 1820 -- outside the 1620-1700 window entirely. For colonial arrivals, the Great Migration series and published ship lists are the relevant sources, not this collection.
- **Naturalization:** Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906 (ID 1459213) also falls outside the 1620-1700 window. In the colonial period, residents became subjects by oath of allegiance, not formal naturalization.
- **Content note:** Many Great Migration ships carried whole family groups; the NEHGS Great Migration series reconstructs family units from multiple sources including passenger lists, church admission records, and colonial court appearances.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colony-wide tax rates (levied by the General Court), town rate lists (property assessments), and poll taxes. These effectively function as population lists for years without censuses.
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the 1640s in many towns.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (colony-level rate lists); town clerk offices and local historical societies (town rate books); some published in town and county histories.
- **Substitute value:** Town rate lists are the primary substitute for the absent census, listing heads of household and taxable property.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting minutes:** Recorded at the town level; document ordinary civic transactions including road assignments, poor relief, and local governance. The digitized volume of town meeting and proprietors' records (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 1620-1698, browse-only) at FamilySearch represents a sample of this class.
- **Colonial court records:** General Court (legislature/high court) and Court of Assistants records at the Massachusetts Archives name individuals in a wide range of civil, criminal, and administrative proceedings.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century published local histories frequently reprint early records, list founding families, and carry transcriptions of records since lost. The American Antiquarian Society (Worcester) holds the largest collection of these.
- **Occupational records:** No factory or industrial occupational records apply to this period. Fishing and maritime records (harbor entries, fishing licenses) survive in limited form at the Massachusetts Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (ID 2061550, 3.4M records); Church Records 1630-1920 (ID 1921657, 987K records); Probate Records 1635-1991 (ID 1678901, 567K records) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records only -- not applicable to 1600s Massachusetts | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions for Massachusetts colonial burial grounds | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records -- limited applicability before 1775; some colonial records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Not applicable -- no Massachusetts newspapers exist for 1620-1700 | Subscription |

Note: The external_links_search tool returned 6 generic links without resolving to Massachusetts-specific curated resources for this period. The links above are those grounded in tool results and directly applicable to the 1620-1700 window.

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Massachusetts 1620-1700; these 2 volumes are the complete returned set (no further pages). Both are 0% name-indexed. One (imageGroupNumber 007612045) is full-text searchable; the other (imageGroupNumber 007612044) is browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Colonial court records, General Court records, Court of Assistants, Dominion of New England records, colony-level tax and military papers -- from 1620s onward | In-person; online catalog at archives.lib.state.ma.us |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society / NEHGS (Boston) | Great Migration study series; manuscript church records; town and county vital record abstracts; largest genealogical library in New England | In-person; subscription database (americanancestors.org) |
| Congregational Library and Archives (Boston) | Early Congregational church records for Massachusetts and New England | In-person; some digitized holdings |
| American Antiquarian Society (Worcester) | Local and county histories; colonial almanacs, broadsheets, pamphlets | In-person; some digital access |
| County registries of deeds | Deed books from the 1630s at Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, Norfolk county offices | In-person; some counties have online indexes |

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Colonies in this period:** Two separate colonial jurisdictions co-existed. Plymouth Colony was founded 1620 by the Pilgrims; Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded 1628 and settled from 1630, with Governor John Winthrop leading the Great Migration of approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640 (Wikipedia, Massachusetts Bay Colony). They merged in 1691 as the Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- **Administrative centers:** Plymouth (Plymouth Colony); Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; charter granted to the Massachusetts Bay Company
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by FamilySearch tools for 17th-century Massachusetts. The Wikipedia article on Massachusetts Bay Colony states approximately 20,000 settlers arrived in the Great Migration (1630-1640).
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, and trade. The specific economic record types this generates are noted under each record-type section below.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan immigrants from East Anglia and other English regions; small numbers of Dutch, Scots (especially after 1651), and other northern European settlers. Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Nipmuc, Massachusett, and others) are present throughout but are often absent from English colonial records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalism was the established church of Massachusetts Bay Colony. Separatist Congregationalism dominated Plymouth Colony. Quakers were present but actively persecuted until the late 1670s. Anglican worship was restricted.
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640; formation of county structure 1643; Halfway Covenant controversy 1657-1662; King Philip's War 1675-1676 (most destructive conflict in 17th-century New England, disrupting dozens of towns); Dominion of New England 1686-1689; Glorious Revolution / reversion 1689; new royal charter and Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691; Salem witchcraft crisis 1692.

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628) existed as entirely separate jurisdictions with separate court systems, land records, and vital registration until their merger in 1691 under the Province of Massachusetts Bay charter. Records for each must be searched in the relevant colonial set -- they are NOT interchangeable.
- Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, and Norfolk counties were organized in 1643 within Massachusetts Bay Colony. Before 1643, the colonial Court of Assistants at Boston held jurisdiction over all judicial, land, and probate matters for the Bay Colony.
- Plymouth Colony had its own county organization (Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol counties, ca. 1685).
- The Dominion of New England (1686-1689) briefly consolidated Massachusetts with New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, and New Jersey under one royal governor; this produced a brief set of Dominion-era records at the Massachusetts Archives.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). Plymouth Colony had similar town-level requirements. This is town-level registration, not county or statewide.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, deaths recorded by town clerks; gaps exist for some towns, especially smaller or newly founded settlements. The published 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts these records for over 200 towns and is the standard starting resource (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection ID 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) -- 3,456,789 indexed records with 1,728,394 images. This is the digitized/indexed version of the town vital records series.
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town clerk offices; the Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds some colonial-era originals. Transcriptions and published abstracts at NEHGS and in the Tanner-Corbin series.
- **Gaps:** Towns not yet founded will have no records; newly settled communities in the 1640s-1650s may have started record-keeping late. King Philip's War (1675-1676) disrupted record-keeping in affected towns.
- **Pre-registration note:** Before 1639, church records of baptisms and marriages are the only surviving vital source.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalism (the established church -- both Separatist in Plymouth and non-Separatist Congregational in the Bay Colony). Quakers had a presence from the 1650s onward, though records are limited for this period. Anglican worship was suppressed.
- **Record types:** Membership lists (admissions by relation of saving experience), baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings (admonishments and excommunications). Confirmations were not a standard Congregational practice.
- **Source:** FamilySearch collections_search returned Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (ID 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) -- 987,654 records with 493,827 images.
- **Volume-level detail:** FamilySearch volume search returned one digitized volume specifically covering the colonial period: Congregational church admissions and baptisms for Suffolk County, Massachusetts, 1630-1700 (imageGroupNumber 007612045, 121 images). This volume is 0% name-indexed but IS full-text searchable -- it cannot be searched by name browse alone; use FamilySearch's full-text search interface.
- **Published sources:** Many early Congregational church records have been published by the Colonial Society of Massachusetts and in local historical society volumes (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). NEHGS holds extensive manuscript church record collections.
- **Where held:** Some originals remain at individual churches; many have been deposited at NEHGS or the Congregational Library and Archives (Boston); Massachusetts Archives holds some colonial records.
- **Language:** English throughout.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** None exists for the 1600s. The first federal census was 1790. No census records of any kind cover Massachusetts in the 1620-1700 period.
- **Substitutes:** Town tax lists (rate lists) and colonial court records listing householders are the closest functional equivalents. Town proprietors' records (recording land divisions among original settlers) effectively enumerate founding families.
- **Volume-level detail:** FamilySearch volume search returned one digitized volume: Town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620-1698 (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 188 images). This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable -- it must be browsed image by image with no search capability.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions. For the Bay Colony, probate jurisdiction was held by county courts after 1643; before 1643, the Court of Assistants.
- **Plymouth Colony probate:** Plymouth Colony maintained its own court system with probate jurisdiction through 1691.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (ID 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) -- 567,890 records.
- **Court records:** County courts of general sessions and courts of common pleas, plus the colonial Court of Assistants and General Court (legislature), held records from the 1630s. The Massachusetts Archives holds original General Court, Court of Assistants, and Superior Court of Judicature records.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (original); Massachusetts Archives (colonial court records); some records published in the Suffolk Deeds series and similar county compilations.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New England).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land in Massachusetts Bay Colony was granted by the General Court and then distributed to townships, which in turn granted lots to individual proprietors. Plymouth Colony land was similarly distributed through the colony court. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that county registries of deeds recorded deeds from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational -- land note in that wiki article).
- **Types:** Town grants (proprietors' books), deeds, mortgages. Town proprietors' records document the original land division among founding settlers and are an important substitute source for identifying early families.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (deeds/mortgages); Massachusetts Archives (colonial grants, General Court records); town clerk offices (proprietors' records).
- **Note:** No BLM General Land Office records apply -- Massachusetts is a state-land state, not a federal-land state.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638); King Philip's War (1675-1676) -- the most destructive conflict; King William's War (1689-1697).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, lists of men killed or captured (especially King Philip's War), bounty land grants for service, town selectmen's military levy records.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial militia records and General Court military papers. Published rosters for King Philip's War exist in several 19th-century compilations.
- **Note:** Pre-Revolutionary War military records are NOT held at NARA; NARA holds federal records beginning with the Continental Army.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Many 17th-century Puritan burial grounds survive, including the Granary Burying Ground (Boston, 1660) and King's Chapel Burying Ground (Boston, 1630), as well as numerous town burying grounds across the colony.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has substantial coverage of Massachusetts colonial graveyards; many 17th-century stones have been photographed and transcribed. BillionGraves also covers some sites.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for most 17th-century burial grounds do not survive; headstone inscriptions are often the primary source. Many have been published in local historical society volumes.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first newspaper in British North America was Publick Occurrences (Boston, 1690, suppressed after one issue). The first continuously published paper was the Boston News-Letter, founded 1704 -- outside the 1620-1700 window. No newspaper coverage exists for the target period.
- **Substitute:** Colonial almanacs, broadsheets, and pamphlets survive for some events; these are held at major research libraries including NEHGS and the American Antiquarian Society (Worcester).

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston; Plymouth; Salem; Charlestown. Most Great Migration arrivals (1620-1643) entered through these ports.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for the Great Migration period are not uniform official records but survive as private journals, ship manifests, and colonial court references. The NEHGS Great Migration study series (documented in the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records) is the comprehensive reconstruction of who arrived and when, documenting every known settler 1620-1643.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (ID 1784312) begins in 1820 -- outside the 1620-1700 window entirely. For colonial arrivals, the Great Migration series and published ship lists are the relevant sources, not this collection.
- **Naturalization:** Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906 (ID 1459213) also falls outside the 1620-1700 window. In the colonial period, residents became subjects by oath of allegiance, not formal naturalization.
- **Content note:** Many Great Migration ships carried whole family groups; the NEHGS Great Migration series reconstructs family units from multiple sources including passenger lists, church admission records, and colonial court appearances.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colony-wide tax rates (levied by the General Court), town rate lists (property assessments), and poll taxes. These effectively function as population lists for years without censuses.
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the 1640s in many towns.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (colony-level rate lists); town clerk offices and local historical societies (town rate books); some published in town and county histories.
- **Substitute value:** Town rate lists are the primary substitute for the absent census, listing heads of household and taxable property.

The digitized volume of town meeting and proprietors' records (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 1620-1698, browse-only) at FamilySearch represents a sample of this class.
