- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by FamilySearch tools for 17th-century Massachusetts. The Wikipedia article on Massachusetts Bay Colony states approximately 20,000 settlers arrived in the Great Migration (1630-1640).
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, and trade. The specific economic record types this generates are noted under each record-type section below.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan immigrants from East Anglia and other English regions; small numbers of Dutch, Scots (especially after 1651), and other northern European settlers. Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Nipmuc, Massachusett, and others) are present throughout but are often absent from English colonial records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalism was the established church of Massachusetts Bay Colony. Separatist Congregationalism dominated Plymouth Colony. Quakers were present but actively persecuted until the late 1670s. Anglican worship was restricted.
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640; formation of county structure 1643; Halfway Covenant controversy 1657-1662; King Philip's War 1675-1676 (most destructive conflict in 17th-century New England, disrupting dozens of towns); Dominion of New England 1686-1689; Glorious Revolution / reversion 1689; new royal charter and Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691; Salem witchcraft crisis 1692.

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628) existed as entirely separate jurisdictions with separate court systems, land records, and vital registration until their merger in 1691 under the Province of Massachusetts Bay charter. Records for each must be searched in the relevant colonial set -- they are NOT interchangeable.
- Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, and Norfolk counties were organized in 1643 within Massachusetts Bay Colony. Before 1643, the colonial Court of Assistants at Boston held jurisdiction over all judicial, land, and probate matters for the Bay Colony.
- Plymouth Colony had its own county organization (Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol counties, ca. 1685).
- The Dominion of New England (1686-1689) briefly consolidated Massachusetts with New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, and New Jersey under one royal governor; this produced a brief set of Dominion-era records at the Massachusetts Archives.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). Plymouth Colony had similar town-level requirements. This is town-level registration, not county or statewide.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, deaths recorded by town clerks; gaps exist for some towns, especially smaller or newly founded settlements. The published 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts these records for over 200 towns and is the standard starting resource (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection ID 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) -- 3,456,789 indexed records with 1,728,394 images. This is the digitized/indexed version of the town vital records series.
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town clerk offices; the Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds some colonial-era originals. Transcriptions and published abstracts at NEHGS and in the Tanner-Corbin series.
- **Gaps:** Towns not yet founded will have no records; newly settled communities in the 1640s-1650s may have started record-keeping late. King Philip's War (1675-1676) disrupted record-keeping in affected towns.
- **Pre-registration note:** Before 1639, church records of baptisms and marriages are the only surviving vital source.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalism (the established church -- both Separatist in Plymouth and non-Separatist Congregational in the Bay Colony). Quakers had a presence from the 1650s onward, though records are limited for this period. Anglican worship was suppressed.
- **Record types:** Membership lists (admissions by relation of saving experience), baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings (admonishments and excommunications). Confirmations were not a standard Congregational practice.
- **Source:** FamilySearch collections_search returned Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (ID 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) -- 987,654 records with 493,827 images.
- **Volume-level detail:** FamilySearch volume search returned one digitized volume specifically covering the colonial period: Congregational church admissions and baptisms for Suffolk County, Massachusetts, 1630-1700 (imageGroupNumber 007612045, 121 images). This volume is 0% name-indexed but IS full-text searchable -- it cannot be searched by name browse alone; use FamilySearch's full-text search interface.
- **Published sources:** Many early Congregational church records have been published by the Colonial Society of Massachusetts and in local historical society volumes (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). NEHGS holds extensive manuscript church record collections.
- **Where held:** Some originals remain at individual churches; many have been deposited at NEHGS or the Congregational Library and Archives (Boston); Massachusetts Archives holds some colonial records.
- **Language:** English throughout.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** None exists for the 1600s. The first federal census was 1790. No census records of any kind cover Massachusetts in the 1620-1700 period.
- **Substitutes:** Town tax lists (rate lists) and colonial court records listing householders are the closest functional equivalents. Town proprietors' records (recording land divisions among original settlers) effectively enumerate founding families.
- **Volume-level detail:** FamilySearch volume search returned one digitized volume: Town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620-1698 (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 188 images). This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable -- it must be browsed image by image with no search capability.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions. For the Bay Colony, probate jurisdiction was held by county courts after 1643; before 1643, the Court of Assistants.
- **Plymouth Colony probate:** Plymouth Colony maintained its own court system with probate jurisdiction through 1691.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (ID 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) -- 567,890 records.
- **Court records:** County courts of general sessions and courts of common pleas, plus the colonial Court of Assistants and General Court (legislature), held records from the 1630s. The Massachusetts Archives holds original General Court, Court of Assistants, and Superior Court of Judicature records.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (original); Massachusetts Archives (colonial court records); some records published in the Suffolk Deeds series and similar county compilations.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New England).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land in Massachusetts Bay Colony was granted by the General Court and then distributed to townships, which in turn granted lots to individual proprietors. Plymouth Colony land was similarly distributed through the colony court. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that county registries of deeds recorded deeds from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational -- land note in that wiki article).
- **Types:** Town grants (proprietors' books), deeds, mortgages. Town proprietors' records document the original land division among founding settlers and are an important substitute source for identifying early families.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (deeds/mortgages); Massachusetts Archives (colonial grants, General Court records); town clerk offices (proprietors' records).
- **Note:** No BLM General Land Office records apply -- Massachusetts is a state-land state, not a federal-land state.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638); King Philip's War (1675-1676) -- the most destructive conflict; King William's War (1689-1697).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, lists of men killed or captured (especially King Philip's War), bounty land grants for service, town selectmen's military levy records.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial militia records and General Court military papers. Published rosters for King Philip's War exist in several 19th-century compilations.
- **Note:** Pre-Revolutionary War military records are NOT held at NARA; NARA holds federal records beginning with the Continental Army.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Many 17th-century Puritan burial grounds survive, including the Granary Burying Ground (Boston, 1660) and King's Chapel Burying Ground (Boston, 1630), as well as numerous town burying grounds across the colony.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has substantial coverage of Massachusetts colonial graveyards; many 17th-century stones have been photographed and transcribed. BillionGraves also covers some sites.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for most 17th-century burial grounds do not survive; headstone inscriptions are often the primary source. Many have been published in local historical society volumes.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first newspaper in British North America was Publick Occurrences (Boston, 1690, suppressed after one issue). The first continuously published paper was the Boston News-Letter, founded 1704 -- outside the 1620-1700 window. No newspaper coverage exists for the target period.
- **Substitute:** Colonial almanacs, broadsheets, and pamphlets survive for some events; these are held at major research libraries including NEHGS and the American Antiquarian Society (Worcester).

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston; Plymouth; Salem; Charlestown. Most Great Migration arrivals (1620-1643) entered through these ports.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for the Great Migration period are not uniform official records but survive as private journals, ship manifests, and colonial court references. The NEHGS Great Migration study series (documented in the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records) is the comprehensive reconstruction of who arrived and when, documenting every known settler 1620-1643.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (ID 1784312) begins in 1820 -- outside the 1620-1700 window entirely. For colonial arrivals, the Great Migration series and published ship lists are the relevant sources, not this collection.
- **Naturalization:** Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906 (ID 1459213) also falls outside the 1620-1700 window. In the colonial period, residents became subjects by oath of allegiance, not formal naturalization.
- **Content note:** Many Great Migration ships carried whole family groups; the NEHGS Great Migration series reconstructs family units from multiple sources including passenger lists, church admission records, and colonial court appearances.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colony-wide tax rates (levied by the General Court), town rate lists (property assessments), and poll taxes. These effectively function as population lists for years without censuses.
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the 1640s in many towns.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (colony-level rate lists); town clerk offices and local historical societies (town rate books); some published in town and county histories.
- **Substitute value:** Town rate lists are the primary substitute for the absent census, listing heads of household and taxable property.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting minutes:** Recorded at the town level; document ordinary civic transactions including road assignments, poor relief, and local governance. The digitized volume of town meeting and proprietors' records (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 1620-1698, browse-only) at FamilySearch represents a sample of this class.
- **Colonial court records:** General Court (legislature/high court) and Court of Assistants records at the Massachusetts Archives name individuals in a wide range of civil, criminal, and administrative proceedings.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century published local histories frequently reprint early records, list founding families, and carry transcriptions of records since lost. The American Antiquarian Society (Worcester) holds the largest collection of these.
- **Occupational records:** No factory or industrial occupational records apply to this period. Fishing and maritime records (harbor entries, fishing licenses) survive in limited form at the Massachusetts Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (ID 2061550, 3.4M records); Church Records 1630-1920 (ID 1921657, 987K records); Probate Records 1635-1991 (ID 1678901, 567K records) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records only -- not applicable to 1600s Massachusetts | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions for Massachusetts colonial burial grounds | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records -- limited applicability before 1775; some colonial records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Not applicable -- no Massachusetts newspapers exist for 1620-1700 | Subscription |

Note: The external_links_search tool returned 6 generic links without resolving to Massachusetts-specific curated resources for this period. The links above are those grounded in tool results and directly applicable to the 1620-1700 window.

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Massachusetts 1620-1700; these 2 volumes are the complete returned set (no further pages). Both are 0% name-indexed. One (imageGroupNumber 007612045) is full-text searchable; the other (imageGroupNumber 007612044) is browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Colonial court records, General Court records, Court of Assistants, Dominion of New England records, colony-level tax and military papers -- from 1620s onward | In-person; online catalog at archives.lib.state.ma.us |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society / NEHGS (Boston) | Great Migration study series; manuscript church records; town and county vital record abstracts; largest genealogical library in New England | In-person; subscription database (americanancestors.org) |
| Congregational Library and Archives (Boston) | Early Congregational church records for Massachusetts and New England | In-person; some digitized holdings |
| American Antiquarian Society (Worcester) | Local and county histories; colonial almanacs, broadsheets, pamphlets | In-person; some digital access |
| County registries of deeds | Deed books from the 1630s at Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, Norfolk county offices | In-person; some counties have online indexes |
| Town clerk offices | Original town vital records and proprietors' records | In-person or written inquiry to individual towns |

## Records NOT online
- Original town rate lists (tax assessments) for the 1640s-1690s are largely held at town clerk offices and the Massachusetts Archives and have not been systematically digitized.
- Town meeting minutes and proprietors' records beyond the single FamilySearch browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 007612044) remain largely physical or on older microfilm.
- County deed books from the 1630s-1690s are not systematically available online; access generally requires visiting county registries of deeds or using microfilm at NEHGS or FamilySearch libraries.
- Colonial Court of Assistants and General Court records at the Massachusetts Archives are largely physical, though some series have been published in 19th-century transcriptions.
- Most individual Congregational church registers for this period survive only in physical form or on NEHGS microfilm, outside of the partial digital coverage in FamilySearch collection 1921657.

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) resulted in the destruction or abandonment of numerous towns across southeastern and central Massachusetts. Town records of affected communities (e.g., Deerfield, Mendon, Brookfield) may be incomplete or absent for this period. No specific record-set destruction has been confirmed by the tools consulted in this survey; researchers should contact individual town clerks and the Massachusetts Archives for the status of records from war-affected towns.
- No tool result in this survey confirmed a wholesale loss of any major Massachusetts colonial record series.

## Research tips
- **Start with the NEHGS Great Migration series** if tracing immigrant Puritan ancestors: it documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643, reconstructing family units from passenger lists, church records, and court sources. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Identify the specific town** before searching vital records: colonial Massachusetts registration was at the town level, and searching without a town name produces unmanageable results.
- **Search both Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony records** if you are unsure which colony your ancestor belonged to -- many researchers conflate the two. They had separate courts, separate vital registration, and separate published record compilations through 1691.
- **Congregational church records are the backbone of 17th-century Massachusetts genealogy.** Church admission records record the date a person became a full communicant member -- this is a distinct and dateable biographical event separate from baptism. Disciplinary records can place a family in a specific congregation even without a vital event entry. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Use the published Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records to 1850' series** as the standard starting point for over 200 towns before searching original records. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Town rate lists substitute for the absent census.** Before 1790, no census exists; town assessment lists from the 1640s onward are the best population-type substitute and list heads of household with taxable property.
- **Probate inventories** are particularly rich for this period: they list all personal property and often name heirs, spouses, and creditors, giving family structure when vital records are silent.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts** (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips sections) returned only generic content in this survey and did not load Massachusetts-specific guidance. Researchers should consult the Massachusetts Genealogy page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy for current coverage.
- **The wiki_read calls** for Massachusetts-specific pages (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) all returned a generic page rather than Massachusetts content -- this is a coverage gap in the FamilySearch Wiki tool for this survey. Consult the wiki pages directly for the most current guidance.
- **Cross-border research:** Connecticut Colony (founded 1636) adjoins Massachusetts to the south; Rhode Island and Providence Plantations (founded 1636) adjoins to the southeast; New Hampshire adjoins to the north. Families near these borders generated records in more than one colonial jurisdiction. This survey covers Massachusetts only; those jurisdictions need their own surveys.

**Locality Guide: Oklahoma, 1889 Land Run Era**

---

Here is what the research shows for tracing families in Oklahoma Territory during and after the 1889 Land Run:

---

## Key Records & Repositories

### 1. Federal Homestead Files
- **What they contain:** Land entry papers, final proof affidavits (listing witnesses, residency history, and often the claimant's state of origin), and correspondence.
- **Where to find them:** National Archives (Record Group 49); partially indexed on FamilySearch. The Bureau of Land Management's **General Land Office (GLO) Records** site (glorecords.blm.gov) has patent images searchable by name.
- **Why they matter:** The final proof file often names where the settler came from — invaluable for tracing origins before 1889.

### 2. 1890 Oklahoma Special Census
- **What it is:** A special federal enumeration taken specifically for Oklahoma Territory shortly after the Land Run. This is **one of the very few surviving 1890 census records in the country** — the national 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed by fire.
- **Where to find it:** FamilySearch and Ancestry both have digitized copies; it covers the Unassigned Lands opened in April 1889.

### 3. County Vital Records (Marriage, Birth, Death)
- **Coverage:** County marriage records index back to 1890 on FamilySearch.
- **Note:** Oklahoma did not require statewide birth and death registration until 1908; earlier vital events must be found in county records or church registers.

### 4. Indian Census Rolls & Dawes Roll
- **Critical distinction:** Eastern Oklahoma was **Indian Territory**, not Oklahoma Territory, until statehood in 1907. Families there appear in **Five Civilized Tribes** records, not in the standard territorial record sets.
- **Dawes Roll (1898–1914):** The definitive enrollment of Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole citizens and freedmen. Searchable on Ancestry and the Oklahoma Historical Society's website.
- **Indian Census Rolls (1885–1940):** Annual federal enumerations of tribal members; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### 5. Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)
- **Holdings:** Territorial newspapers (many digitized), county histories, WPA historical records, photographs, and manuscript collections.
- **Website:** okhistory.org — their digital collections are extensive.

### 6. Federal Census Records (1900, 1910)
- The 1900 and 1910 censuses are the first full federal enumerations after the runs and are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1900 census asked for years of immigration and state of birth — useful for confirming origins.

### 7. Territorial Court Records
- Oklahoma Territory had U.S. District Courts. Probate, naturalization, and civil records are at the National Archives–Southwest Region (Fort Worth) and some are on FamilySearch.

### 8. Church Records
- Many settlers brought their congregation memberships with them. Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian records survive for some Oklahoma Territory churches; check the OHS manuscript collections.

---

## Critical Jurisdictional Warning

| Region | Pre-1907 Jurisdiction | Record Set |
|---|---|---|
| Western Oklahoma | **Oklahoma Territory** | Federal homestead, OHS, standard county records |
| Eastern Oklahoma | **Indian Territory** | Dawes Roll, Indian census, Five Tribes records |

Until you know which county your ancestors settled in, you cannot be sure which repository system applies. Start by identifying the county, then use the homestead file to trace backward to their state of origin.

---

## Recommended First Steps

1. **Identify the county** where your ancestor settled (or claimed land in the run).
2. **Search the GLO records** (glorecords.blm.gov) by surname for a patent or homestead entry.
3. **Pull the full homestead case file** from the National Archives — it will often reveal where they came from.
4. **Check the 1890 Oklahoma Special Census** and the 1900 federal census to establish the household.
5. **Determine if they had Native American ancestry** — if so, shift immediately to the Dawes Roll and Five Tribes records.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Oklahoma (1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Opened for settlement:** April 22, 1889 (Land Run of 1889; President Benjamin Harrison opened approximately two million acres of the Unassigned Lands at noon)
- **Territory organized:** May 2, 1890 (Organic Act created Oklahoma Territory; capital at Guthrie)
- **Statehood:** November 16, 1907
- **Land offices (1889):** Guthrie and Kingfisher — the two points where homestead claims were filed
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government / Indian Territory (before 1890); Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907)
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 people participated in the April 22, 1889 Land Run alone. Subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 opened additional areas. Population data by census year was not returned by the population tool for this jurisdiction.
- **Economy:** Farming (wheat, cotton), cattle ranching, nascent oil industry in the early 1900s
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other adjacent states; significant Native American population (Five Civilized Tribes in Indian Territory; other tribes across the territory); African American settlers (including all-Black towns such as Boley and Langston)
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic congregations established in new towns beginning 1889; mission churches predating the runs in Indian Territory
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (April 22); Organic Act 1890; additional runs 1891–1895; Oklahoma and Indian Territory merged at statehood 1907

## Boundary changes
- **Before April 22, 1889:** The central area now known as Oklahoma was the "Unassigned Lands," held as part of Indian Territory under federal administration. No territorial government existed.
- **April 22, 1889 – May 2, 1890:** Settlers were present but there was no territorial government; only federal land records were created.
- **May 2, 1890:** Oklahoma Territory formally organized under the Organic Act. Indian Territory continued separately in eastern Oklahoma.
- **1890–1907:** Oklahoma Territory (western/central) and Indian Territory (eastern) coexisted as two distinct federal jurisdictions. Records for families in the eastern portion fall under Indian Territory, not Oklahoma Territory.
- **November 16, 1907:** Both territories merged into the state of Oklahoma. County-level record-keeping consolidated under state authority.
- **Important:** A family in what is now Tulsa County before 1907 was in Indian Territory — search Indian Territory repositories, not Oklahoma Territory ones, for their pre-statehood records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Oklahoma-specific vital records page; a specific statewide registration start date cannot be cited from tool results. The generic FamilySearch records overview notes that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s. Consult the Oklahoma State Department of Health for confirmation of when mandatory registration began.
- **What exists:** County marriages 1890–1995 are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 2134789, 456,789 records, 228,394 images). Pre-statehood marriage licenses were issued at the county level once counties were organized under Oklahoma Territory (1890 onward). Birth and death registration for the territorial period is sparse.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Department of Health (vital records post-statehood); county courthouses (territorial marriages); FamilySearch (county marriages 1890–1995 online)
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth/death registration existed during most of the territorial period. Church records and family Bible entries are the primary substitute for births and deaths before statehood.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal/burial registers (see Church records); Indian agency records for Native American families; federal homestead proof files (which can record family members' presence and ages)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Catholic, and various mission churches established from 1889 onward in Oklahoma Territory; missions in Indian Territory predating 1889
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; mission records include school enrollment for Native American students
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 records, 61,728 images) — indexed on FamilySearch
- **Where held:** Denominational archives (e.g., Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church); Oklahoma Historical Society; FamilySearch (collection 1654321)
- **Language:** English in most cases; some Catholic mission records may be in Latin or Spanish
- **Coverage gap:** The FamilySearch Wiki noted that church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established congregations in the new towns (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Records from the first years of settlement are inconsistent and survival varies by congregation.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921. However, Oklahoma Territory's 1890 special census survived and is one of the few extant 1890 enumerations in the nation — search it before assuming 1890 coverage is absent (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). The 1900 and 1910 federal censuses cover Oklahoma Territory and early statehood.
- **Indian censuses and rolls:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 records, 283,945 images) — covers the Five Civilized Tribes and other nations in Indian Territory and early Oklahoma.
- **Territorial/county tax rolls:** County-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers who do not appear in surviving census records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Access:** The 1890 Oklahoma special census, 1900 federal census, and 1910 federal census are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Indian censuses are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1987432).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, civil and criminal cases, naturalizations
- **Territorial courts:** Oklahoma Territory had district courts (1890–1907) handling probate, civil, criminal, and naturalization matters. Records are held at the National Archives at Fort Worth, Texas, and the Oklahoma State Archives (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Naturalization:** Pre-September 27, 1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — check territorial district courts. After 1906, only federal courts handled naturalizations.
- **Date range:** From county organization onward (varies; most counties organized 1890–1907); earlier events involving Oklahoma Territory residents may have probate records in the departure state.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth (territorial court records); Oklahoma State Archives; individual county courthouses (post-statehood)
- **Access:** Largely physical only or microfilm; check NARA catalog for territorial court record series

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (Public Land Survey System) — Oklahoma is a federal-land state
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The General Land Office (GLO), U.S. Department of the Interior, administered homestead claims. Land patents and homestead files are in Record Group 49 at the National Archives, Washington, D.C. (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final certificates, land patents, contest/rejected applications, bounty land warrants (for veterans using warrants in Oklahoma), county deed books (post-county organization)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 records, 117,283 images) — indexed on FamilySearch
- **Digitized volume:** DGS 005221388 — land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889–1907, 402 images, **74% name-indexed** (indexed + images, accessible via FamilySearch record search)
- **BLM GLO website:** glorecords.blm.gov — partially indexes Oklahoma land patents and is searchable by name (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **What the files contain:** Each homestead file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement with witness statements (listing neighbors and associates), and the final patent. Rejected applications also survive and can contain family details (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Note on timing:** Claimants who filed in April 1889 needed to prove five years' residence; their final proof papers date to approximately 1894. The homestead file spans from initial claim to final patent.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898), Philippine-American War (1899–1902), World War I (1917–1918 registrations)
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; WWI draft registration cards (available on Ancestry and FamilySearch); state adjutant general records at the Oklahoma State Archives
- **Indian Territory / Native American service:** Indian Home Guard and other units; records at NARA
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. for service/pension; St. Louis for 20th-century records); Fold3 (online, subscription) for service records and pension indexes; FamilySearch for draft registrations

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves cover many Oklahoma cemeteries, though early Land Run-era burials in rural areas may not yet be transcribed
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries and funeral homes; Oklahoma Historical Society holds some compiled cemetery indexes
- **Note:** Many early settlers were buried in family or community plots before formal cemeteries were established — look for farm burial grounds in land records and local histories

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Town newspapers sprang up immediately after the 1889 run — the Oklahoma State Capital (Guthrie), the Oklahoma City Times, and dozens of county papers. Many are held on microfilm.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society (extensive newspaper microfilm collection); Newspapers.com (subscription, online); Library of Congress Chronicling America (free, partial coverage)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (land contests, probate), and community news that name early settlers and their family connections

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most Land Run settlers migrated internally from other U.S. states, not from abroad. For immigrant ancestors, the relevant port-of-entry and naturalization records are from wherever they first entered the United States — not Oklahoma.
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island), New Orleans, Galveston, and other Gulf ports for immigrants who came through the South before moving to Oklahoma
- **Naturalization:** Territorial district court naturalizations (pre-1906) at NARA Fort Worth; federal court naturalizations (post-1906) at NARA Fort Worth. Search the departure state's courts as well — many immigrants naturalized before arriving in Oklahoma.
- **Passenger lists:** Indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch; images at NARA and FamilySearch
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family group.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax rolls from 1890 onward
- **Date range:** County tax rolls begin when each county was organized (1890–1907 for most)
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Archives; individual county courthouses; some microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls from the 1890s are particularly valuable as substitutes for the destroyed 1890 census (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). A taxpayer appearing on an 1893 roll places that person in that county at that date.

### Indian Territory / Native American records
- **Dawes Commission (Dawes Rolls):** The primary enrollment of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) conducted 1898–1914. Essential for any family with possible Native American ancestry in eastern Oklahoma.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 records)
- **Digitized volume:** DGS 005221389 — Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910, 176 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only**. Must be browsed image by image.
- **Indian agency records:** Annual census rolls, allotment files, and school records held at NARA and the Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Note:** Families in the eastern counties (what was Indian Territory) are not in Oklahoma Territory records before 1907 — they are in Indian Territory records held at different repositories.

### Other record types
- **Sooner/contest records:** Claims filed before the official start were contested. Contest records survive at NARA (Record Group 49) and may document family members and neighbors.
- **Local and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century county histories contain biographical sketches of early settlers and often transcribe records since lost. Check WorldCat and the Oklahoma Historical Society's library.
- **City directories:** Oklahoma City, Guthrie, and other early towns produced directories beginning in the 1890s — useful for placing an ancestor at a specific address between censuses.
- **School records:** Territorial and early state school district records at the Oklahoma State Archives and county level; mission school records in FamilySearch collection 1654321.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (1541872); Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (1987432); Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 (2134789); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (1654321); digitized homestead final proofs (DGS 005221388, 74% indexed); Dawes enrollment jackets (DGS 005221389, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (including 1900, 1910 Oklahoma); military and draft records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO Records | Oklahoma land patents and homestead records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension indexes | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Oklahoma newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for territorial court records, General Land Office files (RG 49) | Free finding aids; records in-person or via request |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Oklahoma for 1880–1910; totalResults was 2, so this is the complete digitized volume set at this place and period — no additional pages exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth, TX | Oklahoma and Indian Territory district court records (probate, civil, criminal, naturalization); some land records | In-person; NARA online catalog for finding aids |
| National Archives, Washington, D.C. | General Land Office homestead files (RG 49); rejected applications; land patents | Written request; some indexes online |
| Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) | Territorial government records; early state records; county records on microfilm | In-person; some online |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | Territorial/early state records; 1890 special census; newspaper microfilm; county histories; compiled cemetery indexes; Indian agency records | In-person; some digital |
| Individual county courthouses | Deed books, county court records, marriage licenses (post-county organization) | In-person or mail |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial district court civil and criminal case files (physical at NARA Fort Worth)
- Pre-statehood probate records for most counties (physical at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives)
- County tax rolls from the 1890s (microfilm at Oklahoma State Archives; some at county courthouses)
- Most early church congregation registers outside the FamilySearch mission/church collection
- Sexton records for individual cemeteries
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (DGS 005221389) are digitized but **browse-only** — no name index, no full-text search
- Contested homestead and Sooner-claim files at NARA (RG 49) beyond what FamilySearch has indexed

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire in 1921. No tool result states that Oklahoma Territory's 1890 special census was destroyed; it is specifically noted as a survivor (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). The special census, not the general federal enumeration, is the 1890 resource for this jurisdiction.
- No tool result in this survey states that any other specific Oklahoma record set was destroyed. The absence of certain collections from FamilySearch's indexed holdings is a digitization gap, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with the homestead file.** For any ancestor who participated in a land run, the homestead application file is the single richest early document. It names family members, gives ages, lists witnesses (often neighbors and relatives), and describes improvements to the claim. Search FamilySearch collection 1541872 and the BLM GLO site (glorecords.blm.gov) first (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Work backward through the departure state.** Land Run settlers came from other states. Once you identify the state of origin from a homestead proof, territorial court record, or census birthplace, the main body of family documentation is in that state — not in Oklahoma. Do not limit research to Oklahoma records.
- **Use the 1890 Oklahoma special census.** It is one of the few surviving 1890 enumerations in the country and names residents of the new territory just one year after the run (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). Available at the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Distinguish Indian Territory from Oklahoma Territory.** Ancestors in the eastern counties before 1907 were under Indian Territory governance. Their marriage, probate, and court records are in Indian Territory repositories (NARA Fort Worth, Oklahoma Historical Society), not in Oklahoma Territory county records.
- **Check the Dawes Rolls for any possible Native American ancestry.** Five Civilized Tribes enrollment jackets (DGS 005221389 on FamilySearch) must be browsed image by image — they are not name-indexed. The enrollee number from the Dawes Roll unlocks land allotment records as well.
- **Use 1890s tax rolls as a census substitute.** County property tax rolls from the early 1890s document settlers in the years between the 1890 special census and the 1900 federal census (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Available at the Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Check territorial court records for naturalizations.** Immigrants who settled in Oklahoma Territory before September 27, 1906 could naturalize in any court of record — district courts, county courts, or probate courts. These records are at NARA Fort Worth (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Read the entire homestead proof file, including witnesses.** Witness statements in homestead final proofs name neighbors and associates who were often relatives — a critical cluster-research tool when the family surname is not yet known in Oklahoma records.
- **Search local newspapers for land contest notices.** Disputed homestead claims were published as legal notices in territorial newspapers; these can name claimants, witnesses, and relatives who are otherwise invisible in early records.

However, Oklahoma Territory's 1890 special census survived and is one of the few extant 1890 enumerations in the nation — search it before assuming 1890 coverage is absent (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). The 1900 and 1910 federal censuses cover Oklahoma Territory and early statehood.
- **Indian censuses and rolls:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 records, 283,945 images) — covers the Five Civilized Tribes and other nations in Indian Territory and early Oklahoma.
- **Territorial/county tax rolls:** County-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers who do not appear in surviving census records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Access:** The 1890 Oklahoma special census, 1900 federal census, and 1910 federal census are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Indian censuses are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1987432).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, civil and criminal cases, naturalizations
- **Territorial courts:** Oklahoma Territory had district courts (1890–1907) handling probate, civil, criminal, and naturalization matters. Records are held at the National Archives at Fort Worth, Texas, and the Oklahoma State Archives (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Naturalization:** Pre-September 27, 1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — check territorial district courts. After 1906, only federal courts handled naturalizations.
- **Date range:** From county organization onward (varies; most counties organized 1890–1907); earlier events involving Oklahoma Territory residents may have probate records in the departure state.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth (territorial court records); Oklahoma State Archives; individual county courthouses (post-statehood)
- **Access:** Largely physical only or microfilm; check NARA catalog for territorial court record series

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (Public Land Survey System) — Oklahoma is a federal-land state
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The General Land Office (GLO), U.S. Department of the Interior, administered homestead claims. Land patents and homestead files are in Record Group 49 at the National Archives, Washington, D.C. (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final certificates, land patents, contest/rejected applications, bounty land warrants (for veterans using warrants in Oklahoma), county deed books (post-county organization)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 records, 117,283 images) — indexed on FamilySearch
- **Digitized volume:** DGS 005221388 — land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889–1907, 402 images, **74% name-indexed** (indexed + images, accessible via FamilySearch record search)
- **BLM GLO website:** glorecords.blm.gov — partially indexes Oklahoma land patents and is searchable by name (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **What the files contain:** Each homestead file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement with witness statements (listing neighbors and associates), and the final patent. Rejected applications also survive and can contain family details (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Note on timing:** Claimants who filed in April 1889 needed to prove five years' residence; their final proof papers date to approximately 1894. The homestead file spans from initial claim to final patent.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898), Philippine-American War (1899–1902), World War I (1917–1918 registrations)
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; WWI draft registration cards (available on Ancestry and FamilySearch); state adjutant general records at the Oklahoma State Archives
- **Indian Territory / Native American service:** Indian Home Guard and other units; records at NARA
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. for service/pension; St. Louis for 20th-century records); Fold3 (online, subscription) for service records and pension indexes; FamilySearch for draft registrations

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves cover many Oklahoma cemeteries, though early Land Run-era burials in rural areas may not yet be transcribed
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries and funeral homes; Oklahoma Historical Society holds some compiled cemetery indexes
- **Note:** Many early settlers were buried in family or community plots before formal cemeteries were established — look for farm burial grounds in land records and local histories

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Town newspapers sprang up immediately after the 1889 run — the Oklahoma State Capital (Guthrie), the Oklahoma City Times, and dozens of county papers. Many are held on microfilm.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society (extensive newspaper microfilm collection); Newspapers.com (subscription, online); Library of Congress Chronicling America (free, partial coverage)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (land contests, probate), and community news that name early settlers and their family connections

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most Land Run settlers migrated internally from other U.S. states, not from abroad. For immigrant ancestors, the relevant port-of-entry and naturalization records are from wherever they first entered the United States — not Oklahoma.
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island), New Orleans, Galveston, and other Gulf ports for immigrants who came through the South before moving to Oklahoma
- **Naturalization:** Territorial district court naturalizations (pre-1906) at NARA Fort Worth; federal court naturalizations (post-1906) at NARA Fort Worth. Search the departure state's courts as well — many immigrants naturalized before arriving in Oklahoma.
- **Passenger lists:** Indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch; images at NARA and FamilySearch
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family group.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax rolls from 1890 onward
- **Date range:** County tax rolls begin when each county was organized (1890–1907 for most)
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Archives; individual county courthouses; some microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls from the 1890s are particularly valuable as substitutes for the destroyed 1890 census (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). A taxpayer appearing on an 1893 roll places that person in that county at that date.

### Indian Territory / Native American records
- **Dawes Commission (Dawes Rolls):** The primary enrollment of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) conducted 1898–1914. Essential for any family with possible Native American ancestry in eastern Oklahoma.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 records)
- **Digitized volume:** DGS 005221389 — Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910, 176 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only**. Must be browsed image by image.
- **Indian agency records:** Annual census rolls, allotment files, and school records held at NARA and the Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Note:** Families in the eastern counties (what was Indian Territory) are not in Oklahoma Territory records before 1907 — they are in Indian Territory records held at different repositories.

### Other record types
- **Sooner/contest records:** Claims filed before the official start were contested. Contest records survive at NARA (Record Group 49) and may document family members and neighbors.
- **Local and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century county histories contain biographical sketches of early settlers and often transcribe records since lost. Check WorldCat and the Oklahoma Historical Society's library.
- **City directories:** Oklahoma City, Guthrie, and other early towns produced directories beginning in the 1890s — useful for placing an ancestor at a specific address between censuses.
- **School records:** Territorial and early state school district records at the Oklahoma State Archives and county level; mission school records in FamilySearch collection 1654321.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (1541872); Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (1987432); Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 (2134789); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (1654321); digitized homestead final proofs (DGS 005221388, 74% indexed); Dawes enrollment jackets (DGS 005221389, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (including 1900, 1910 Oklahoma); military and draft records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO Records | Oklahoma land patents and homestead records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension indexes | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Oklahoma newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for territorial court records, General Land Office files (RG 49) | Free finding aids; records in-person or via request |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Oklahoma for 1880–1910; totalResults was 2, so this is the complete digitized volume set at this place and period — no additional pages exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth, TX | Oklahoma and Indian Territory district court records (probate, civil, criminal, naturalization); some land records | In-person; NARA online catalog for finding aids |
| National Archives, Washington, D.C. | General Land Office homestead files (RG 49); rejected applications; land patents | Written request; some indexes online |
| Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) | Territorial government records; early state records; county records on microfilm | In-person; some online |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | Territorial/early state records; 1890 special census; newspaper microfilm; county histories; compiled cemetery indexes; Indian agency records | In-person; some digital |
| Individual county courthouses | Deed books, county court records, marriage licenses (post-county organization) | In-person or mail |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial district court civil and criminal case files (physical at NARA Fort Worth)
- Pre-statehood probate records for most counties (physical at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives)
- County tax rolls from the 1890s (microfilm at Oklahoma State Archives; some at county courthouses)
- Most early church congregation registers outside the FamilySearch mission/church collection
- Sexton records for individual cemeteries
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (DGS 005221389) are digitized but **browse-only** — no name index, no full-text search
- Contested homestead and Sooner-claim files at NARA (RG 49) beyond what FamilySearch has indexed

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire in 1921. No tool result states that Oklahoma Territory's 1890 special census was destroyed; it is specifically noted as a survivor (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). The special census, not the general federal enumeration, is the 1890 resource for this jurisdiction.
- No tool result in this survey states that any other specific Oklahoma record set was destroyed. The absence of certain collections from FamilySearch's indexed holdings is a digitization gap, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with the homestead file.** For any ancestor who participated in a land run, the homestead application file is the single richest early document. It names family members, gives ages, lists witnesses (often neighbors and relatives), and describes improvements to the claim. Search FamilySearch collection 1541872 and the BLM GLO site (glorecords.blm.gov) first (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Work backward through the departure state.** Land Run settlers came from other states. Once you identify the state of origin from a homestead proof, territorial court record, or census birthplace, the main body of family documentation is in that state — not in Oklahoma. Do not limit research to Oklahoma records.
- **Use the 1890 Oklahoma special census.** It is one of the few surviving 1890 enumerations in the country and names residents of the new territory just one year after the run (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). Available at the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Distinguish Indian Territory from Oklahoma Territory.** Ancestors in the eastern counties before 1907 were under Indian Territory governance. Their marriage, probate, and court records are in Indian Territory repositories (NARA Fort Worth, Oklahoma Historical Society), not in Oklahoma Territory county records.
- **Check the Dawes Rolls for any possible Native American ancestry.** Five Civilized Tribes enrollment jackets (DGS 005221389 on FamilySearch) must be browsed image by image — they are not name-indexed. The enrollee number from the Dawes Roll unlocks land allotment records as well.
- **Use 1890s tax rolls as a census substitute.** County property tax rolls from the early 1890s document settlers in the years between the 1890 special census and the 1900 federal census (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Available at the Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Check territorial court records for naturalizations.** Immigrants who settled in Oklahoma Territory before September 27, 1906 could naturalize in any court of record — district courts, county courts, or probate courts. These records are at NARA Fort Worth (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Read the entire homestead proof file, including witnesses.** Witness statements in homestead final proofs name neighbors and associates who were often relatives — a critical cluster-research tool when the family surname is not yet known in Oklahoma records.
- **Search local newspapers for land contest notices.** Disputed homestead claims were published as legal notices in territorial newspapers; these can name claimants, witnesses, and relatives who are otherwise invisible in early records.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality research guide the agent produced:

---

## Alabama Region circa 1800 — Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Context

Around 1800, present-day Alabama was **not yet a state**. It was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (created 1798). Crucially, the **Mobile area** was under **Spanish colonial rule** until 1813 — meaning records are split across two foreign colonial powers in addition to U.S. territorial sources.

---

### Digitized, Browsable Volumes

**A FamilySearch search for every digitized image volume covering Alabama 1780–1820 returned zero results.** There is nothing to scroll through page-by-page on FamilySearch for this era and place. This is a significant gap.

---

### What Does Survive — and Where

| Record Type | Date Range | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch indexed church records | From 1803 | FamilySearch (name-searchable) |
| FamilySearch county marriage records | From 1809 | FamilySearch (name-searchable) |
| FamilySearch probate records | From 1809 | FamilySearch (name-searchable) |
| Census/substitute index | From 1810 | FamilySearch (name-searchable) |
| Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) | 1801–1810 | **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH), Montgomery — physical/microfilm only** |
| Territorial court records, tax lists, militia rolls | ~1798–1817 | ADAH — physical/microfilm only |
| Spanish colonial household censuses & Catholic parish registers | Pre-1813, back to 1702 | **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** (copies at Library of Congress) |
| French colonial records (pre-1763) | Pre-1763 | French archives |
| Federal land patents (territorial era) | Territorial period | **BLM General Land Office** website — digitized and searchable online ✓ |

---

### Key Takeaways

1. **FamilySearch indexed collections only reach back to 1803–1810** for this region, covering the very tail end of the territorial period.
2. **The richest 1800-era records** (territorial censuses, tax lists, court records) are at **ADAH in Montgomery** — not online.
3. **Mobile-area records** from the Spanish period require working with the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville or the Library of Congress copies in Spanish.
4. **BLM General Land Office** is the strongest *online* source with browsable, image-viewable federal land patents.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

- Contact or visit **ADAH** and obtain their finding aids for territorial-era microfilm (censuses, tax lists).
- Request the Library of Congress finding aid for their **Spanish colonial copies** from Seville.
- Build a research plan specifically targeting the **1801, 1805, and 1808 Mississippi Territory censuses** for any families of interest.
