# Locality Guide: Alabama Region — Territorial Period (ca. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Governing jurisdiction at 1800:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817). Alabama achieved statehood in 1819, preceded by the Alabama Territory (1817–1819).
- **Administrative center:** No dedicated Alabama-portion capital during the Mississippi Territory period; the territorial capital was near Natchez (present-day Mississippi). After 1817, St. Stephens (Washington County) served as the Alabama Territory seat.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (from the Province of Georgia cession and cessions from Spanish West Florida)
- **Population during period:** Population figures for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory were not returned by the place_population tool in this survey. The region was sparsely settled in 1800; growth accelerated sharply after the Creek War (1813–1814).
- **Economy:** Frontier agriculture, fur trade, early cotton production in river valleys, trading posts at Mobile and along the Tombigbee and Alabama rivers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Indigenous Creek and Cherokee nations (dominant through most of the territory); European-American settlers migrating from Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia; French Creole and Spanish Creole communities in the Mobile area; enslaved African Americans. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama)
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist and Baptist circuit riders served the growing settler population; Catholic parish at Mobile (established under French rule ca. 1702 and continuous through Spanish rule); some Presbyterian presence. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Alabama-specific denominational data for this period in this survey.
- **Key historical events:** Creek War (1813–1814), U.S. seizure of Mobile from Spain (1813), organization of the Alabama Territory (1817), Alabama statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes

- **Pre-1763:** Mobile area under French colonial rule (Province of Louisiana).
- **1763–1780:** Mobile area under British rule (British West Florida).
- **1780–1813:** Mobile District under Spanish rule (Spanish West Florida). Spain controlled Mobile and the surrounding region.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory created, covering the eastern (Alabama) lands ceded from Georgia. The Spanish retained Mobile.
- **1804 and 1812:** Mississippi Territory expanded to encompass all of present-day Alabama and Mississippi.
- **1813:** United States seized Mobile from Spain. The entire Alabama region passed to U.S. territorial authority.
- **1817:** Mississippi Territory divided: western half became the State of Mississippi; eastern half became the Alabama Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama admitted as a state.

**Research implication:** A person living in present-day Alabama in 1800 generated records under the Mississippi Territory; in 1815 under U.S. authority succeeding Spanish Mobile; by 1820 under the new State of Alabama. Records for the same individual may be filed under three or more successive jurisdictions. Search all layers.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** No civil registration system existed in Alabama during the territorial period (pre-1819). The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Alabama-specific civil registration start dates in this survey; the Alabama_Vital_Records wiki_read returned only a generic fallback page.
- **What exists for this period:** FamilySearch's "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" (collection 1598408, 612,345 records, 306,172 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) begins in 1809, at the very end of the territorial period. It captures marriages recorded at the county level as new counties were organized in the final territorial years.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers and court records are the primary sources for vital events before 1809. See Church Records and Court Records sections.
- **Gaps:** No FamilySearch collections cover births or deaths before statehood. Pre-1809 marriages, where recorded at all, appear in territorial court records or church registers.

### Church records

- **What exists:** FamilySearch's "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (collection 1986396, 156,789 records, 78,394 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) begins in 1803 — the earliest name-searchable FamilySearch collection for the region.
- **The Mobile Catholic parish:** The Catholic parish at Mobile maintained continuous registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from the French colonial period (ca. 1702) through the Spanish period and into U.S. jurisdiction. These sacramental registers predate the territorial period by nearly a century and are among the earliest surviving records for any Alabama community.
- **Language:** Catholic registers from the French period (pre-1763) are in French; from the Spanish period (1780–1813) in Spanish. Protestant circuit-rider records are in English but may be sparse and discontinuous.
- **Where held:** Mobile Catholic diocese archives hold local originals. French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, France, and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish records of the Mobile District — including church registers — are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for collection 1986396 (from 1803); browse-only or physical for pre-1803 colonial church registers.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The Mississippi Territory was enumerated in the 1800 and 1810 federal censuses; Alabama as a territory in 1820. The 1800 enumeration covered heads of household only.
- **Territorial (non-federal) censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (collection 2016756, 287,634 records, no images — index only; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756). This begins at 1810, capturing the last territorial census year.
- **Digitization level:** Index only (no images) for collection 2016756; the territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 are physical only at ADAH.

### Probate and court records

- **What exists on FamilySearch:** "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (collection 1537764, 438,210 records, 219,105 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) begins in 1809. This is an indexed + images collection.
- **Pre-1809 territorial court records:** Records from the Mississippi Territory district courts (which handled the Alabama portion before county organization) predate the county-level records. The volume_search returned zero digitized volumes for Alabama dated 1780–1820 — meaning no browse-only digitized image volumes exist on FamilySearch for the territorial period. Physical territorial court records are held at ADAH.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Both wills (testate) and administrations (intestate) would appear in collection 1537764; only the very end of the territorial period (from 1809) is covered.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal-land state. Lands were surveyed under the rectangular (township-range) system and distributed through the General Land Office (GLO).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government held authority over public land distribution in the territorial period. Federal land patents for Alabama, including those issued during the territorial period, are searchable and image-viewable online at the BLM General Land Office website (https://glorecords.blm.gov/). This is the primary digitized online source for Alabama land records in this era.
- **Spanish and British land grants:** The Mobile District contained prior Spanish and British land grants that required U.S. confirmation after 1813. Originals are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville); U.S. confirmation records are at NARA. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Territorial records:** The wiki_search confirmed that land grants are among the territorial records held at ADAH. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Note:** The Alabama_Land_and_Property wiki_read returned only a generic fallback page in this survey; Alabama-specific land record details from the FamilySearch Wiki are limited to what the wiki_search returned.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Creek War (1813–1814) is the most directly relevant conflict. The War of 1812 also generated service records for men in the region. Militia service was a feature of territorial life throughout the period.
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls and service records; federal service records for the Creek War; pension files; bounty land warrants at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA, Record Group 94 (Adjutant General's records). The wiki_search confirmed militia rolls as a category of territorial records at ADAH. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records) Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) indexes many pre-Civil War military records including War of 1812 and Creek War records.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some Alabama cemeteries including early 19th-century burials, but coverage for the territorial period (pre-1820) is sparse — many graves from this era have no surviving marked stone.
- **Physical records:** The oldest cemeteries in the Mobile area have records held by the City of Mobile or the diocese. Rural pioneer cemeteries in the territorial period rarely had formal records.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Newspapers in the Alabama region before statehood were extremely rare. No newspaper coverage from around 1800 is expected. The earliest Alabama newspapers date from approximately 1811–1813, near the very end of the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and ADAH hold early Alabama newspapers, but these are primarily from statehood onward.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant context:** Most settlers in the Alabama region around 1800 arrived overland from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia — not through a single port. Passenger arrival records are not the primary tool for tracing this internal migration. Researching the family's origin state may reveal church or court records predating the Alabama arrival.
- **For Mobile:** Spanish-era Mobile had maritime traffic, but systematic U.S. passenger manifests began only with the Passenger Act of 1819. The Mobile port's records for the post-1820 period are at NARA.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including territorial courts. These would be in NARA or ADAH holdings.
- **Note on manifests:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) beginning systematically after 1820 record every person aboard, including infants traveling with parents — a full family survey of the manifest is essential when one is located for a slightly later period.

### Tax records

- **What exists:** Territorial tax lists for the Mississippi Territory (Alabama portion) exist for some years. The wiki_search confirmed tax lists as a category of territorial records held at ADAH. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from the territorial period (ca. 1800–1817) are among the best substitutes for census coverage in years when no federal or territorial enumeration was taken.
- **Digitization level:** The volume_search returned zero digitized volumes for Alabama 1780–1820. Territorial tax lists are physical at ADAH or on microfilm.

### Other record types

- **Militia rolls:** The Mississippi Territory raised militia units whose muster rolls and enrollment lists survive at NARA and ADAH. These name men who appear in no other surviving record for this period.
- **Indian affairs records:** The Creek and Cherokee nations generated treaty records, annuity rolls, and federal agent reports that sometimes name adjacent non-Indian settlers and traders. These are at NARA (Bureau of Indian Affairs records) and have been partially microfilmed.
- **Spanish colonial census (padrones):** For the Mobile District specifically, Spain conducted parish-level household censuses and maintained land grant records. These are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories from the 19th and early 20th centuries sometimes transcribe early territorial records since lost. ADAH holds many such volumes; they can also be located through WorldCat.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1803-1950 (col. 1986396); County Marriages 1809-1950 (col. 1598408); Probate Records 1809-1985 (col. 1537764); Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (col. 2016756) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents including territorial period; searchable and image-viewable | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | War of 1812 and Creek War military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records: land confirmations, military service, Indian affairs, naturalization | Free finding aids; some records digitized |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records; limited pre-1820 coverage | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 0 digitized volumes for Alabama dated 1780–1820 (the query was also run under Mississippi Territory, United States, and also returned 0). There are no browse-only digitized image volumes on FamilySearch specifically covering the pre-statehood period. The four FamilySearch collections listed above are indexed collections whose earliest dates range from 1803 (church records) to 1810 (census substitutes). They are the only FamilySearch online resources with data reaching into the territorial period, and they cover only its final years.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); territorial court records; tax lists; militia rolls; land records; state records from 1819 | In-person; ADAH online catalog at adah.alabama.gov; some records on microfilm |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington, DC and Southeast Region (Morrow, GA) | Federal land records; military service and pension records (Creek War, War of 1812); Indian affairs records; naturalization records | In-person; NARA online catalog; some on Fold3 |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | French colonial church records on microfilm; local Mobile records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records from Archivo General de Indias | In-person; some digitized at loc.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial census, church, and land records for the Mobile District | In-person or written inquiry; some digitized at pares.mcu.es |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile area (pre-1763) | In-person or written inquiry |

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for this period but are not in any online database, or exist only as physical records:

- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (physical at ADAH; returned by wiki_search but not by volume_search or collections_search)
- Territorial court records predating county organization (physical at ADAH)
- Territorial tax lists and militia rolls for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory (physical at ADAH; volume_search returned zero results for 1780–1820)
- Spanish colonial padrones (parish censuses) and land grant records for the Mobile District (Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress)
- French colonial records for Mobile (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; Mobile Municipal Archives on microfilm)

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey stated that any specific record set for this period and place was destroyed. The absence of digitized volumes in the volume_search for 1780–1820 is a digitization gap, not evidence that the physical records do not exist. ADAH should be consulted directly about the completeness of surviving territorial records. County courthouses in Alabama have experienced fires at various points in their histories; which counties and which specific record sets were affected is not confirmed by any tool result in this survey and should not be assumed either way.

## Research tips

- **Start with ADAH.** The Alabama Department of Archives and History is the primary repository for territorial-era Alabama records. Its online catalog and microfilm holdings should be the first stop after exhausting FamilySearch's early collections. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Search under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama.** Federal records created before 1817 are filed under the Mississippi Territory. NARA holdings, microfilm finding aids, and catalog searches indexed under "Alabama" may miss records filed under the territorial designation.
- **For Mobile-area ancestors, search Spanish and French colonial sources.** The Mobile District had continuous European-American settlement from 1702, and its records (Catholic church registers, colonial household censuses, land grants) run decades before the territorial period, in French and Spanish. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (French) and the Archivo General de Indias (Spanish) hold the originals; the Library of Congress holds copies of the Spanish series. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Land records are the strongest digitized online source for this period.** The BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) provides searchable, image-viewable federal land patents including those issued during the territorial period — this is the deepest fully online coverage for this era.
- **Use the 1810 federal census and the 1810 territorial census together.** Both enumerate present-day Alabama households. They may overlap or diverge; using both increases coverage.
- **Tax lists substitute for missing census years.** For 1801–1809 (between federal censuses), territorial tax lists at ADAH are the best substitute — they document taxable adults by name and locate them in the territory.
- **No browse-only digitized image volumes exist on FamilySearch for Alabama before 1820.** The volume_search returned zero results for this place and period. FamilySearch's holdings here are indexed collections (searchable by name), not page-by-page image volumes — and even those indexed collections begin only in 1803–1810. Anyone hoping to browse unindexed image volumes will need to go to ADAH or obtain microfilm.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama-specific pages did not return Alabama-specific content in this survey.** All four wiki_place_page sections and all wiki_read fetches for Alabama-specific URLs returned a generic fallback page. The wiki_search results (cited with specific source URLs above) are the only FamilySearch Wiki content grounding this guide.

- **Local papers:** Newspapers in the Alabama region before statehood were extremely rare. No newspaper coverage from around 1800 is expected. The earliest Alabama newspapers date from approximately 1811–1813, near the very end of the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and ADAH hold early Alabama newspapers, but these are primarily from statehood onward.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant context:** Most settlers in the Alabama region around 1800 arrived overland from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia — not through a single port. Passenger arrival records are not the primary tool for tracing this internal migration. Researching the family's origin state may reveal church or court records predating the Alabama arrival.
- **For Mobile:** Spanish-era Mobile had maritime traffic, but systematic U.S. passenger manifests began only with the Passenger Act of 1819. The Mobile port's records for the post-1820 period are at NARA.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including territorial courts. These would be in NARA or ADAH holdings.
- **Note on manifests:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) beginning systematically after 1820 record every person aboard, including infants traveling with parents — a full family survey of the manifest is essential when one is located for a slightly later period.

### Tax records

- **What exists:** Territorial tax lists for the Mississippi Territory (Alabama portion) exist for some years. The wiki_search confirmed tax lists as a category of territorial records held at ADAH. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from the territorial period (ca. 1800–1817) are among the best substitutes for census coverage in years when no federal or territorial enumeration was taken.
- **Digitization level:** The volume_search returned zero digitized volumes for Alabama 1780–1820. Territorial tax lists are physical at ADAH or on microfilm.

### Other record types

- **Militia rolls:** The Mississippi Territory raised militia units whose muster rolls and enrollment lists survive at NARA and ADAH. These name men who appear in no other surviving record for this period.
- **Indian affairs records:** The Creek and Cherokee nations generated treaty records, annuity rolls, and federal agent reports that sometimes name adjacent non-Indian settlers and traders. These are at NARA (Bureau of Indian Affairs records) and have been partially microfilmed.
- **Spanish colonial census (padrones):** For the Mobile District specifically, Spain conducted parish-level household censuses and maintained land grant records. These are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories from the 19th and early 20th centuries sometimes transcribe early territorial records since lost. ADAH holds many such volumes; they can also be located through WorldCat.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1803-1950 (col. 1986396); County Marriages 1809-1950 (col. 1598408); Probate Records 1809-1985 (col. 1537764); Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (col. 2016756) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents including territorial period; searchable and image-viewable | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | War of 1812 and Creek War military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records: land confirmations, military service, Indian affairs, naturalization | Free finding aids; some records digitized |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records; limited pre-1820 coverage | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 0 digitized volumes for Alabama dated 1780–1820 (the query was also run under Mississippi Territory, United States, and also returned 0). There are no browse-only digitized image volumes on FamilySearch specifically covering the pre-statehood period. The four FamilySearch collections listed above are indexed collections whose earliest dates range from 1803 (church records) to 1810 (census substitutes). They are the only FamilySearch online resources with data reaching into the territorial period, and they cover only its final years.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); territorial court records; tax lists; militia rolls; land records; state records from 1819 | In-person; ADAH online catalog at adah.alabama.gov; some records on microfilm |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington, DC and Southeast Region (Morrow, GA) | Federal land records; military service and pension records (Creek War, War of 1812); Indian affairs records; naturalization records | In-person; NARA online catalog; some on Fold3 |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | French colonial church records on microfilm; local Mobile records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records from Archivo General de Indias | In-person; some digitized at loc.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial census, church, and land records for the Mobile District | In-person or written inquiry; some digitized at pares.mcu.es |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile area (pre-1763) | In-person or written inquiry |

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for this period but are not in any online database, or exist only as physical records:

- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (physical at ADAH; returned by wiki_search but not by volume_search or collections_search)
- Territorial court records predating county organization (physical at ADAH)
- Territorial tax lists and militia rolls for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory (physical at ADAH; volume_search returned zero results for 1780–1820)
- Spanish colonial padrones (parish censuses) and land grant records for the Mobile District (Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress)
- French colonial records for Mobile (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; Mobile Municipal Archives on microfilm)

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey stated that any specific record set for this period and place was destroyed. The absence of digitized volumes in the volume_search for 1780–1820 is a digitization gap, not evidence that the physical records do not exist. ADAH should be consulted directly about the completeness of surviving territorial records. County courthouses in Alabama have experienced fires at various points in their histories; which counties and which specific record sets were affected is not confirmed by any tool result in this survey and should not be assumed either way.

## Research tips

- **Start with ADAH.** The Alabama Department of Archives and History is the primary repository for territorial-era Alabama records. Its online catalog and microfilm holdings should be the first stop after exhausting FamilySearch's early collections. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Search under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama.** Federal records created before 1817 are filed under the Mississippi Territory. NARA holdings, microfilm finding aids, and catalog searches indexed under "Alabama" may miss records filed under the territorial designation.
- **For Mobile-area ancestors, search Spanish and French colonial sources.** The Mobile District had continuous European-American settlement from 1702, and its records (Catholic church registers, colonial household censuses, land grants) run decades before the territorial period, in French and Spanish. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (French) and the Archivo General de Indias (Spanish) hold the originals; the Library of Congress holds copies of the Spanish series. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Land records are the strongest digitized online source for this period.** The BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) provides searchable, image-viewable federal land patents including those issued during the territorial period — this is the deepest fully online coverage for this era.
- **Use the 1810 federal census and the 1810 territorial census together.** Both enumerate present-day Alabama households. They may overlap or diverge; using both increases coverage.
- **Tax lists substitute for missing census years.** For 1801–1809 (between federal censuses), territorial tax lists at ADAH are the best substitute — they document taxable adults by name and locate them in the territory.
- **No browse-only digitized image volumes exist on FamilySearch for Alabama before 1820.** The volume_search returned zero results for this place and period. FamilySearch's holdings here are indexed collections (searchable by name), not page-by-page image volumes — and even those indexed collections begin only in 1803–1810. Anyone hoping to browse unindexed image volumes will need to go to ADAH or obtain microfilm.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama-specific pages did not return Alabama-specific content in this survey.** All four wiki_place_page sections and all wiki_read fetches for Alabama-specific URLs returned a generic fallback page. The wiki_search results (cited with specific source URLs above) are the only FamilySearch Wiki content grounding this guide.

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide, 1860–1900

### Core County: Schuylkill County (formed 1811)

Population grew from ~90,000 to ~173,000 during this period, driven almost entirely by coal mining. Large numbers of Irish Famine-era immigrants and their children settled here.

---

### Critical Finding: No Statewide Civil Registration

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil birth or death registration** during the entire 1860–1900 window. This means:
- **Catholic and Protestant parish registers are the only systematic record** of baptisms and burials for this era.
- Schuylkill County Catholic records are held by the **Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives** (not Scranton — the diocese boundary matters), for all events before 1961.

---

### Specialized Coal-Region Resources

The FamilySearch Wiki page on **Pennsylvania Coal Region Records** identifies three sources unique to the anthracite field:

1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** — ~41,000 colliery workers by name, 1855–1898. Focused on Luzerne and Lackawanna counties (not Schuylkill), but essential for cross-county research.
2. **Pennsylvania Triennial Tax Assessments (from 1853)** — list occupation and sometimes nativity; useful for locating Irish miners.
3. **Diocesan archive routing** — Schuylkill County Catholic registers go to **Philadelphia**, not Scranton. A common research error.

---

### FamilySearch Digitized Volumes

Of five digitized FamilySearch volumes for Schuylkill County in this period:
- **Four are browse-only** (no name index) — must be examined image by image.
- Only the **deed records volume (007936752)** carries any indexing, and that only at ~22%.

---

### The Other Four Coal Counties

Each needs its own locality survey:

| County | Key Note |
|---|---|
| **Luzerne** | Pre-1878 Lackawanna records sit here |
| **Lackawanna** | Not formed until 1878; earlier records under Luzerne |
| **Carbon** | Separate survey needed |
| **Northumberland** | Separate survey needed |

---

### Recommended Next Step

Build a **research plan** using this locality guide as the foundation. The subagent suggests the `research-plan` skill as the logical next move. If you have a specific ancestor in mind (a name, approximate dates, county), share that and we can sequence which record sets to hit first.

quirks: Lackawanna County was formed from Luzerne County in 1878 — records for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre area before 1878 are filed under Luzerne County; search Luzerne first for events before that year.

Before 1868, all five anthracite coal counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) fell under the Catholic Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna transferred to the Diocese of Scranton, Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg; Schuylkill and Carbon stayed with Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. The diocesan archive holding a Catholic baptismal or marriage register depends on the county and the year — for Schuylkill County events, search the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives for records prior to 1961.

Pennsylvania statewide death certificates begin in 1906 — deaths during 1860–1905 are documented only in church burial registers, cemetery sexton records, and newspaper obituaries, none of which are systematically indexed online for this county.

No statewide civil birth registration existed in Pennsylvania during the target period. Church baptismal registers are the primary source; volume 007936751 (church records, 1842–1895, 187 images) is browse-only and includes German-language registers — some records require reading German.

Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853; the assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — directly useful for locating Irish-born miners between census years. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)

Company payroll indexes (which name individual colliery workers) are distinct from mine-inspection and accident reports (which are organized by colliery, not by person). Use payroll-derived indexes as the direct genealogical tool; accident reports require first knowing which colliery the ancestor worked at. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)

The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898) names approximately 41,000 colliery workers from the lower anthracite field (Luzerne/Lackawanna area), not Schuylkill County. Researchers should consult it when tracing a family across county lines within the region.

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. If an ancestor is not found in Schuylkill County's naturalization volume (007936750, browse-only), check adjacent county courts and the federal courts in Philadelphia.
The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed — use the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses and the Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments of the early 1890s to place families in the gap years.
One FamilySearch collection returned for this place is labeled 'synthetic test fixture' (ID SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) — verify its actual availability on FamilySearch before relying on it.

The unsurveyed coal counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland — each require their own locality survey. A family following the anthracite field likely generated records in multiple counties.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:**
  - 1860: 89,510
  - 1870: 116,428
  - 1880: 129,974
  - 1900: 172,927
  (Source: U.S. Census via FamilySearch place_population)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the dominant industry. Colliery work — loading, hauling, breaker work — employed most male immigrants. The Reading Railroad served the county and shaped settlement patterns along its lines.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant population from the 1840s Famine wave onward; also Welsh, English, Pennsylvania German (from earlier settlement), and by the 1880s–1890s a growing Eastern European presence (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak communities).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish immigrants), Welsh Congregationalist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Evangelical Lutheran, German Reformed.

- **FamilySearch volume:** Volume 007936752 — Schuylkill County Deed Records 1815–1900, 543 images. **22% name-indexed** (partially indexed + images available). This is the only Schuylkill County volume in this survey with meaningful indexing.
- **Access:** Partial name index at FamilySearch; the remaining ~78% must be browsed. County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville, holds originals.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); coal-region Irish-Americans served in Pennsylvania volunteer regiments. Spanish-American War (1898) falls at the edge of the target period.
- **Record types:** NARA Civil War service records and pension files; Pennsylvania State Archives regimental records; Civil War draft registrations (NARA provost marshal records); Spanish-American War records at NARA.
- **Access:** Civil War pension files and service records at NARA; many are digitized on Fold3 (subscription) and Ancestry (subscription). State adjutant general records at Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Catholic, Protestant, and nondenominational cemeteries established for coal-mining communities; sexton records held by individual cemeteries and parishes.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves provide headstone images and transcriptions for many Schuylkill County cemeteries; coverage varies by cemetery.
- **Value for this period:** Cemetery records are a primary source for deaths 1860–1905 given the complete absence of civil death registration.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville), established 1825, was the dominant regional newspaper through the target period. It carried obituaries, birth notices, marriage announcements, mine accident reports, and Molly Maguires trial coverage.
- **Where held:** Held by the Schuylkill County Historical Society and partially available on microfilm through the Pennsylvania State Library. Online availability of the Miners' Journal was not confirmed by any tool result in this session.
- **Content value:** Mine accident reports name victims and their workplaces; labor-dispute coverage names union officers and Molly Maguires defendants; community notices record Irish immigrant social and religious life.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Irish immigrants typically arrived through Philadelphia (closer), New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island from 1892), or Baltimore. Passenger lists are at NARA and indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA Series M237 for New York, M425 for Philadelphia); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions at Schuylkill County courts (volume 007936750, browse-only, 1849–1915).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest page for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. Pre-1895 manifests contain limited detail; post-1895 manifests add birthplace, nearest relative in country of origin, and contact person in the U.S.
- **Access:** Naturalization volume (007936750) is browse-only at FamilySearch. Passenger lists are name-indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Tax records
- **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments** (from Pennsylvania Coal Region Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records): State assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. Directly useful for identifying Irish-born miners and placing families between census years.
- **External link (pre-period context):** FamilySearch curated an Ancestry link to 'Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801' (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/). This collection predates the target period by 60+ years and is background context, not a prime source for 1860–1900.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; some county assessor records may survive at the Schuylkill County Historical Society.
- **Substitute value:** The triennial assessments covering the early 1890s are especially valuable as a substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census.

### Specialized coal-region records
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898** (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records): Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field (Luzerne/Lackawanna counties), drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. **This index covers the lower anthracite field, not Schuylkill County**, but is essential when following a family across county lines within the region.
- **Payroll vs. accident reports:** Per the coal-region wiki page: 'company payroll indexes (which name individual colliery workers) [are distinct] from mine-inspection and accident reports (which are organized by colliery, not by person).' Payroll-derived indexes are the more direct genealogical tool.
- **Molly Maguires trial records:** The 1876–1877 trials generated extensive court records, newspaper coverage, and Pinkerton Detective Agency reports, many naming Irish-born Schuylkill County miners. Held at the Schuylkill County courthouse and covered in published regional histories.
- **Labor union records:** Workingmen's Benevolent Association and United Mine Workers membership and benefit records may survive in union archives or local historical societies; not confirmed in tool results.

### Other record types
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published local histories often carry biographical sketches of founding families and reprint early records. The Schuylkill County Historical Society and WorldCat/OCLC are the starting points.
- **City directories:** Pottsville city directories can place an ancestor at a specific address in years between censuses.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Probate Records 1851–1930 (vol. 007936749, 412 images, browse-only); Naturalization Records 1849–1915 (vol. 007936750, 298 images, browse-only); Church Records 1842–1895 (vol. 007936751, 187 images, browse-only, incl. German); Deed Records 1815–1900 (vol. 007936752, 543 images, 22% indexed); Marriage Records 1870–1910 (vol. 007936753, 94 images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (coll. 1999196, 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (coll. 1921317, 524,189 indexed records with images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (coll. 1571957, 312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (coll. 1502909, 198,765 index records, no images) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/); federal census years 1860–1900; Civil War service records and pension files (Fold3, same parent company) | Subscription |

**Note:** One collection returned by FamilySearch collections_search is labeled 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)' (ID SYNTH-PA-CHURCH). This label indicates a test fixture; verify whether it represents a real browsable collection before relying on it.

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized volumes match Schuylkill County for the target period; all 5 are detailed above (this was the complete result set — volume_search returned no nextPageToken and totalResults was 5).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, marriage licenses, court records, naturalization petitions, will books | In-person; many series microfilmed at FamilySearch |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Miners' Journal microfilm, local histories, family files, cemetery transcriptions | In-person; contact for remote research services |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Statewide vital records (post-1906), military records, state tax assessments, land office records | In-person; partial online access via Pennsylvania Digital Archives |
| Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County (pre-1961, when Diocese of Allentown was erected) | Contact archives for access |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill and Carbon counties after 1961 diocese erection | Contact diocese for access |
| National Archives (NARA), Philadelphia & Washington DC | Civil War service records and pension files, passenger lists, naturalization records post-1906 | In-person; Fold3/Ancestry for digitized records |

## Records NOT online

- **Civil birth records:** No civil birth registration during 1860–1900 in Pennsylvania at the statewide level. Church baptismal registers are the only systematic source; volume 007936751 (1842–1895, 187 images) is browse-only.
- **Civil death records:** Pennsylvania statewide death certificates begin in 1906. Deaths 1860–1905 are in church burial registers, cemetery sexton records, and newspaper obituaries — none systematically indexed online for this county.
- **Naturalization petitions:** Volume 007936750 (1849–1915, 298 images) is browse-only; no name index exists online.
- **Church records (full set):** Volume 007936751 is browse-only and covers only 187 images. Many parish registers remain in physical custody of individual parishes and the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives.
- **Miners' Journal newspaper:** Online availability was not confirmed by any tool result in this session.
- **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (1853 onward):** Not confirmed as available in any online database in this session. Physical holdings at Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index:** Online availability was not confirmed by tool results. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records for current access details.
- **Company payroll books / colliery employment records:** Physical records; access depends on whether they survived consolidation events and where individual coal company archives are held.

## Known record losses

No tool result in this session stated that a specific Schuylkill County record set was destroyed or lost. The FamilySearch wiki page https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records notes that the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index was drawn from company payroll books 'that survived a 1903 records consolidation,' implying other payroll books were lost in that consolidation — but this applies to the Lackawanna Valley (Luzerne/Lackawanna counties) specifically, not to Schuylkill County. For Schuylkill County company payroll records, the fate of individual colliery records was not stated by any tool result.

The near-complete destruction of the 1890 federal census is a national-level loss affecting all jurisdictions.

## Research tips

- **Consult the specialized coal-region wiki page first.** The FamilySearch Wiki page 'Pennsylvania Coal Region Records' (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) describes the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, diocesan archive boundaries, and the triennial tax assessments — sources unique to the anthracite field that do not appear in standard county guides.
- **Distinguish payroll indexes from accident reports.** Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records: 'company payroll indexes (which name individual colliery workers) [are distinct] from mine-inspection and accident reports (which are organized by colliery, not by person).' Payroll-derived indexes are the direct genealogical tool; accident reports require already knowing which colliery the ancestor worked at.
- **Triennial tax assessments list nativity.** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853, listing occupation and sometimes nativity. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records.) A 'nativity: Ireland' notation is confirmatory evidence and places a person in the county in non-census years, including the gap years around the destroyed 1890 census.
- **Catholic diocesan archive routing depends on the year.** For Schuylkill County Catholic parish records: all records created during the target period (1860–1900) belong to the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives; the Diocese of Allentown was not erected until 1961. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records.)
- **Search both anglicized and original Irish surname spellings.** Irish immigrants were frequently indexed under anglicized or phonetically inconsistent spellings (Flynn/Flinn, Murphy/Morphey, Sullivan/Sulivan/Solivane). Try all plausible variants in every indexed collection before concluding a person is absent.
- **The 1890 census gap is severe — use triennial assessments.** Pennsylvania's triennial tax assessments for the early 1890s are especially valuable in the coal region for bridging the destroyed 1890 census. Also search the 1880 mortality schedule and 1880 Soundex/Miracode index.
- **Church records volume (007936751) includes German-language registers.** Not all Schuylkill County church records are in English. German Reformed and Evangelical Lutheran registers may require reading German or engaging a translator.
- **Naturalization before 1906 can be in any county court.** Volume 007936750 (Schuylkill County, 1849–1915, browse-only) is the primary source, but if an ancestor is not found there, check adjacent county courts and the U.S. Circuit and District Courts in Philadelphia.
- **Deed records are the most indexed source available online.** Volume 007936752 (Deed Records 1815–1900, 22% indexed) is the only Schuylkill County volume with significant name indexing. Even tenants and boarders sometimes appear as witnesses or grantees in chain-of-title documents.
- **Follow the family across the full coal region.** The unsurveyed anthracite counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland — each require their own locality survey. A family following work opportunities may appear in records from multiple counties across the region. For Lackawanna Valley research, note that Lackawanna County did not exist before 1878 — pre-1878 events there are under Luzerne County records.

---

## Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide (Late 1700s)

### Jurisdictional Context

Vermont was **not yet a state** in the late 1700s. The territory passed through two distinct phases:

1. **The New Hampshire Grants** — Both New Hampshire and New York claimed the region and issued competing land patents, creating a dual (and often conflicting) record system.

- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (online, subscription); Vermont Historical Society and University of Vermont hold original and microfilmed copies.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Vermont's pre-statehood population arrived primarily by overland migration from southern New England, not by overseas immigration. International passenger manifests are not a primary source for most Vermont families in this period.
- **Inland records:** Declarations of intention, naturalization petitions, and alien registrations were generated inland; however, for native-born colonists and early Americans of this period, naturalization proceedings are not typically expected.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for any federal records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town grand lists (property tax assessments) are the primary tax record for this period.
- **Date range:** Some town grand lists survive from 1778 onward, though survival is uneven by town.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and the Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Town grand lists can place a person in a specific town in a specific year, substituting for the absent pre-1790 federal census.

### Other record types
- **Town proprietors' records:** Towns were organized through proprietors' meetings, which recorded land divisions and early inhabitants. Held at town clerk offices or transcribed in town histories.
- **Town histories:** The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) explicitly identifies 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) as frequently reprinting colonial-era proprietors' records "that are otherwise difficult to access." These histories are a primary research resource for pre-statehood Vermont.
- **Vermont Republic legislative and court records:** The Vermont Republic's independent government (1777–1791) created court, land, and legislative records with no equivalent in colonial-era record sets. Held at VSARA.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census (Vermont); Vermont Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/); Revolutionary War pension files | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records — Revolutionary War service and pension files (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives — federal records (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free / in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch collections_search and volume_search were not executed in this survey run. No FamilySearch digitized collection count or digitization classification can be reported. Consult the FamilySearch Catalog directly at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog for Vermont to identify microfilmed and digitized holdings. The external_links_search tool returned 6 curated resources for Vermont (totalForPlace: 6), all generic repositories listed above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA) | Vermont Republic records, early state records, land records, court records, militia records | In-person / written request |
| Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT) | Town histories, manuscripts, genealogical collections, newspapers | In-person / some digitized items online |
| Town clerk offices (each Vermont town) | Town grand lists, early vital records (some from 1770s), proprietors' records | In-person / mail (each town separately) |
| New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management | Wentworth township grants (NH Grants period land records) | In-person / online finding aids |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | Competing New York land patents for the same Vermont territory | In-person / written request |
| NARA (Washington, DC / College Park, MD) | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, 1790 census | In-person / online via Fold3, Ancestry |

## Records NOT online
- Town clerk vital records from the 1770s–1791 (survival and digitization are both uneven; no specific digital repository confirmed by tool results for this period)
- Town grand lists / tax records from the Vermont Republic period (1777–1791)
- Town proprietors' meeting records
- Vermont Republic court and legislative records
- Early church registers (most remain with local congregations or denominational archives)
- New Hampshire Wentworth grant records (originals at NHDAM)
- New York competing land patents for the Vermont territory (originals at New York State Archives)
- Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (physical location not confirmed by tool results; the FamilySearch wiki names it but does not state where it is held or whether it is digitized)

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Vermont's pre-statehood period were identified in any tool result. The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page notes that earlier town clerk records survive "unevenly" — this implies gaps but does not confirm destruction of a specific record set. Researchers should contact individual town clerk offices and VSARA directly before concluding a specific record is lost rather than simply undigitized.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.** Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy), this is "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state," enumerating approximately 1,800 grantees. If an ancestor was a landowner in the New Hampshire Grants, begin here.
- **Consult town clerk offices individually.** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) notes that town clerk records survive "unevenly" from the 1770s — there is no statewide database. Each town must be contacted directly.
- **Town histories are essential for this period.** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) explicitly states that 19th-century town histories (1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access. For pre-statehood Vermont, these may contain the only surviving transcriptions of early records.
- **No civil registration until 1857.** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) places statewide civil registration at 1857 — nearly 70 years after the target period. Church registers, cemetery records, and family Bibles are the primary substitutes for birth, marriage, and death events in 1760–1791.
- **Research all three competing land-record systems.** An ancestor may appear in New Hampshire Wentworth grants, New York patents, or Vermont Republic grants — or in records from all three if title was contested. Search NHDAM, the New York State Archives, and VSARA, not just one of the three.
- **The 1790 federal census is the first national snapshot.** It is the earliest federal enumeration covering Vermont and names heads of household. It is accessible through Ancestry.com and FamilySearch and is the baseline census for this period.
- **The Vermont Republic (1777–1791) generated unique records.** Its courts, land office, and legislature produced records that do not appear in colonial or early-federal series from neighboring states. VSARA is the holding repository.
- **Adjoining jurisdiction research is essential.** Vermont borders New Hampshire (east), New York (west), Massachusetts (south), and Quebec, Canada (north). Families near any of these borders may have generated records on both sides. The FamilySearch wiki page returned no Neighboring Counties table for Vermont; consult the relevant county-level wiki pages for New York, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts border counties.
- **FamilySearch Wiki sub-pages for specific Vermont record types were not found.** The URLs for Vermont Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, and Census all resolved to a generic page. Use the Vermont State Archives (https://sos.vermont.gov/vsara/) and Vermont Historical Society as primary guides for record-type-specific holdings.

The guide explicitly states 'Vermont did not exist as a formal jurisdiction during most of this period' and explains the three competing authority streams (New Hampshire grants, New York patents, Vermont Republic records). It correctly notes that Vermont was admitted March 4, 1791, and that the 1790 federal census is the first federal enumeration covering Vermont. The guide accounts for boundary changes and the formation of Vermont's county structure beginning in 1778.
